We've developed a novel probability theory that outlines the average case behavior of two-layer neural networks by investigating their performance on random data sets. The theory specifically examines generalization errors in stochastic gradient descent, and we've discovered that for two-layer networks with weight matrices of uniformly distributed entries, the generalization error scales logarithmically with the dimensionality of the data set. Notably, this result surpasses previous theories' predictions. Furthermore, we've proven that our lower bound on the generalization error is essentially tight by deriving an upper bound with a similar logarithmic scale factor. Additionally, we've extended our theoretical framework to analyze the performance of two-layer neural networks with non-uniformly distributed weight matrices, and our findings reveal that for such networks, the generalization error scales linearly with the dimensionality of the data set. We've also used our theoretical framework to investigate the performance of two-layer neural networks in the regime of extremely large data set sizes, and our results indicate that for such scenarios, the generalization error either remains constant or scales logarithmically with the inverse of the data set size, depending on the architecture of the network. We've verified our theoretical findings by means of numerical simulations. By combining our study with prior research in the field, we've gained insights into the average case behavior of three-layer neural networks, and our results indicate that the generalization error scales linearly with the product of the data set size and the logarithm of the dimensionality of the data set for such networks. We've also obtained numerical evidence supporting our theoretical findings by means of an analysis of the loss landscape of three-layer neural networks. Our in-depth analysis of the largest cosmic ray dataset ever assembled reveals the existence of significant anisotropic patterns within extremely high-energy cosmic rays. The measured anisotropy patterns, obtained from the largest dataset of the Pierre Auger Collaboration, describe a changing cosmic ray arrival direction that varies with energy and the direction on the sky. The amplitude of this anisotropy significantly increases above an energy threshold of 4 EeV for the dominant Galactic magnetic field alignment, but remains relatively stable below this threshold. The measured anisotropy patterns are composed of two distinct anisotropies: one with small-scale arrangements and an arrival energy of approximately 8 EeV, and another with large-scale arrangements that operates across various energy ranges up to at least 40 EeV. The findings presented in this study contradict earlier anisotropy measurements that indicated no anisotropy above 8 EeV and show an isotropic arrival pattern for cosmic rays above this threshold. The anisotropy amplitude patterns derived from this study exhibit an energy dependence that follows a logarithmic law and displays a change in sign for specific arrival directions on the sky that are aligned with the center of the Galactic disc. The measured scales of the anisotropies, characterized by the clumpiness and arrangement patterns, remain stable across various energy ranges. The findings in this study are consistent with, but also offer more precise constraints on, earlier simulations that investigated the anisotropy patterns of cosmic rays using hadronic interactions for hadron-nucleus interactions, but reveal discrepancies with simulations that involved an energy-dependent fragmentation function. The anisotropy amplitude patterns derived from this study set an upper limit on hadron-nucleus interaction expectations in the energy range of 5-60 EeV, but also confirm that the selected simulation, which is known as Sim-SD, can accurately describe the measured anisotropy patterns across all energy ranges examined in this study. The findings presented in this study provide significant new constraints on the models of cosmic ray anisotropy and scale of the ultra-high energy cosmic rays. The anisotropy amplitude patterns derived from this study offer new avenues for investigating the properties of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays. The anisotropy patterns derived from this study offer new evidence that confirms the validity of Sim-SD, a simulated model of cosmic ray anisotropy, which is based on the models of ultra-high energy cosmic ray sources and propagation. Our solution to these challenges lies in an integrated digital platform that allows for the storage, digitization of tissue sections, generation of tumor infiltrating lymphocyte data, and comprehensive analysis of immune cell expressions across diverse cancer patient groups. Our approach has been proven effective through a comprehensive evaluation of immune cell expressions across 36 cancer types and their surrounding tissues, gathered from the CytoScape platform's comprehensive dataset of immune cell expressions. These findings have been freely shared with the scientific community via the BioFork platform. Furthermore, we have made available a set of analytical tools, including the LymphoAnalyzer, for detecting and quantifying tumor infiltrating lymphocytes, as a contribution to the broader research community. Our digital platform has been designed to be highly versatile and adaptable, enabling researchers to expand its capabilities by contributing their own data analysis methods and associated tissue information. Our ultimate aim is to establish a unified standard for digital tools and procedures across the cancer research community, thereby facilitating seamless sharing of results and general-purpose research applications. As such, we invite the research community to contribute their knowledge and expertise to our initiative. Moreover, researchers can replicate our work by visiting our dedicated website at https://lympho.cytoscape.org/. It shows that applying circularly polarized light can create unique quantum states and control the mechanical movement, ultimately leading to the creation of entangled states between photons and mechanical objects. It's also demonstrated that changing certain characteristics in the material can make the quantum system more resilient to external influences. We present a method for creating a robust and resilient quadrupedal gait in reinforcement learning that doesn't rely on reward functions. By training a policy that generates feasible gaits using reinforcement learning, we overcome the challenge of crafting a reward function that simultaneously enables efficient baselining and myopic optimization for quadrupedal robots. To achieve long-term goal alignment, we introduce a training approach that gradationally intensify optimization obstacles while introducing discrepancies between the model's observations and target trajectories. This method leads to the emergence of quadrupedal gaits through policy optimization alone, as demonstrated by our quadrupedal robot's successful navigation of a challenging terrain, synchro-recovery from disturbance, and precise landing from a series of mid-air motions. We exhibit good generalization to diverse and dynamic environments by simulating recovery scenarios with substantial deviations in sensor data and task parameters. This research showcases the potential of reinforcement learning for creating highly resilient quadrupedal robots capable of withstanding complex in-service environments. Additionally, we observe that models trained in this manner exhibit prolonged lifespan but can deteriorate with repair operations that restore normal performance at the expense of loss of resilience. We provide an insightful explanation for this observation through an analysis of local optima and gaits that exhibit distinct phases. This research presents an innovative approach to creating quadrupedal gaits in simulation that can be seamlessly transferred to real-world applications, marking an important milestone for developing quadrupedal robots that can operate independently in various environments. In addition to this, we introduce open-source software to implement the MCPC algorithm, providing a valuable resource that can be utilized by researchers and developers. The wind interacts with the surrounding gas in the disk, creating shock waves that produce the observed X-ray emission. This research utilizes the full simulation model of the Detector, incorporated in the ROOT framework, to assess its performance. I have developed an advanced program to evaluate the Detector's effectiveness in identifying narrow energy gaps within high energy electron pairs, achieved by systematically analyzing the energy differences in numerous electron pair configurations. This program employs a versatile root toolkit to create two-dimensional histograms of energy relationships, which are then used to calculate the probability of detecting such energy differences. We conducted an in-depth analysis of tononzintla 2's chemical composition by comparing its metal levels and elemental ratios to a large reference database of cluster spectra. Our findings indicate exceptional metal levels within the cluster, exceeding those in 47 Tucanae and Omega Centauri. Additionally, the spread of metal levels and elemental ratios in tononzintla 2 surpasses those in other high-metallicity clusters. The large metallicity dispersion and abundance variations in tononzintla 2 are likely the result of multiple inhomogeneous metal mixing events or alternative explanations such as internal dynamics or interactions with the host galaxy. Further research is needed to distinguish between these possibilities and to investigate the cluster's complex chemical composition. Based on the metal levels analysis, we estimate tononzintla 2's distance from the galactic plane to be around 2-3 kiloparsecs. The estimated rate of chemical composition spread variation over time in tononzintla 2 is surprisingly low, at less than 20 percent per generation. This is comparable to other globular clusters but contradicts the hypothesis suggesting heavier elements composition spread in the galactic plane due to longer exposure to star-forming events. Ultimately, tononzintla 2's unique chemical composition and its relatively small size make it an exceptional and likely ancient remnant from the early galaxy. Its unique characteristics position it as an ideal candidate to further explore alternative theories on early galaxy metal mixing compositions. Additionally, we report new elemental ratio findings for the elements manganese, yttrium, zirconium, and barium within the cluster. Our findings refine their previously measured abundance levels within the cluster and match or exceed the abundance levels of their respective solar neighborhood counterparts. This is particularly evident in the relatively low yttrium to iron ratio and the relatively high manganese to iron ratio within the cluster. The spread variation in the ratios of these elements to iron within the cluster is quite small, less than 0.15 dex. This small variation indicates a uniform metal mixing event and likely reflects a uniform metal mixing event and homogeneous early metal mixing within the cluster. Conversely, the larger spread variation in the ratios of other elements to iron within the cluster may indicate that these elements were introduced to the cluster at a later time via multiple inhomogeneous metal mixing events or alternative explanations such as internal dynamics or interactions with the host galaxy. We investigate the utility of this task by pre-training on real-world projects, comparing its effectiveness with established pre-training strategies and finding that it yields more beneficial downstream performance in code completion and bug detection. Additionally, we discuss how the proposed task captures essential aspects of the programming edit operation and suggest its integration as a standard method in the development of pre-trained coding models. The differing shapes of galaxies, governed by the law of uniform density, have led to a longstanding debate about how galactic discs and spheres form.  Discs are characterized by their thinness and relatively low surface brightness in the center, while spheres exhibit the opposite.  We propose two mechanisms, dampened and shaken, to account for the distinct formation processes of these galactic structures.  In the dampened process, massive stars form early in the galaxy's life, producing radiation and heat that cool into massive globular clusters, thereby suppressing the growth of the galaxy's disc.  Simultaneously, dark matter in these early clusters settles into tight, rotating halos that will eventually comprise the galaxy's sphere.  As the galaxy's disc finally forms, its outer regions are consumed by these halo clusters, leaving behind ring structures.  In the shaken process, spiral arms form in a galaxy's disc, but are destroyed by periodic galactic mergers, thereby repeating the cycle of disc destruction and reformation.  However, in contrast to the dampened process, these reformed discs retain their original features.  Consequently, galaxies with discs are abundant, while those with spheres are scarce.  On the other hand, the shaken process can account for the abundance of both galactic discs and spheres.  We present observations and simulations supporting these theories, including Hubble's views of M101 $\mu$ Cen, M82, and our own Milky Way, as well as simulations of these processes, to substantiate these claims.  Further research is needed to confirm these theories and explore the inherent complexities of these galactic structures.  Ultimately, our goal is to elucidate the intricate development of the vast, sparkling expanse of our own galaxy, the Milky Way.} \begin{theight}4.5cm} {\it Keywords:} galaxies; galactic structures; star formation; supermassive stars; galactic mergers; dark matter; globular clusters. \end{theight} }

This research demonstrates the effectiveness of using wide-field photometry observations from night-time sky to estimate the vertical distribution of aerosols without the need for absolute instrument calibration. A complex model based on grey radiative transfer is developed to analyze how observed photometry is affected by atmospheric conditions. By applying this model in wide-field photometry data collected over Montsec (Spain), we derived a vertical profile of aerosol optical depth with an accuracy of ~0.01 for the lowest 10 km of the atmosphere. This new technique enables the monitoring of aerosol vertical distribution over large areas with a monitoring network of wide-field photometers. This facilitates the identification of regions affected by large-scale desert dust or pollution transport. By integrating our aerosol optical depth measurements with satellite imagery, we demonstrated the capability to identify the shape and movement of aerosol plumes. Furthermore, we compared our aerosol optical depth results with collocated in situ measurements to validate the accuracy of our technique, which is used to map the aerosol spatial distribution and diurnal variations. This new method provides valuable information to improve the interpretation of satellite data, such as IR and laser backscatter, with potential applications in climate and pollution studies. Additionally, it provides vertically resolved information essential for understanding biogeophysical and biogeochemical processes related to vegetation, fires, biomass, and heat islands. This new wide-field photometry technique enables the simultaneous monitoring of atmospheric and geophysical variables, enhancing our understanding of the relationship between the atmosphere and the Earth's surface. In contrast, a triplet plus singlet sector requires a mass scale separation by at least one order of magnitude to achieve comparable Higgs boson mass predictions. In this paper, we examine the performance of mmWave multicasting by incorporating multiple antennas at both the basestation and receivers. To maximize system efficiency, we utilize a hierarchical transmission approach and optimize power allocation, phase shifts, and beamformers through an iterative minimax approach. This method guarantees optimal performance in the presence of interference and quantization errors. Our results demonstrate the system's resilience to changes in mmWave channel conditions and show significant improvements in system quality and coverage area with the addition of antennas at the receiver. Moreover, we find that more than double the system capacity can be achieved when using more than eight antennas at the receiver. Additionally, we validate the optimality of our approach through comparison with benchmark methods. Finally, we provide key design insights and suggestions for both practical and theoretical applications. A comprehensive simulation environment is included to facilitate further research in this domain. Contributions and related works are outlined in the section on discussion. Based on our findings, we recommend the use of hierarchical transmission as a robust approach to mmWave multicasting. This methodology can serve as a foundation for future research in this area and can be applied in various communication scenarios. For instance, it may be useful in emerging applications involving virtual reality and robotic communications. Furthermore, our analysis can be extended to other transmission strategies and performance metrics in future studies. Additionally, we have made the simulation code accessible on the GitHub repository listed at the end of this paper for the benefit of the research community. In computer vision, model compression via one-shot pruning has proven to be effective.
This research expands on this technique by integrating it into Federated Learning and Federated Distillation to accelerate convergence and reduce communication costs. We introduce Compressed Federated Distillation, a novel approach that combines model compression and Federated Distillation, thereby bypassing the need for data transmission and reinforcement of weak connections among models. Experimental results demonstrate that Compressed Federated Distillation yields superior performance compared to both Federated Distillation and Federated Averaging, and reduces communication requirements by 90% while increasing accuracy. Additionally, we find that Compressed Federated Distillation is resilient to issues of data imbalance and model heterogeneity. We publicly release our research framework at https://github.com/ashaykns/Compressed-Federated-Distillation.

We examine a two-dimensional herringbone lattice with hexagonal structures, featuring chiral properties rooted in their non-symmetric shapes, and show how specific perturbations can alter the lattice's characteristics. The system's dynamics are modeled using a Hamiltonian-based equation with random fluctuations represented by a white noise term, and the subsequent evolution of the system is governed by a stochastic flow that emerges from the application of the Strichaner flow. The findings highlight the emergence of a particular flow regime, characterized by a quasi-stationary equilibrium with distinct chiral properties, and demonstrate that the lattice's chirality can be quantified using the determinant of the transported hexagonal structure, resulting in a natural metric for categorizing the system's states according to their level of chirality. The analysis further reveals that the determinant serves as a effective biasing field to manipulate the system's chiral characteristics, and the derived metric offers a valuable approach for assessing the level of chirality in more complex systems, offering a promising tool for investigating chiral phenomena in two-dimensional lattice systems. The research is further expanded to consider the emergence of chiral condensates in more complex systems by increasing the dimension of the lattice. The derived results are validated through the analysis of numerical simulations, resulting in a thorough understanding of the system's dynamics under the influence of random fluctuations. The research contributes to the broader field of nonlinear dynamics, particularly in the study of chiral phenomena in lattice systems, and offers valuable insights for analogous studies in the field of condensed matter physics. The research is documented in a peer-reviewed article, and the associated code is publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/abhishek-jaiswal/stochastic-herringbone. Replay-based algorithms excel in risk-sensitive reinforcement learning, and our research expands upon this by exploring their performance in dynamic environments with episodic changes. We first establish a theoretical framework for understanding the effectiveness of replay in dynamic settings, and then devise new algorithms combining restarts with optimal control methods. Through analysis and experimentation, we demonstrate that restart-based algorithms can successfully navigate changing environments, and find that a particular algorithm, often considered the most effective in stationary environments, underperforms in dynamic scenarios. By tuning its hyperparameters, we identify an improved configuration that achieves better performance. Our empirical evaluation showcases the robustness of restart-based methods across diverse risk-sensitive reinforcement learning tasks in dynamic environments. By expanding upon prior work, where restart-based algorithms were found to be the first to solve problems in changing worlds, we verify that they remain superior in risk-sensitive tasks, even when augmented with new algorithms. We provide open-source implementations of our research to facilitate replication and future advancement in the field. Additionally, our analysis highlights the need for more sophisticated evaluation methods in dynamic environments, as current Spencer-style tests may not adequately capture the performance of learned policies. Thus, we propose an alternative dynamic sparsity test to assess the efficacy of restart-based algorithms in dynamic settings. The study examines how WPM affects sparsity and the regularity of the data, and its impact on the local convergence rate and the number of communication rounds required. The convergence rate of the WPM-based SGD algorithm under specific data assumptions is demonstrated to be O(1/k), and even attains the optimal value under more stringent conditions. The merits of the proposed aggregation technique are exemplified through experiments involving sparse vector recovery and the distributed training of neural networks on a node partitioned data set. Our innovative approach represents a polymer as a manageable structure by identifying its fundamental monomer components using sequential sub-polymers and a unique alignment technique. This versatile method can be applied to a wide range of systems, such as massive polymers with complex internal structures, tiny polymbers composed of a few residues, or even experimental observations of polymer behavior. Additionally, it enables the calculation of precise probabilities for each proposed monomer configuration on small polymers, allowing for a reliable evaluation of inaccurate but plausible scenarios in large polymers. Our method is further illustrated by determining the fundamental monomer configurations of a protein, a ribosomal RNA component, and an observed lung cancer-related protein modification. It demonstrates the ability to accurately infer a complex polymer's structure, even when only partial observational data is available, and can be used to validate existing structures. This approach provides a fundamental building block for inferring the internal structures of massive objects composed of smaller components, such as astronomical bodies, called steinwayas. Furthermore, it can be applied to various fields, such as biology, chemistry, computational theory, and astrophysics, to name a few. The behavior of surface roughness during a machining operation can be complex, largely due to the interconnected effects of cutting conditions, tool geometry, and material properties. The precise prediction of surface roughness from first principles is not feasible due to the intricate nature of the removal process that involves many parameters. However, various models are in use that simplify the complex interaction between cutters and workpiece materials to estimate surface roughness values. The main objective of this research was to assess the accuracy of four surface roughness prediction models for different workpiece materials and to investigate how their input parameters affect the quality of the prediction they produce. Four widely applied surface roughness prediction models were tested: Chen's model, Dvort-Schmidt model, Mogtader's model, and Zinger's model. A set of experimental data collected from machining operations in a laboratory were used as the basis for the comparison of these models. The effect of varying tool orientations, cutting conditions, and workpiece materials on the surface roughness values was also investigated. The results showed that the choice of tool orientation, cutting speed, and cutting depth had a weaker impact on the quality of prediction produced by the models, while the effect of tool geometry and workpiece materials was more significant. The comparison of the models revealed that the accuracy of surface roughness prediction produced by the models varied depending on the type of workpiece material used. The validity of the models was verified through the use of the mean absolute error (MAE) metric. Based on the results, Mogtader's model provided the best prediction for aluminum workpieces, while the Dvort-Schmidt model produced the most accurate prediction for titanium workpieces. The effect of varying tool orientations on the quality of prediction produced by the models was also investigated. The results showed that the choice of tool edge radius and tool land had a weaker impact on the quality of prediction produced by the models, while the effect of tool cutting edge angle was more significant. The results of this research can be used to inform researchers and engineers about the accuracy of surface roughness prediction produced by the models for different workpiece materials and to guide further investigations in this area. The results can also be employed by developers of simulation software to inform their choice of tool path generation strategies and to evaluate the feasibility of employing simulated cutters with specialized geometries in machining operations. The results can also be used by manufacturers to evaluate the effectiveness of employing different cutting tools in machining operations based on the quality of the prediction produced by the models. This note establishes the fact that the Ahlfors regular conformal dimension of a graph's distance metric is equal to its topological dimension. Furthermore, we have derived a new criterion for determining whether a graph's distance metric is Ahlfors regular. Our methods involve examining the behaviour of Borel measurable mappings between graph metric scales. Additionally, we have derived exceptions to known results in metric measure spaces. Our work is in part a response to questions and challenges posed by Airhart and S. Lang, as well as in part a continuation of our own research. Some of the conclusions in this note are sharp, requiring the particular choice of the Poincar\'e inequality exponent 'p'. Our research sheds new light on the conformal dimension of graphs, and may be generalised to certain topological spaces called uniform spaces.

A study on a modified galactic chemical evolution model reveals that pre-enrichment by asymptotic giant branch stars is insufficient to explain nitrogen's distribution in the Milky Way. The model assumes that nitrogen is primarily generated through hydrogen burning in the core and mixed into the star's envelope, resulting in a nitrogen-to-oxygen ratio ([N/O]) that increases more slowly than would be expected through simple core-mass interactions. However, even within the model's initial mass function parameters, we find that [N/O] ratios rise more quickly at lower metallicity levels than at higher levels, matching the findings of various [N/O] versus [O/H] relations observed in the Milky Way and a number of external galaxies. The discrepancy between our model predictions and observed [N/O] ratios in the Milky Way's disk begins to emerge at [O/H] > or equal to -1.15. When considering initial mass functions with mass limits, we find that [N/O] ratios are significantly lower and decrease more slowly than would be expected for a mass-free evolution scenario, in which all massive stars enrich the gas. However, even within the limited mass range of 20 solar masses, our model predicts that [N/O] ratios are only marginally lower and decrease more slowly than would be expected for a mass-free evolution scenario. Consequently, we propose that [N/O] ratios in the Milky Way's disk are primarily limited by the low mass range of the initial mass function. Furthermore, we find that [N/O] ratios in the Milky Way's bulge are higher than those at the disk's edge, in agreement with observations, indicating that the initial mass function's low mass range may also be responsible for the [N/O] versus [O/H] relations in the Milky Way's bulge. The presence of simpler stellar populations with [O/H] up to -0.80 in the Milky Way's bulge also suggests that supernovae from low and intermediate mass stars enriched the gas in the bulge. The absence of such simple stellar populations with [O/H] up to -1.0 in the SAURON team's [O/H] versus [N/O] map of the NGC 4565 bulge disc however, suggests that the Milky Way's disc and NGC 4565's bulge disc may have different chemical and stellar evolution patterns. This robust method can be adapted to various graph systems, where it can identify critical components for efficient problem-solving. In the near future, computational methods are anticipated to harness the potential of upcoming low-precision hardware technologies. This progression is driven by the efficiences of neural networks in such environments. High-precision computational frameworks, including deep learning systems, will eventually be based on predictable yet precision-limited hardware components, where the optimal distribution of between precision levels will be crucial. This paper introduces the Precice framework, an innovative tool for designing and managing precision in computational methods across diverse frameworks. The Precice framework is comprised of three key modules. Firstly, it's found through statistical analysis that significant decreases in precision for neural network parameters are feasible in the initial stages of training, providing a foundation for its second module - an algorithm that dynamically adjusts precision levels by analyzing data and adapting accordingly. The third module is an automated tool that identifies and optimizes the most effective precision configurations for each computation method. The Precice framework is extensively tested on various deep learning workloads and has yielded a 3x speedup on average when compared to the standard precision setting, achieving this improvement through a 50% reduction in average precision usage. This research focuses on estimating the pose of an object based on image features that are affected by random sensor errors. We propose a novel optimization approach that accounts for the full range of potential errors among image features. This technique involves incorporating a correlation matrix that maps pairs of features to their expected related error margins. We found that limiting the correlation matrix to the variance of individual features only provides insufficient error margins, leading to suboptimal results. By contrast, our studies demonstrate that including the full correlation matrix yields more accurate pose estimations, even when the number of features is relatively low. We further examined the relationship between the optimization problem's objectives and found that a lower correlation matrix determinant results in better pose estimation accuracy. This led us to employ a determinant minimization method, which significantly improved the efficiency of the optimization process. As a result, we were able to solve this problem in a manner that is both more accurate and faster. We verified the effectiveness of this technique through extensive simulation studies. When used for pose estimation from image features, our method achieved a significant improvement in accuracy, amounting to a 4-fold reduction in position error and a 2-fold reduction in orientation error compared to a standard method that does not account for the full range of errors. We also successfully applied this technique to a real-world problem of estimating the shape and position of a object based on its shadow in an image. By using our proposed method, we were able to determine the shape and position of the object with a high level of accuracy, specifically a square with a side length of 15 cm, and further verify that the chosen values for its position and shape are statistically reliable. We examine how the structure of the multi-temporal universe affects the behavior of dark matter at various scales, extending from the cosmic vastness to individual organisms and pathogens. Our research builds upon the findings of Arzoumanian et al. (2020), where a dual-time framework for dark matter is established. In this study, we delve deeper into how dark matter cross-sections are influenced by the universe's evolutionary stages. Our numerical analysis centers on evaluating indirect dark matter signatures using gamma-ray emissions from dwarf galaxies, but also expands to consider dark matter interactions with neutrons within neutron stars and, for the first time, with the stars' outer layers. Our results indicate that dark matter-neutron star interactions may generate thermal gradients within these celestial bodies, potentially influencing their cooling processes. As such, we recommend incorporating such phenomena in neutron star cooling models to refine existing constraints on dark matter parameters, especially for cross-sections associated with spin-dependent interactions. By broadening the scope of dark matter physics to encompass both cosmic and micro-cosmic scales, our research enhances our understanding of dark matter, thereby promoting more precise dark matter modeling and related observational analyses. In addition, we outline potential future research paths that combine dark matter physics with astrophysical knowledge, as exemplified by neutron star dark matter interactions and the multi-temporal universe framework. Such an approach can foster the development of innovative methods to investigate dark matter, as exemplified by the potential for future neutron star observations to constrain dark matter parameters with far greater precision. In this light, we suggest that the multi-temporal universe theory and associated dark matter astrophysics have substantial potential for future breakthroughs in both dark matter and nuclear astrophysics, as these fields are intricately connected, even in the universe's earliest stages. In particular, we explore how the universe's initial conditions influenced the formation of dark matter particles and relate this to the distinct properties of dark matter across different scales, as exemplified by the contrast between neutron stars, which are composed primarily of dark matter, and galaxies, for which dark matter constitutes only a fraction of the total mass. In conclusion, we emphasize that the multi-temporal universe theory offers an exceptional opportunity to investigate the intricate connections between dark matter, nuclear astrophysics, and the universe's evolutionary stages, as exemplified by the potential future research into dark matter-neutron star interactions. By leveraging such an innovative framework, we may be able to uncover novel, correlated signatures in the observations of dark matter, nuclear astrophysics, and the universe's early stages,

Researchers have released an updated analysis of same-sign W boson pair production, providing more precise data and additional detection criteria in a previous study. In this new investigation, the researchers utilized high-energy proton-proton collisions occurring at 13 TeV and collected a substantial dataset of 36.3 fb^-1, using the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Within the recorded data, two identical W bosons were detected in isolated leptonic decays, yielding a data-to-simulation count of 4.2 standard deviations above expected values. In line with predictions, the observed results did not exhibit any notable discrepancies in terms of kinematical characteristics of the W boson pair system. Additionally, the researchers analyzed potential anomalous triple-W boson couplings, but did not discover any deviations from standard model forecasts at a 95% confidence level in any examined scenario. The task of colorizing grayscale images through learning-based methods has received significant attention in computer vision research, and recent contributions have established baseline expectations for the field. This paper innovates upon prior work by introducing an unsupervised colorization method that leverages a hierarchical structure to unify multiple features and constraints. Prior approaches have either focused on a single image or paired images, restricting flexibility; our method surpasses existing techniques by incorporating new constraints such as multi-image colorization with hierarchical features, achieving superior results on public datasets, while also demonstrating improved efficiency through reduced required examples. We present an extensive evaluation of our approach, along with accompanying source code and dataset creations. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy and generalizability, and can effectively colorize images even when the provided examples significantly differ from the target image. This includes suitable applications in art style translation and image inpainting. Furthermore, our method achieves notable performance on colorizing individual images when provided with relevant example images, compared to pure supervised learning approaches. Through thorough ablation studies, we analyze the impact of different architectural components on the overall performance, and present insightful qualitative results that highlight the potential and limitations of our approach. In terms of computational efficiency, our method compares favorably to prior GAN-based approaches, making it suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments. In addition to these contributions, we present a new benchmark for colorizing individual images, along with relevant code and dataset creations. In order to facilitate reproducibility, our source code is publicly available at the repository address listed at the end of this paper. This includes the code for our method and baseline approaches, along with generated results, to enable exact replication of our findings. Moreover, our dataset creations for the individual image colorization task can be accessed through the listed repository address. Lastly, our technical report is available at the listed address for reference.

We analyze the properties of a specific primordial power spectrum, represented by $P(q)$, in cosmological models with non-flat backgrounds and fixed angular scale power spectrum amplitude $A_L=1$. Our study, based on the combined 2015 Planck data and uncalibrated WMAP data, reveals the significance of $q$-parameter in distinguishing between flat and non-flat cosmologies. Notably, employing the standard LCDM model results in a 2.6 sigma preference for non-flat geometries, in contrast to a 0.8 sigma preference within the flat $\Lambda$CDM framework. However, when considering a broader $wCDM$ model, our findings indicate a 1.1 sigma preference for non-flat geometries, in addition to a 0.8 sigma preference within the flat $wCDM$ model. Introducing more data from future surveys like Euclid and Hicksgate will be essential in resolving the nature of $r_s$ and ultimately addressing whether non-flat geometries are required in the cosmological context. \\

Specifically, studies of paired spins show that weak magnetic interactions arise between carriers on neighboring sites, and these interactions are indicated to be responsible for the formation of local magnetic moments in pure materials. The results are then related to experiments that have investigated the properties of local magnetic moments in pure materials, and the findings show that the local magnetic moments are consistent with predictions made in earlier studies. We investigate strong symmetries in quantum field theories, specifically within the context of two dimensional scalar field theories where a U(1) symmetry is present. The presence of explicit symmetry breaking terms, linear in the field, precludes the conservation of U(1), yet permit the development of a U(1) current operator. Nonetheless, conservative U(1) symmetries can be compromised by quadratic interactions that generate a anomaly. We focus on determining the minimum requirements for such an anomaly to arise within a given theory and to what extent it can be controlled by the theory's parameters. Using both Lagrangian and path integral approaches, we establish that the U(1) current is consistently unitary when the theory encompasses a conservative U(1) symmetry. We then develop an explicit method for determining the path integral generating function, which includes an explicit parameter controlling the symmetry breaking term. The resulting function facilitates the determination of correlation functions associated with the U(1) current. Utilizing these correlation functions, we study the spatial fluctuations of the U(1) current within an inhomogeneous cosmic string background. The resulting data indicate significant spatial fluctuations in the U(1) current, which could potentially impact cosmological magnetic fields. The presence of magnetic fluctuations is also explored in a geometric approach, which supports our path integral findings. Our research demonstrates that cosmic strings can generate significant magnetic-induced fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background, which could be verified through observational data. The primary contribution of our research lies in providing a precise mathematical framework that can control anomalies in symmetric field theories and offer valuable insights into the related technical methods. The research also extends the existing technical methods to better accommodate magnetic background-induced correlations, which could potentially impact cosmological magnetic fields, while providing a precise geometric analysis of these effects. Furthermore, our research develops a mathematical framework to precisely study the fluctuations of the U(1) current in the presence of a cosmic string background. When robots learn from experts, they can easily fall prey to biases present in the teaching data. Our approach introduces a novel hierarchical Bayesian model that enables a robot to effectively eliminate confounding factors influencing demonstration data and improve its teaching efficiency. This method considers the expert teacher as a fellow student, modeling their actions as informed by varying levels of task knowledge. By assuming that demonstrations are partially informative, but ultimately insufficient to guarantee optimal solutions, the robot relies on its internalized task structure to bridge gaps in the data and achieve better results. This research was conducted as part of the Association for Computing Machinery's Conference on Human Robot Interaction 2021, using a planning problem from the RoboSales domain with simulated confounding factors, resulting in significantly improved robot performance when working without biases compared to standard learning approaches. This finding has important implications for future research in robot learning from humans. This paper introduces a novel motion planning system combining deep reinforcement learning and level of detail (LOD) technology. The motion planning stage in this framework differs from traditional methods, as it relies on a policy model learned through deep reinforcement learning in contrast to the conventional optimization-based approach. The framework tackles the complexity of the simulation environment by employing an LOD technique, similar to level of detail in video games, but from a computational complexity perspective. This setup involves a simple, fixed model for the environment that remains unchanged regardless of the motion object's size, with complex geometric details only loaded when within a certain proximity threshold of the sensor range. The feature complexity is also adjusted by reducing the number of features for objects outside a certain threshold distance, with only essential features maintained for distant objects. The framework's efficiency in generating motion trajectories is evaluated through comparison with other optimization-based methods. The evaluation shows that this new approach can create realistic motion trajectories with reduced computation time. Furthermore, the framework's flexibility enables easy substitution of the level of detail setup to facilitate the evaluation of various complexity scenarios. The success of this framework in generating natural motion trajectories for a simulation environment with limited geometric details also indicates potential application in real-world scenarios with similar characteristics. The developed system is now accessible through the open-source project page at https://github.com/ChaserFSE/MDO_MPC. This study offers a precise measurement of a research paper's impact on its citers based on cross-platform analysis of preprints and traditional publications. Contrasting the rapid posting of preprints with standard publication timelines, our findings show that preprints significantly accelerate and boost the research article's own citation count. Additionally, our data indicates that authors of preprints are more likely to cite earlier, overlapping work compared to authors of traditionally published research. The advantages of preprints stem from their rapid dissemination: both the speed of publication and reach resonate strongly with researchers, ultimately influencing their behavior and promoting open science practices. Our investigation spans multiple years and diverse fields, offering insights into the evolving benefits of preprints within an ever-changing scientific landscape. By leveraging both machine reading and human annotation, our dataset comprises 47 million author-affiliation records, 1.3 million research articles, and 13 million citations. Our cross-platform analysis provides long-term perspectives on preprint usage, extending previous studies by multiple years and offering an unparalleled view of the rapidly growing preprint ecosystem. Our findings position preprints as an indispensable component of the open science movement, enhancing scientific collaboration and facilitating innovative research through rapid dissemination of ideas. By comprehensively examining preprints, we aim to illuminate their potential and illustrate the importance of measuring open access initiatives, ultimately informing data-driven open access policies. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/mdpi/complementarystudy/tree/main/preprints. The conversion to electronic laboratory documentation has made it possible to streamline the documentation process, but significant challenges remain, particularly in data management. This has led to the development of automated, rule-based data management systems. This paper examines the benefits of using such an automated system in clinical chemistry laboratories, evaluating its effectiveness in a multi-disciplinary setting. A comparative study between manual and automated data management was conducted over a six-month period in two laboratories, one specializing in clinical chemistry and the other with a diverse range of disciplines. The findings reveal that the automated system significantly reduced errors associated with data management, including both minor and major mistakes. Notably, this advantage extended to situations where new testing protocols were introduced. The implementation of an automated data management system was shown to be both efficient and flexible, unaffected by changes in laboratory procedures or staff. This technology is likely to benefit a wide range of laboratories, regardless of their size or scope. This innovative approach can be used to develop and implement standardized, automated data management processes, thereby minimizing errors and ensuring consistency in both small and large-scale clinical and chemical testing laboratories. This technology holds great potential for other fields, such as medicine and bioinformatics. By combining this technology with established standards in these areas, it may be possible to develop fully automated, IT-based decision support systems. This combination could ultimately lead to the creation of centralized, automated data management systems, capable of integrating multiple disciplines and supporting decision-making at both the individual and population levels. This vision is within reach, and the development of modern information technology, coupled with carefully designed automated data management processes, may one day revolutionize the field of bio-medical information technology. This dream is not just a possibility, but a necessary step towards creating a seamless, high-quality health care system, supported by efficient and innovative information technology. This goal is both important and achievable, and the key to its success lies in the careful design of both the computer technology and the biological models underpinning it. This chapter is a summary of the research conducted in this field over the past twenty years, and is intended to inspire further study in this area. This effort is ongoing, and the findings presented herein represent only a portion of the research completed to date. We uncover relationships between the completeness of Sidon sets on these curves and the properties of hyperbolas and ellipses in a geometric sense. Noticing that extreme eigenvalues from random Gaussian matrices conform to specific patterns led researchers to apply this knowledge to estimate the thresholds for various statistical physics models and computer science problems, like constraint satisfaction problems and binary graph models. We expand upon this research by developing a new approach for identifying threshold functions based on sampling methods. By applying the principle of maximum entropy, we determine a non-uniform probability distribution for binary matrix entries, resulting in an significant improvement in the accuracy of threshold estimates compared to standard uniform sampling methods. Furthermore, this new approach is adaptable to various matrix structures, like sparse matrices, and can be applied to find threshold functions for probabilistic graphical models, demonstrating its potential usefulness in studying statistical physics models and computer science problems. We illustrate the methodology's effectiveness by calculating the thresholds for the following models: the satisfiable instances of the 3-SAT problem, the planted-satisfiability of random 3-SAT, and the sparse random 4-SAT. We also analyze the properties of the non-uniform probability distribution and its relationship to the matrices' extreme eigenvalues. By applying this new approach, we obtain threshold estimates that closely resemble those derived from analyzing the matrix's extreme eigenvalues, resulting in precise predictions for some of these models' threshold functions. We verify these predictions through extensive numerical simulations. Moreover, this approach allows us to obtain probabilistic bounds on the threshold functions, providing a new type of phase transition pattern, known as "fuzzy," in the boolean xOR function on sparse random graphs. We discuss the methodology's potential generalization to other probability distributions and explore its connections to variational methods and mean-field theories in statistical physics. We also analyze the approach's complexity, including the computational requirements for each simulation. We conclude by reviewing the methodology's potential applications, including its uses in predicting phase transitions, testing conjectures, and designing algorithms, and discuss potential areas for further research. We collect the necessary mathematical tools used in this approach in an appendix. We also provide an independent explanation of how the non-uniform probability distribution can be determined, along with numerical simulations used to verify its effectiveness. We demonstrate that the symmetric group $S_\infty$ and its enlargements, such as $S_\infty$ acting on the countable set of integers, possess a characteristic subgroup $S_\infty^1$ exhibiting specific random properties. This subgroup, known as $S_\infty^1$, consists of countable sequences of elements from $S_\infty$, has the ability to be generated by a collection of elements $\{\sigma_i\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$ where each $\sigma_i$ acts on the $i-th$ coordinate as a non-trivial element of $S_{\pm 1}(i)$, a subgroup of $S_\infty$ consisting of elements that differ from the identity only in the $i-th$ coordinate and possibly in adjacent coordinates, and is faithful with almost everywhere preservation of its action on any probability measure preserving action. Additionally, $S_\infty^1$ possesses a collection of specific generators $\{\tau_i\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$, which exhibit a linear pattern, establishing a new model for a linearly independent permutation group with a specific structure. Similarly, we apply the same approach to establish a characteristic subgroup $S_\infty^2$ with additional random properties, such as weak mixing and faithfulness, by introducing a new collection of specific generators $\{\tau_i^2\}_{i\in\mathbb Z}$, which exhibit a quadratic relationship, providing a new model for a quadraticly independent permutation group with a specific structure. Furthermore, we show that $S_\infty^1$ and $S_\infty^2$ are minimal in their respective categories. Lastly, we formulate two open questions regarding the development of a randomized subgroup with even more random characteristics.

This newfound understanding is not only consistent with the holographic duality but also unlocks a crucial connection between the change in boundary entropies and the geometric properties of the boundary, unlocking a valuable tool for developing precise predictions of boundary entropies through classical geometric characterizations. This geometric property, referred to as the cross-sectional entropy density, is the key factor that determines the allowed range of boundary entropies, providing a valuable insight that will contribute to the development of precise predictions of boundary entropies, thereby providing a clearer understanding of holographic constraints on bulk entropies. Furthermore, this concept is not limited to entanglement entropies alone but can also be extended to holographic quantities, such as bulk energy, providing valuable insights that will aid in the development of precise predictions of these properties as well. An interesting extension of this concept is the dual geometric property, referred to as the root-mean-square entropy density, that arises from cross-sectional entropy densities. A notable finding is that the difference between cross-sectional entropy density and root-mean-square entropy density serves as a precise indicator of higher-order corrections to the entanglement entropy theorem. A general method is developed to compute the local state probabilities of solvable lattice models based on the branching rule from representation theory. The method is demonstrated through specific examples including the XXZ spin chain, the fermionic XX spin chain, and the fermonic Razumov-Shhamanov model. The derived local state probabilities are analyzed using conformal field theory to confirm their scaling properties at criticality. Furthermore, the low-lying excitations of the XXZ spin chain are computed using this method in combination with the fusion rules of conformal field theory. The findings agree with prior studies on the fusion hierarchy and the correlation function of the XXX spin chain. The newly computed excitations of the XXZ spin chain reveal a hierarchical structure of the low-lying excitations with a previously unknown level. The overlap between adjacent levels contains physical excitations characterized by a half-integer spectral index. These spectral indices were used to compute the asymptotic probability density function of the local state probabilities, which exhibits a symmetric, bell-shaped profile regardless of the type of solvable lattice model. The observed density function is found to approach a Gaussian distribution in the scaling limit. The methodology established here can be applied to compute local state probabilities for increasingly complex solvable lattice models as well as the low-lying excitations of these models. Additionally, the method has potential applications in the broader fields of representation theory and conformal field theory. The associated computer code is available in the public domain at https://github.com/jaeschner/local_state_prob. A copy of the local_state_prob MATLAB package is included in the back matter of this thesis. Additionally, the underlying Python code that was used to generate the figures and tables presented in this thesis can be found at https://github.com/jaeschner/thesis_code. Both repositories are maintained at https://github.com/jaeschner.

The study further evaluates the numerical outcomes of various signal recovery algorithms, focusing on specific applications like compressive sensing, sparse logistic regression, and sparse regression with quadratic penalties. We've developed an innovative approach to a non-linear co-addition technique, 
which precisely maintains a consistent point spread function (PSF) across the 
image and is capable of effectively handling data from diverse instruments 
and various photometric bandages. Current methods, such as median and clipped-mean, 
fail to achieve this consistency. Our new algorithm, 'Wilmlow', uses a robust 
section-wise calculation process to combine multiple images. It accommodates 
images with differing data types and noise levels, while being able to handle 
images taken at the same time as well as those taken at different times. 
We compare the performance of Wilmlow with a widely used linear algorithm, 
'Weighted Mean', and demonstrate through realistic simulations that it delivers 
similar or better results in terms of signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) and retains 
a consistent PSF. Furthermore, Wilmlow exhibits significant time savings, 
mainly due to its ability to handle images independently without needing 
intermediate temporary images. This novel algorithm is now available under 
the BSD 3-clause license at https://github.com/astromax/wilmlow. We welcome 
any feedback or contribution towards further development to make it a 
versatile and reliable tool for astronomers.

We establish that chordal Schramm–Loewner evolution (CSLE) corresponds to the advancement of a family of imaginary surfaces within the 3D hyperbolic space under the influence of a real field that represents time. This results in an extension of the established relationship between SLE and the Yang–Mills equation, to the more complex chordal version. This finding is also accompanied by a discovery regarding the connection between the volume of a CSLE domain at a particular time and the integral of the imaginary field within that time frame. This relationship is akin to that observed between a typical SLE domain and the integral of its driving function. Furthermore, it has been discovered that the convergence of an evolving domain towards a boundary point occurs at a specific power law, with the rate of convergence dictated by a smaller power of the distance to that point compared to the one governing the point's interior points. This new discovery is, however, contingent upon the point in question lying outside a specific 'exclusion zone', defined earlier for SLE in relation to its key excursions. The theory developed here is not limited to CSLE but can also be applied to more general versions of evolution, thereby offering additional insights into their properties and behaviors. Additionally, a discovery was made linking the field that drives a CSLE to a solution of the Loewner equation with a specific characteristic of uniqueness, thus establishing that its domain remains fixed over time. This solution, in turn, is linked to a family of conformal mappings, used to define a particular type of curve, known as the Stoll curve, under the influence of the driving field in question. The theory developed here finds applications in various fields, such as the study of random fractals, functional equations and systems, as evidenced by previously established connections between SLE and these areas. The existing research in these fields is not only used to support the presented results, but some of the obtained findings are also stated to be strong enough to replace some of the existing theories and results in these fields, therefore they are also considered to be useful for their potential application in future research. The presented results are also independent and can be applied to various driving fields and thus are expected to be generalizable to other fields that share similarities with the driving field in question. This paper focuses on obtaining an optimal Lr maximum norm bound for the Navier-Stokes equations, with $ 2 < r < \infty$, for a short time period in a bounded domain. It addresses concerns raised by the absence of a final maximum norm bound established for the Navier-Stokes equations by Wu and Yuan (2011), specifically in a bounded domain. By utilizing an optimal Lr maximum norm criterion for the heat equations in the half-space established by Zhang (2019), we derive the desired short time maximum norm bound, and consequently, the long time maximum norm bound by combining it with a logarithmic inequality. Furthermore, we obtain an Lr maximum norm bound for the spatial derivatives of the Navier-Stokes equations, and demonstrate that the maximum norm of the solution's derivatives decay at a faster rate than the initial data. Additionally, we obtain an Lr maximum norm bound for the time derivatives of the Navier-Stokes equations, and establish the optimal decay rate of the maximum norm of the time derivatives. By employing a similar approach, we also obtain an Lr maximum norm bound for the time derivatives of the viscous heat-conduction equation. Furthermore, we extend our results to the Stokes equations with variable viscosity. Utilizing our established results, we obtain an Lr maximum norm bound for the Navier-Stokes equations in a bounded domain for any $ 2 < r < \infty$, which improves and extends the results of Wu and Yuan (2011), and also fills the gap in Chen and Zhang (2016). To the best of our knowledge, the present paper provides the first Lr maximum norm bound for the spatial derivatives of the Navier-Stokes equations for any $ 2 < r < \infty$, which complements the results of Wu and Yuan (2011). Lastly, we obtain an Lr maximum norm bound for the Navier-Stokes equations in a bounded domain for any $ 2 < r < \infty$ under the assumption of Sobolev embedding, which improves and extends the results of K. Abe (2017). The study introduces an alternative method to derive the maximum norm of the solution in a bounded domain, which can be applied to derive the maximum norm of the solution in a bounded domain with non-constant boundary conditions. Furthermore, the study derives the maximum norm of the solution to the Navier-Stokes equations in a bounded domain with constant boundary conditions for any $ 2 < r < \infty$. Implementing quantum algorithms on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices remains challenging. We introduce an approach to run a quantum circuit on multiple devices and guarantee the correctness of its output through verification. Our verification process involves checking if the output of the circuit, run multiple times, matches the expected result. If the outputs from the different runs consistently match each other, but do not agree with the incorrect value, we can be sure that the correct output has been obtained. We tested this approach using the Berthier et al.'s estimate-angle estimate (EA) protocol, but encountered issues in getting it to work due to noise on the devices. An alternative protocol was developed, but it required significant modifications and resource increases. We discovered however that the angle-based phase estimation in quantum circuit learning protocols can be used as an alternative and reliable solution to verify the circuit. We successfully tested this approach on noise-resistant devices, achieving an accuracy of 99.96% across seven devices and contrasted it with existing protocols, finding that our method provides faster verification, especially when dealing with a large number of circuits that need to be executed. The CVQC protocol and associated tools are available on GitHub at https://github.com/QIHLQ/CVQC, free for public use.

Recurring concepts in reinforcement learning tasks, like geometric shapes, have been discovered by agents applying similar policies across different episodes, leading to the exploration of multi-episode persistence in learning. We investigate how agents leverage persistent features, like shape contours, to perform tasks such as navigation and target detection. A recent finding suggests that persistent features significantly impact an agent's performance, and we verify this effect in various challenging, geometric tasks. We introduce a new method to identify and utilize persistent features, which leads to near-optimal performance, and find that this approach is more efficient than traditional reinforcement learning. Interestingly, our results indicate that persistent features are beneficial only when the task requires an agent's interaction with the environment, and we verify this effect in navigation and target detection tasks. To study the effect of persistent features, we created a new suite of persistent tasks, consisting of three challenging scenarios, such as circulation around a closed shape, pressing a button in a hole or a depression, and finding a small object in a complex environment. Our research shows that persistent features, like shape contours, can be discovered by agents and utilized to excel in various geometric tasks, and we developed a new, more efficient strategy, called persistence exploration, to tap into their potential. Furthermore, our results indicate that existing reinforcement learning techniques can be enhanced by incorporating a module that tracks persistent features. We introduce a Newtonian version of the Eccentrically Ordered Cluster Multipole Calculation (ECMC) algorithm for rapidly simulating long-range interactions in three-dimensional systems, specifically to address dynamic freezing in dipolar models. Unlike previous implementations, our variant maintains high accuracy by incorporating the effects of eccentricities in a systematic manner. Building upon a recent breakthrough, our simulations successfully eliminate the dynamic arrest in three-dimensional dipolar models across a broad range of polarities. Moreover, the method can be applied to various Newtonian dipolar models with minimal modifications. Furthermore, a crucial parameter in the algorithm has been identified, affecting accuracy, and efforts are made to minimize its impact. Several strategies are explored to refine the calculation and minimize variability. The results obtained using ECMC match those from direct summation with high precision. Lastly, a theoretical foundation for the algorithm is laid by analyzing the effects of clustering on the dipolar interaction for various system configurations. By leveraging this understanding, the relationship between accuracy and clustering parameters can be established, thus enabling a more efficient search for optimal parameters. All the above advancements are made available in an open-source code, known as Newtonian ECMC, for the community to use and extend. Furthermore, a comprehensive guide is provided to facilitate the adaptation of our algorithm to other Newtonian dipolar models, with a view to their application in simulation tools. Additionally, a detailed tutorial is included to help new users set up and run successful simulations using Newtonian ECMC. Data augmentation has gained significant attention in recent years as an efficient method to enhance the performance of neural network-based sound event detection systems. In this research, we introduce an innovative framework called Data Augmentation by Magnetic Rotation (DAMR) that utilizes magnetic rotation to successfully accommodate broad applications of augmentation techniques. By applying a magnetic rotation operation, the DAMR method seamlessly integrates various data augmentation techniques including time-stretch, shift, and mixing methods, thereby yielding excellent results for sound event detection tasks. Our experiments conducted on the DCASE 2021 benchmark demonstrate that DAMR significantly outperforms a non-augmented baseline system; furthermore, interesting findings related to magnetic rotation parameters and data augmentation degrees are discussed. Additionally, the effectiveness of DAMR is evaluated on two distinct datasets, showing superior performance compared to time-stretch and mixing methods. Our open-source implementation of the proposed approach is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/tzengchun/DAMR.

The detection and estimation of signals within an unknown environment are critical problems, often addressed by considering the spectrogram based on a continuous time signal, with its entries being randomly distributed according to a complex law. By utilizing a level-set approach, we develop a detection and estimation technique for signals within an unknown environment, with associated spectral analysis. This level-set methodology leads to the development of an efficient numerical method, comprised of an optimization problem and a spectral analysis technique, effectively tackling the difficulties posed by non-differentiable data and unknown signal structure. This approach has been successful in various signal processing domains, such as radar, ultrasonic imaging, image denoising, and audio analysis. Moreover, we establish a conditional asymptotic analysis to evaluate the level-set technique's performance, with corresponding results confirmed through extensive numerical experiments. Ultimately, this level-set method yields significant improvements in performance, particularly in the domains of radar signal detection and image denoising. This research is an expanded version of previous work presented at the 2019 International Conference on Signal Processing, Imaging and Infrared Spectroscopy. This study investigates the jamming transition in a confined environment using dense packs of disks with varying weights, placed within a narrow channel. A weight gradient is maintained to ensure that lighter disks can easily escape and heavier ones remain jammed at the point of highest tension. Observations indicate that jamming occurs not only through the collapse of individual disks but also through the simultaneous jamming of pairs, particularly when disk weights have a significant variation. In channels that are not extremely narrow, the jamming transition caused by pair interactions is evident, whereas in very tight channels, the primary cause of jamming is the collapse of individual disks. Specifically, when channel heights are around 5 times thicker than disk diameters, the jamming transition is predominantly driven by pair interactions, whereas in very tight channels, it is mainly caused by individual disk collapses. Conversely, when disk weights are relatively similar, the jamming transition in confined environments is primarily caused by the collapse of individual disks. Furthermore, the jamming transition in this scenario is found to be insensitive to channel dimensions and disk shapes. In particular, when channels are around 5 times thicker than disk diameters, the transition point is around 0.73 times the channel thickness. On the other hand, when disk weights are relatively similar, the transition point is significantly lower at approximately 0.45 times the channel thickness. In very tight channels, the transition point can be as low as 0.1 times the channel thickness, mainly caused by individual disk collapses. Our research investigates how heavy black holes are created within the framework of the fuzzy spin-down theory. We discover that the mass spectra of black holes formed through the motion of massive particles across event horizons differ significantly when the particles either collide with existing black holes or get swallowed whole, resulting in a lower number of light black holes and a higher number of heavy black holes in the former scenario. In contrast, the mass spectra of black holes formed through the light seeding pathway exhibit a broader and more complex distribution, affecting the overall mass function and causing it to deviate from standard predictions at higher mass points. We propose the development of tailored mass function analysis methods for distinct heavy black hole formation mechanisms and demonstrate the feasibility of applying such an analysis to the masses of observed black holes using the motion of massive particles across event horizons, resulting in a more nuanced understanding of the process. We discover that a more nuanced application of our analysis to the masses of observed black holes in groups of up to 10 objects reveals an overall consistency with the predictions of the fuzzy spin-down theory, including a notable lack of light black holes and a significant negative slope at high mass points, consistent with the standard mass function analysis. Additionally, we apply our analysis to the masses of observed black holes from the central region of clusters and find evidence for a distinct heavy black hole formation mechanism, resulting in a higher number of light black holes and a lower number of heavy black holes in this scenario, caused by the influx of less massive particles from the surrounding gas. We speculate that the differing constraints imposed by the environment on the motion of massive particles across event horizons may be the primary factor distinguishing the properties of the mass spectra of heavy black holes formed through the motion of massive particles across event horizons and those of less massive particles. We also explore the potential for further research to investigate the role of the cosmic web in shaping the distribution of black hole masses and the inherent diversity of heavy black hole formation mechanisms at the heart of cosmology. In this further research, we outline an exciting array of theoretical and observational questions that could be tackled in the future to further our understanding of the subject. Comprehensive fiscal support for this further research would be necessary to fully exploit the forthcoming datasets, ultimately enabling us to pinpoint the precise theoretical black hole formation mechanisms responsible for creating the diverse range of massive black holes at the heart of cosmology. In turn, this in-depth understanding will enable us to constrain the underlying cosmology more precisely than is currently possible, while also uncovering new and significant facts about the development of massive black holes

Historically, models predicting click-through rates in online advertising have relied on linear combinations of features. This approach uses data from multiple sensors to estimate the parameters of an aerosol-filled atmosphere, relying on the fundamental principles of light propagation and radiation to guide the model. By incorporating knowledge of the aerosols' effects and the structure of the atmosphere, this method improves the accuracy of wavelength-dependent optical distortion predictions, especially in situations where the distortion is small. We evaluate the benefits of this more sophisticated model by comparing its ability to predict optical distortion from wildfires in 2020, using either ground-based sensor data or satellite sensor data, to a simpler model that relies solely on sensor data. By incorporating the effects of light absorption and scattering by aerosols, this method offers a more comprehensive understanding of the aerosols' impact, and could eventually be used to monitor the impact of persistent wildfires on the atmosphere and aerosols. This study examines the impact of inter-site variability on functional network connectivity by comparing two simultaneous EEG recordings from the same subjects. We analyzed the collected data from the NFP100 dataset, focusing on individual and group differences. Our investigation revealed that inter-site effects can influence the accuracy of detecting these differences, particularly in frequency-specific network patterns. We addressed this issue by incorporating an intermediate step in our analysis, aiming to stabilize the inter-site variability and refine our findings. This approach involved applying the StableEEG package to reduce inter-site fluctuations and improve the reliability of our conclusions. We compared two methods of network construction, derived from raw EEG signals and corrected EEG signals, to assess their respective performances. Our results showed that the correction method successfully enhanced the accuracy of functional network connectivity, leading to more precise individual and group differentiation in the current study. We hope this research promotes the development of more reliable EEG-based network construction methods. Additionally, we have made available on GitHub a script integrating StableEEG, used for frequency-specific functional network connectivity analysis. This resource can be utilized for exploratory data mining purposes.
