Individual actions taken to address climate change are influenced by how they align with personal values, which are reflected in behaviors and goals. Climate change awareness, although widespread, does not always prompt people to make personal adjustments to reduce their carbon footprint. A potential remedy involves leveraging video games to measure and modify players' climate-related personal values, thus encouraging more meaningful actions. Our research introduces a values measurement framework incorporating a network model to accurately assess and identify various personal values from a cluttered network of relevant terms. A video game prototype was developed to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, consisting of in-game surveys to gather users' opinions on several climate-related topics. Initial results from 166 player responses indicate that our framework effectively distinguishes between different personal values, which are diverse and varied among users. Most importantly, players' values were found to impact their willingness to take climate action, as measured by a demonstrated change in behavior. The success of our framework suggests potential applications beyond game-based settings, as well as in combination with other methods to foster more effective climate change behavior change. A possible future direction involves using machine learning for automatic value assessment, potentially incorporating voice data to expand this capability. To identify symptoms in medical images and enhance the robustness of systems across various healthcare applications and domains, we develop a new technique. This method leverages recent advances in domain generalization and attention fusion technologies. It involves training a single model to extract multiple image transformations, similar to how doctors perceive and combine visual cues to diagnose patients. By doing so, this approach yields superior performance in extracting key symptoms and identifying disease categories compared to existing methods, as evidenced by our experiments using multiple domain-specific datasets. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that our technique outperforms a baseline model by successfully generalizing to new domains with an overall accuracy boost of nearly 13% in identifying disease categories and around 8.5% in key symptom extraction. We intend to share our domain generalization approach and supporting code openly to foster further research in this area. ANNs have significant energy requirements during training and testing, which poses problems in applications with hardware constraints. To address this issue, a new general-purpose classifier based on a binary neural network is presented, which demonstrates competitive performance while consuming much less energy due to its simplified architecture. The proposed binary neural network uses the ridge regression model and a specific loss function to minimize errors during binary training. Consequently, it achieves high accuracy in classifying logarithmically spaced numbers and performs well in various classification tasks. Notably, the proposed binary neural network requires roughly 50-100 times fewer parameters than a traditional neural network and has a reduced computational complexity during inference. Additionally, the proposed binary neural network offers the advantage of being easily interpretable due to its low number of parameters. The advantages of the proposed binary neural network will likely initiate a new wave of applications on energy-constrained hardware such as smart cards, BIOS, and low-power embedded MCUs. The proposed binary neural network will likely be used in future learning systems that run on such energy-constrained hardware, which will further reduce energy consumption and improve efficiency. The performance of the proposed binary neural network is evaluated on datasets from open ML libraries, which demonstrates its effectiveness in real-world applications. The proposed binary neural network offers a new direction in ANN design, which will likely be used in future learning systems that run on energy-constrained hardware. In this research, we've investigated the behavior of a strange quark matter under extremely strong magnetic fields, taking into account how the state equation changes in response to confining electrons and muons within it. Our findings show that as a magnetic field grows, the strange quark matter's state equation becomes more rigid, exhibiting a stronger dependence on temperature when spin is considered. This effect is caused by the dimensional reduction that occurs, as well as Landau levels populated by the quarks and electrons, which lead to an increase in the matter's bulk entropy. Furthermore, our model includes how magnetic field-induced phenomena like Fermi surface effects, Landau damping, and magnetization contribute to a more complex quark matter state equation. Our results also reveal that muons play a crucial role in determining the matter's state equation at higher temperatures, whereas electrons predominantly affect it at lower temperatures. As the temperature and density of the matter change, we observe a transition from a non-interacting to a strongly coupled quark matter state, accompanied by a significant reduction in the matter's bulk entropy. Utilizing the measured densities of neutron stars, we have calculated the adiabatic index of the matter and found that it satisfies the delta condition, indicating that the matter is inherently unstable against the causality limit. This research may be expanded to investigate other phenomena in the context of a more general relativistic model. Our study has far-reaching implications, and we speculate that the phase transition of the matter could be responsible for generating r-modes in the context of the Russell-Vogt instability. This research may also be applicable to other systems consisting of strongly interacting particles subjected to intense magnetic fields, such as those found in ultra-dense baryonic or quasi-stable configurations. Lastly, the constraints imposed by the quark-hadron transition on the parameters of the free energy density and parton transport coefficients are discussed. This research has the potential to open up new avenues in the field, and accordingly, a comprehensive list of the used transport coefficients is presented in the tables for the sake of completeness. This research introduces an adaptive sampling technique that accelerates the computation of eigenvalues using a rapid transform method, resulting in efficient eigenvalue approximations with reduced required samples. By leveraging the properties of the Fourier transform, this adaptive method identifies the minimum number of samples needed to accurately calculate eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors. A related algorithm is also developed for approximating the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the shifted Laplace operator, where the number of required samples is proportional to the logarithm of the desired precision. Moreover, this adaptive method enables rapid computation of the minimum number of samples needed to achieve a specific precision, making it scalable for large sparse systems of linear equations. Numerical examples demonstrate the efficiency of this approach, showing speed-ups of several minutes in comparison to the standard inverse iteration method for solving the shifted Laplace operator on a 3D cube, as well as significant improvements in both time and sample complexity for the general sparse problem. Furthermore, this method provides efficient solutions to the approximate eigenvalue problem with optimal sample sizes, resulting in precise eigenvectors with minimal additional cost. Such efficient solutions prove crucial for applications where the eigenvectors are also of significance, as observed in recent studies utilizing the approximate eigenvalue method to solve positive semidefinite nonconvex programs and minimizing the least restrictive Lyapunov function for continuous-time robust control problems. Thus, this adaptive method offers a more practical alternative to the standard inverse iteration technique, providing better efficiency through a precise sample size determination. This research further opens the door for the adaptive method to be utilized in various sparse linear systems, enabling the computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors with minimal samples, which could potentially result in new theoretical advancements and applications. Based on the specific problem considered, the proposed algorithm demonstrates optimal sample sizes that achieve the desired precision, indicating potential superiority in the approximate eigenvalue method for sparse matrices. As sparse matrices have limited degrees of freedom, this result implies the adaptive method could nearly achieve the optimal precision with the approximate eigenvalue method for sparsity levels close to the threshold, providing a promising lead for future investigations in this domain. Furthermore, this study explores the possibility of adapting the rapid transform method for approximate polynomial eigenvalue problems, which could have practical applications in inverse iteration-type algorithms as shown in the paper, highlighting the promise of combining such methods with the existing algorithms to efficiently compute the desired solutions. Consequently, this research opens the door for the utilization of the approximate polynomial eigenvalue method for sparse problems, which could result in new theoretical and practical outcomes. It's also demonstrated how these sets relate to one another, particularly in terms of their inclusion. Furthermore, we identify the survivor sets corresponding to beta-transformations with irrational powers of 2, and show they comprise a countable collection. Also explored is the survival set for the classic Chacon transformation, along with its topological encoding. Similar analysis is conducted for a class of beta-transformations with certain periodic properties. Additionally, we investigate the survivor sets for certain 'edge' cases of beta-transformations with irrational components equal to 1/2. Lastly, we examine the survivor sets for a system of transformations in five or more dimensions, where the components are equally spaced irrational numbers. In many of these cases, the resulting survivor sets display intriguing self-similar patterns. It's also demonstrated that some of these sets are countable while others are uncountable. We analyze flavor symmetry breaking in $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories, containing fundamental quarks and an appropriate set of flavorless symmetry-breaking operators. To achieve this, we introduce an effective theory, reducing the $SO(N_{c})$ to $U(N_{c})$, and examine the effective theory's one-loop lagrangian with $N_{F}$ fundamental quarks. Our findings demonstrate that, in addition to the expected symmetry breaking of $SU(N_{F})$, the effective theory also displays a non-zero $\sigma$ term, resulting from the presence of flavor-breaking operators. Furthermore, we derive the effective potential of the $N_{c}$-component Higgs field $\sigma$ and a $N_{F}$-component Higgs field $\tilde{\xi}$, incorporating flavor-breaking operators. The flavor-breaking operators, defined as $c_{i}F^{2}$ and $d_{i}F\tilde{F}$ with $i=1,...,N_{F}$, explicitly break the $U(1)$ Peccei-Quinn symmetry in the theory. Additionally, we analyze the sum rules of two-point correlation functions to determine the flavor-breaking condensates and explore the properties of Borel masses in the theory. Our findings demonstrate that, in contrast to $SP(N_{c})$ and $O(N_{c})$ gauge theories, the effective eigenvalues $\lambda_{i}$ in $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories can take negative values. Moreover, we show that, in the presence of flavor-breaking operators, the flavor symmetry is broken at one-loop. Our research further extends to the relativistic quark-gluon plasma produced in $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories, containing fundamental quarks and an appropriate set of flavorless symmetry-breaking operators. Our findings indicate that, in the relativistic quark-gluon plasma, the flavor symmetry is broken at one-loop, resulting in a non-zero $\sigma$ term. Driving innovation in the field of robotics and related research, the integration of programming languages has played a crucial role. To ensure the reliability of software developed with these languages, testing is indispensable. Unfortunately, a strong testing culture is hindered by the limitations of embedded devices, where traditional testing methods fall short. To address this, we present a novel testing approach that combines unit testing and driver testing on resource-constrained microcontrollers. Our proposal, MCU Test, includes a tiny kernel, an emulator that mimics the behavior of a microcontroller, and a testing framework that supports multiple programming languages. By enhancing the quality of drivers and promoting a robust testing culture, MCU Test has the potential to revolutionize the development of robotics and related research. Additionally, its versatility makes it an ideal tool for educating students in computer science. 

MCU Test is now available under the permissive MIT License at: https://mcutest.dev/ 

We welcome contributions from the community to further develop MCU Test. Please follow our contribution guidelines at: https://mcutest.dev/contribution/

To begin, we will set up a new project using MCU Test, followed by creating a unit test that verifies the functionality of a parameterized driver. Subsequently, we will modify the driver using an established development environment, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our solution through a sample test scenario. By participating in this demo, viewers will gain hands-on experience with MCU Test and its capabilities. Furthermore, we anticipate that the demo session will foster meaningful interactions, enabling attendees to explore additional features and share their own experiences with the technology.

This paper presents an innovative method for securing application-specific kernel capabilities without necessitating direct user involvement. The research demonstrates that a series of carefully crafted malicious actions in applications written in interpreted languages can deceive the kernel into granting undesired access privileges. To counter this risk, we've created Timeloops - a novel kernel module designed to provide secure system call filtering for interpreted applications. Unlike existing solutions, Timeloops operates seamlessly without requiring user intervention and can effectively block malicious system calls made by such applications. Its unique dynamic analysis technique enables it to develop application-specific call filters in real-time, thereby ensuring timely and accurate protection. Experimental results from evaluating Timeloops on PHP and Python applications indicate a significant reduction in false positives and positive rates. Further integration with existing security modules can enhance Timeloops' performance and scalability. As an innovative solution for securing interpreted applications, Timeloops offers a versatile approach applicable to other system components. All related code and data have been made available on GitHub at the specified URL. Feedback can be provided to [yjxu@umich.edu](mailto:yjxu@umich.edu). Future research can adapt Timeloops' analysis technique to static languages and implement its analysis at the source level. Additionally, developing methods for reversing and mitigating malicious kernel modules is another area of exploration. Additional information can be found in our technical report (Section 5). Finally, research into detecting security vulnerabilities within kernel modules can be an important area of study. This work was partially supported by funding from the National Science Foundation. However, due to the high-dimensionality and sparsity of the data, as well as the inherent variability between cells, developing effective classification systems is an intricate task. Most existing approaches utilize traditional Euclidean distances between cells to classify them, which leads to considerable classification errors. Alternatively, we demonstrate that representing cells in the context of a learned, low-dimensional space built using a neural network called protom. This new method significantly outperforms current approaches, achieving superior classification accuracy and reduced error rates for existing datasets. Furthermore, we illustrate the applicability of protom in tasks beyond cell-type classification, such as cell labeling and transfer learning, thereby showcasing its utility as a versatile tool for supervised classification tasks involving complex, high-dimensional data. Additionally, our method can be applied to other tasks by substituting the classification module with a different mathematical operation. Studies of a supermassive black hole's influence on nearby stars through gravitational force have been conducted using data from the Galaxy Evolution Explorer, which observed a region of high density in the center of the Milky Way.  Analyzing the number of stars at various distances from the black hole under the assumption that stars are evenly distributed across different energy levels, researchers discovered an uneven distribution of stars within the innermost 12 light-years of the high-density region, as calculated using data from a reliable star mass database.  However, this discrepancy may be attributed to measurement inaccuracies. By employing sparse measurement matrices that are effectively unmixing matrices, CIICA reduces the dimensionality of data and facilitates efficient independent component recovery, while also tolerating the presence of noise. Moreover, CIICA outperforms traditional ICA algorithms in terms of output sparsity, misalignment, and average squared error, while requiring significantly fewer computations and memory resources. Given its versatility and efficiency, CIICA has significant practical implications for signal processing applications involving large datasets and real-time processing requirements. We offer a novel proof of Greenberg's strong approximation theorem for one-dimensional local rings with a specific equivalence regarding Steinberg representations. This proof is built upon earlier work by Krauel and Nekov\'a\v z, which examined the case of a single place. Our argument is divided into two primary components. Firstly, we establish that the sum of certain composite functorial maps is equivalent to the diamond product of corresponding symbols, achieved through an induction process over the length of the local ring. Secondly, we prove a refined version of a previous theorem by Krauel and Nekov\'a\v z, which relates to the representation theory of the absolute Galois group in the case of a one-dimensional local ring. The refinement involves the use of a specific decomposition, which is then applied to derive the desired expression for Greenberg's strong approximation theorem. Additionally, we offer a cohomological formulation of this theorem, which is analogous to earlier work by Kahn--Srinivas for a regular local ring. Furthermore, we extend this result to include the case of a one-dimensional local ring with a specific property regarding its absolute Galois group and a certain decomposition. This paper investigates the duality of graphs represented by the class of spectra, a concept introduced by Asser, and reveals that his conjecture holds true for a specific subset of graphs. Asser originally suggested that the dual spectrum class contains a graph's inverse spectrum class. While this is generally the case for most graph classes, certain exceptions do exist. This paper confirms the validity of Asser's conjecture for the particular class of undirected bipartite graphs. Additionally, the paper introduces new methods for determining the duality of graphs classified under the 'extremal' class, and uses these methods to prove Asser's conjecture for this class as well. The confirmation of Asser's conjecture for two distinct graph classes (the class of undirected bipartite graphs and the extremal class) involved reexamining and refining previous concepts, including the notion of superfluous graphs. This led to the discovery of key insights, a new definition for superfluous graphs, and the development of a criterion for identifying non-superfluous graphs. This paper further explores superfluous graphs and their potential connections to 'families of extremal graphs'. It also contains examples of non-superfluous graphs, and proves that the class of superfluous graphs is closed under various graph operations while the class of non-superfluous graphs is still undefined. Lastly, the paper proposes an approach for identifying and determining the spectrum and dual spectrum relations for specific graph classes, and uses this approach to confirm Asser's conjecture for the class of extremal graphs. This method involves selecting representative graphs from a given class and examining their inverse spectrum relations. This simple yet effective approach has the potential to be applied to a wide range of graph classes in the future. Some examples of this application are provided in the paper, including the confirmation of Asser's conjecture for the class of graphs with a specific 'tree-type' structure. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions, including the development of efficient algorithms for identifying superfluous and non-superfluous graphs and applying these concepts to 'families of extremal graphs'. One such potential family is the set of graphs with a specific 'block-type' structure. This paper does not provide a definitive answer but does offer some preliminary insights. This paper develops a general framework to analyze computation in any physical system, which encompasses quantum computation and goes beyond it by examining other computational mechanisms present in nature. We apply this framework to quantum measurement processes, calculating the minimum number of clicks from a click-stream to reconstruct a state within a specific subspace or to evaluate a target operator as accurately as possible. These calculations reveal that quantum computation and measurement are closely connected but also differ in fundamental ways. Furthermore, comparisons between the computational powers of classical, quantum, and other physical systems are explored, including the use of non-linearity and contextual properties. These findings offer insights into the unique roles of these physical systems in computation and the relationships between their computational and fundamental properties. In particular, we discover that other physical systems can perform computations that are at least as powerful as quantum computation, but cannot evaluate certain operators as accurately as quantum measurement can. Additional research directions are suggested, focusing on the other predictive tasks and non-obvious examples of other physically fundamental computations. Additionally, the source code for reproducing the results is provided at https://github.com/other-physical-computation.

We introduce a straightforward, high-performance counting process for random walk positions in $d$ dimensions that significantly reduces memory usage. The traditional method, proposed by Aldous and Shields in 1987, uses $d+1$ independent random walks to track a random walk's visits in a $d$-dimensional space, resulting in $\binom{n+d}{d}$ visits counted $n$ steps. Their method facilitates counting but lacks efficiency, particularly in high-dimensional spaces. Our new approach involves merging visits from $d$ dimensional walks to reduce the number of counted visits from $\binom{n+d}{d}$ to $n^d$, achieving significant memory savings. The process is now efficient enough to enable statistical analysis of a random walk's visits in a $d$-dimensional space $n$ steps with $n$ a million and $d$ a dozen through our C++ implementation. The approach has potential applications, such as tracking a random walk's influence, distributing tasks among units in a $d$-dimensional space, and simulating a company's competition in a $d$-dimensional market where strategies are given weights. 

Our method also makes it easy to generalize visits counting to a mixture of $d$ and $d+1$ dimensional random walks, which has applications in its own right. The approach also led to a new general method for counting visits in a random walk in a toric $d$-dimensional space, where bounces are considered visits, offering another potential application. According to our findings, the reduced specific heat capacity stems directly from the normalized quasiparticle velocity, specifically as it relates to the nonlinear energy dispersion of Dirac fermions, effectively reflecting the collective behavior of interacting electrons through the corrected density of states. Furthermore, our research demonstrates how temperature-dependent self-consistent adjustments to the interaction strength influence thermal conductivity in the absence of lattice disorders. The quality of text-to-speech systems can significantly benefit from a speech database tailored to the language in question, which serves as a foundation for the training process. Unfortunately, building such a comprehensive speech database from scratch is an expensive endeavor due to the need for professional recording equipment and expertise. In this research, we introduce a novel system called MaskedSpeech that leverages publicly available audio clips, which are often inexpensive and easily accessible. This innovative training method utilizes a transformer-based approach to accurately predict speech characteristics by focusing on specific traits, such as speech type, and applying a masking technique to ensure the generated speech meets the requirements of the given trait. When evaluated using the TTS-quality-mean-objective-direction (TTS-QMOD) metric, which measures the perceived quality and naturalness of speech, our MaskedSpeech system consistently outperformed traditional approaches. Additionally, we assessed the expressiveness of the synthesized speech using a subjective evaluation and found that MaskedSpeech led to a notable improvement in this dimension as well. Notably, our system proved particularly effective in generating speech with a specific level of vocal pitch, which is a critical factor in creating a more natural and engaging listening experience. Based on these results, we conclude that MaskedSpeech represents a vital addition to the field of voice cloning, as it enables the accurate translation of a broad range of vocal attributes into synthesized speech. We introduce a novel Bayesian variable selection method that builds on the sparse Bayesian learning framework by incorporating an additional penalty term in the log-marginal likelihood to guide the selection of variables. The proposed approach, LFSB, utilizes the posterior uncertainties from the original model and ensures that selected variables retain their original posterior uncertainties. The inclusion of the new penalty term enhances the interpretability of the selected variables by accounting for their relative importance in the predictive model. The effectiveness of LFSB is demonstrated through comprehensive simulations involving both synthetic and real-world datasets, which showcase its superior performance in variable selection and prediction compared to existing methods. The associated code to reproduce these results can be accessed on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/lfsb-labs/LFSB. Deep Neural Network's vulnerability to adversarial examples has garnered significant interest. A recent study, however, has explored the impact of Man-in-the-Middle attacks on DNNs, which involves compromising the integrity of inputs and outputs transmitted through public channels. Unlike traditional adversarial example attacks, M-i-M attacks manipulate the physical environment or physical inputs/outputs, and can be carried out without the need for sophisticated computational power. While M-i-M attacks are challenging to execute, they are also highly effective, and can be applied to various DNN applications, including robots and autonomous vehicles. This study aims to investigate the effectiveness and detectability of M-i-M attacks, and proposes a mitigation approach to prevent such attacks. Firstly, we examined the success rate of M-i-M attacks in relation to different attack strategies, and discovered that these attacks can indeed compromise DNN accuracy without requiring sophisticated post-processing. Secondly, we explored various methods to identify M-i-M attacks, which typically involve physical anomaly detection, and discovered that both image and text data shared specific characteristics that differentiate them from legitimate inputs. Notably, the use of images and text data in M-i-M attacks can be identified by analyzing the consistency of uploaded images with the target DNN's performance. Based on this insight, we developed an unsupervised detection method, which involves monitoring the performance of a target DNN on M-i-M data, and uses anomaly detection to identify such attacks. Thirdly, we assessed the efficacy of our detection method in detecting M-i-M attacks, which involves training the detector using both clean data and adversarial examples, and discovered that it can be effectively used to identify M-i-M attacks across various attack strategies and input/data types. Lastly, we estimated the cost implications of our detection method, which involves calculating both false positive and negative rates, and discovered that the benefits of identifying M-i-M attacks outweigh the costs. Overall, this study has provided valuable insights into the characteristics and detectability of M-i-M attacks, which can be utilized to develop more effective mitigation approaches in the future. Specifically, our method can potentially identify spoofing attacks, which involve compromising the integrity of inputs/outputs transmitted through public channels, and are challenging to differentiate from M-i-M attacks. Our study addresses this gap using machine learning tools to regularly analyze and categorize relevant social media content on Twitter. From February to May 2021, we found that the most active group circulating climate change conspiracy theories consisted mainly of automated accounts. These accounts primarily propagated theories that deny the core assertion of climate change, whereas human accounts primarily engage in theories that undermine the need for climate action. Notably, we found that the former group tends to be more active. Our findings are based on the analysis of 1123 unique conspiracy theory-related tweets, which we believe can inform the effectiveness of counter-narrative strategies. Recent data from the Direct Detection experiments have revealed that the signal observed by DAMA remains anomalous even after considering the latest results from AXEL and XENONnT. In this study, we present a scenario where the observed effect can be attributed to the interaction of Dark Matter with 81Ni, a nucleus that lacks standard model predictions in many analytical models. We develop a cross-section limit for this specific interaction by comparing measurements of solar/supernova Dark Matter absorption to those from Direct Detection experiments. Our analysis indicates that Dark Matter interacting with 81Ni through a spin-dependent or spin-independent mechanism is possible within this framework, especially when considering the latter in conjunction with constraints from MONOP data. In the case of Dark Matter interacting with 81Ni via a spin-dependent mechanism, we find that our results match those derived using other analytical methods, such as helicity and heavy meson mass analysis methods. Furthermore, we illustrate the impact of differing Dark Matter interaction cross-sections on Dark Matter induced 81Ni absorption within the Standard Model, as well as within Non-Standard model scenarios. In the case of Dark Matter interacting with 81Ni via a spin-dependent mechanism, we find that Dark Matter induced 81Ni absorption within the Non-Standard model scenario is less pronounced, with an estimated rate roughly two orders of magnitude lower, at a cross-section of approximately 10^-10 GeV^2, compared to its Standard Model counterpart. In contrast, at a cross-section of approximately 10^-11 GeV^2, we observe an increased rate of approximately three orders of magnitude within the Non-Standard model scenario. In the case of Dark Matter interacting with 81Ni via a spin-independent mechanism, we find that Dark Matter induced 81Vi absorption within the Non-Standard model scenario is less pronounced, at a cross-section of approximately 10^-10 GeV, compared to its Standard Model counterpart, with an increased rate of approximately two orders of magnitude within the Non-Standard model scenario at a cross-section of approximately 10^-12 GeV. We establish that for categories with Serre duality, the condition of having a Serre dual is equivalent to the existence of a dual approximate sequence. By utilizing this equivalence, we derive a criterion for a perfect pair to have a Serre dual in terms of a descending sequence of subcategories. This framework enables us to determine Serre duals for specific pairs of perfect subcategories, including relative semisimple categories and categories of Gorenstein projective modules. Moreover, we utilize this criterion to investigate the existence of Serre duals for categories of first-order approximations in relation to Grothendieck invariants. Specifically, for Gorenstein projective modules, the existence of Serre duals corresponds to the Grothendieck invariant being nilpotent, and for first-order approximations, it corresponds to the Grothendieck invariant being radical. Furthermore, we establish that for relative pure-injectivity pairs, the existence of Serre duals is consistent with the Grothendieck invariants being nilpotent. Finally, we illustrate with examples that the proposed criterion is necessary and sufficient. Additionally, we establish that for Gorenstein artin algebras, the perfect pairs with Serre duals correspond to the Trivald duality pairs, and the corresponding Grothendieck invariants are nilpotent. Finally, we establish that for abelian categories with Serre duality, the condition of having a Serre dual is equivalent to the existence of a dual approximation sequence. This study provides a detailed description of Norwegian higher education fields of study earnings return on investment (ROI) from 2007 to 2017, also including comparisons with neighboring Denmark and the UK. Our analysis is based on a unique dataset linking higher education fields of study to earnings in Norway. To ensure the validity of our findings, we employed several methods including regression decomposition, analysis of the gender differences in ROI, and examining variations in ROI across distinct regions within Norway. Our analyses indicate that Norwegian fields of study earnings ROI display limited movement over time but show notable discrepancies when compared to Denmark and the UK. Our findings suggest significant implications for informing decision-making in higher education fields of study choices and guiding policy initiatives, particularly those aimed at promoting field of study selection and financial compensation schemes such as study grants. To aid policy makers in identifying fields of study with potential rewards, our results also include a user-friendly visualization tool allowing users to assess and compare various fields of study return on investment in Norway, Denmark, and the UK from 2007 to 2017. This tool is accessible via the website roinorvikt.no. Our research is the first to apply marginal treatment comparison and regression decomposition to analyze fields of study earnings ROI. To facilitate further research, we also provide an open-source replication code available on github. Our work is, however, hindered by several significant challenges including incomplete education fields of study earnings data and a comprehensive census limiting our ability to thoroughly consider field of study selectivity. Our analysis is also restricted by our failure to fully capture other crucial field of study characteristics including degree awarding institutions and individual academic achievement, both crucial in informing decision-making in higher education fields of study choice and guiding policy initiatives. Our research is further limited by our consideration of return on investment in fields of study as a multifaceted concept encompassing both monetary earnings and non-monetary benefits. Our failings to full capture non-monetary benefits of education fields of study earnings, especially in the context of fields of study choice and decision-making, is a significant area requiring further research and inquiry. Our research is lastly restricted by our classification of fields of study earnings return on investment as deterministic, although our analysis indicates that these returns on investment are highly varied and may be influenced by multiple factors including gender, geographic location, and degree awarding institutions. Initially, the smaller binary orbits around the center of the system, which is occupied by a stable stellar mass black hole. The formation of cosmic structures is directly linked to the fluctuations within the universe's matter density. Our research examines how these matter fluctuations influence the universe's large-scale structure, focusing specifically on how its size and spatial distribution change over time. Using a linear fluctuation model, we calculate the expected power spectrum of the universe's matter density at any given time, taking into account the impact of its velocity and second derivative. Our analysis shows that at late times, the power spectrum is primarily determined by the universe's matter density, while the effects of its velocity and second derivative become negligible. Additionally, we observe that on large-scale distances, the power spectrum is largely independent of time. However, on smaller scales, we find that the power spectrum increases slightly over time due to the growth of infrared fluctuations. A detailed comparison with N-body simulation data supports our theoretical findings, confirming that our model accurately predicts the power spectrum on large scales at different redshifts. Our work highlights that on large-scale distances, the power spectrum is largely stable and can serve as a consistent standard, useful in comparing data across different redshifts. The traditional Mumford-Shah model has been widely utilized for image segmentation. However, it falls short in dealing with corrupted images, making it necessary to modify and adapt it. This study introduces a new approach - a piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model - to achieve accurate segmentation in the presence of image corruption. The proposed method efficiently handles high levels of noise and is suitable for images with different color channels. The key to this model's effectiveness lies in its decomposition into an efficient approximation of the image boundaries and the segmentation dividing the image into homogeneous regions. The boundary optimization is reformulated as a nonconvex, geodesic distance-based split problem, addressed using an alternating minimization algorithm. The model's performance is comprehensive, covering various types of image corruption, including additive noise, multiplicative noise, motion deblurring, and low-resolution images. The results demonstrate the significance of preserving edges when segmentation, as it leads to a more accurate and robust segmentation. The proposed model outperforms current methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, as evidenced by the provided examples and comparisons with other segmentation techniques. Recent research suggests that dark matter may be composed of ultra-light particles, potentially in a Bose-Einstein condensate state. Theoretical calculations of condensed dark matter density are complex due to the need to solve an elliptical equation, leading to limited existing solutions. This study derives new closed-form solutions for condensed dark matter equations in different astrophysical contexts, including constant pressure and distinct boundary conditions. The solutions reveal how mass and ultralight particle coupling constant interact and lead to theoretical estimates of critical masses for particle condensation. The findings also enable the analysis of condensed matter properties across various scales, from individual stars to galaxy clusters. The new solutions facilitate the computation of condensed matter effects on light emission, a crucial aspect for testing dark matter hypotheses through the observation of dark matter effects. The research demonstrates that condensed matter effects are significant in small astrophysical systems but gradually decrease in larger systems. In neuromorphic computing, the goal of on-chip learning is to enable neurons on a single hardware component to adapt their properties through systematic adjustments, like weight changes.  Unlike conventional learning, which relies on back-propagation, on-chip learning techniques aim to make this process more efficient by reducing communication between hardware layers.  This work presents a new on-chip learning method that uses spiking neurons and exploits their local, self-contained mechanism for adapting neuron properties and learning algorithms like Hebbian learning.  A specific implementation, called Local Vector-Quantized Distortion Moving Average (LVQ-DMA), combines vector quantization with a competitive learning rule, effectively achieving vector learning within a single hardware layer.  Using an integrated circuit version of this method, trained models were compared with those obtained through standard supervised learning on an image classification task, showing comparable results with only a fraction of the training data required for the on-chip method.  This performance, along with compact, efficient implementations of neuromorphic learning systems, makes this method suitable for various real-world applications. A powerful radio storm, identified as a source of a low-frequency burst, was observed at 284 MHz by the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA). The duration of this burst, known as a low-frequency giant pulse, was under 10 seconds, exceeding typical intervals between such pulses by an order of magnitude. The burst displayed a complex morphology consisting of two distinct components, one resembling a narrowband fan-shaped structure and the other a wideband arc-shaped feature, observed in multiple frequency bands. The arc-shaped feature showed an increase in intensity with decreasing frequency, and the distance between the components increased as the frequency decreased. The shape and size of the storm, as well as its intensity, varied in relation to each other, displaying a nonconstant scaling effect. The narrowband fan-shaped structure had a stable shape and size across different frequencies, but the wideband arc-shaped feature showed an increase in size with decreasing frequency, and the storm's intensity in this region was observed to be an inverse power of the frequency, specifically proportional to $1/\sqrt{f}$. A near-zero-gravity environment is created for a magneto-optical trap (MOT) by setting it in a plane perpendicular to the laser beam's propagation direction. This novel arrangement eliminates the laser beam's deflection due to gravity and reduces motional energy. A detailed analysis of the system's physics is presented, along with a proposed design for a planar-integrated MOT setup. One of the enduring enigmas in astrophysics is why powerful black holes like those at the center of our galaxy or the Large Magellanic Cloud don't emit large amounts of radiation, given their high energy output potential.
For nearly seven decades, various explanations have been tried, but none resolve the issue completely. A recently proposed concept, active--passive electromagnetic depletion, may hold the key and is explored here in the context of accretion hot spots on black holes. This phenomenon is likely responsible for hot spots on stellar-mass black holes, possibly producing gamma-ray bursts, and could also account for the low radiance of supermassive black holes, such as those in our galaxy's center or the Large Magellanic Cloud's center, by removing accretion energy via magnetic reconnection and leaving behind a trail of trapped particles. This process not only produces synchrotron radiation but also accelerates and traps abundant electrons and positrons, which could provide the observed excessive radiation in some supercritical accretion disks. Additionally, this phenomenon may influence the structure and composition of accretion disks by creating magnetospheric atmospheres. A moving neutral atom within a cavity of a single mode will undergo motion-induced correlation when interacting with the emitted photons, especially in systems involving a mirror. This correlation becomes evident in the form of quantum-squeezed vacuum components and is typically observed in research contexts using solid matter systems. This study focuses on a novel approach where a non-relativistic mirror and a rigidly attached atom interact and exhibit coherent motion. This is achieved through a semi-classical method of reduced description, utilizing coherent states and imposing a rigid constraint on the system. This results in the derivation of a non-trivial vacuum state with well-defined momentum, displaying quantum-squeezed vacuum components. This result is further expanded to a system of N identical atoms, resulting in logarithmic attenuation of the vacuum coherence as N increases. This study suggests that similar approaches can be applied to the study of relativistic mirror-atom systems, particularly in the context of particle physics. This is achieved through a fully quantum field theoretical treatment, beginning with a description of a free scalar field subject to a constant background velocity. This results in the creation of a coherent state with a non-zero vacuum expectation value for the scalar field, accompanied by a logarithmic attenuation of the vacuum coherence as the number of particles increases. This finding is analogous to that observed in the neutral atom-mirror system studied above. This research further extends to a study of a mirror-like soliton in a waveguide, described by a non-linear wave equation. This results in the creation of a coherent state with a non-zero vacuum expectation value for the scalar field, accompanied by a logarithmic attenuation of the vacuum coherence as the number of particles increases. This finding is independent of whether the soliton is localized or extends indefinitely, making up a significant portion of the field's energy density. This result is further validated to be stable through an analysis of fluctuations around the soliton solution. This research demonstrates that similar approaches can be applied to various physical systems, offering a valuable contribution to the field of theoretical physics. The 45-year expansion of supernovae from the young and rich cluster Westerlund 2 has caught scientists' attention, as several stars in the cluster have gone missing while no new ones have been discovered within a specific brightness threshold. Researchers analyzed 22 billion electromagnetic waves collected from the sky region containing the cluster to better understand its stellar population, and by using the cluster's center of mass as a reference point, calculated the movement of individual stars within it. Data revealed that stars on the outskirts of the cluster take significantly longer to traverse the same distance as those closer to the center, indicating a substantial discrepancy of about 2 minutes in time for every arcsecond. This large difference in time is primarily attributed to the uneven distribution of brighter, more massive stars within the cluster, as their expulsion mechanisms are yet to be efficiently activated. Scientists believe that the rate at which these massive stars are ejected from the cluster needs to increase by at least 5 times to explain the missing energy discrepancy, and it is likely that the cluster's interior is experiencing more violent events such as the expansion of supernovae, star mergers, and ejections within it. Further study is required to understand the recent and future events within the cluster and how they contribute to the observed expansion and energy discrepancy, as well as to determine the potential impact of a future supernova from the cluster on its stellar population, gravitational force, and expansion rate. Researchers are looking forward to using the New Generation Virtual Observatory tools to further examine the cluster and its stellar population, as well as to monitor the cluster more closely over the next 10 years with the help of space-based telescopes that will likely detect more stars in the cluster. Conversely, it is also possible that the cluster is actually smaller than previously thought, as the brighter stars within it may be responsible for the observed expansion and energy discrepancy through gravitational force, and further study is required to understand the cluster's structure, its stellar population, and the implications of this new theory. Ultimately, the main goal of this research is to understand the recent and future events within the cluster Westerlund 2, as well as to determine the potential impact of a future supernova from the cluster on its stellar population, gravitational force, and expansion rate, and with the help of the New Generation Virtual Observatory tools and future space-based telescope observations, scientists can better understand the cluster and its stellar population, and make comparisons with other young massive clusters at much greater distances. This study delves into a minimax variational problem with constraints that form a convex hull. The minimax problem's (quasi-) existence is examined when the constraints are defined by a partial differential operator and further investigated with regard to perturbations of the operator. The existence of solutions in these cases is linked to specific properties of the operator, including compactness and coercivity, and the results are also generalized to the setting of $p$-Laplacian. The main findings of this research are applied to a specific type of free boundary problem, yielding new (quasi-) existence results that were previously unknown. The paper further analyzes a perturbed version of this problem, providing criteria for the minimax problem's solutions to be unique. The existence and minimaxity of the solutions to these problems are also investigated under specific topological changes in the domain, and the results are demonstrated with the help of examples. The primary techniques employed in this research involve the reformulation of the minimax problem as a homotopy in the relevant topological space, the utilization of the fundamental group to investigate changes in the problem's solution set, and the application of the Fredholm alternative to introduce conditional perturbations of the problem operator. The conclusions of this research are presented in six separate theorems, each addressing a distinct generalization of the original variational problem. The theorems provide criteria for the minimax problem's solutions to exist, be unique, and unique minimax in the relevant topological space, and the results are also extended to the setting of $p$-Laplacian and used to introduce new criteria for the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a free boundary problem in the presence of perturbations. The results are finally demonstrated with the help of examples, illustrating the precision of the introduced criteria. The research is primarily based on the works of Benci and Benetti, but also draws inspiration from the works of Capoferri, Pogreba, and the research on the $p$-harmonic measure by Gris Ardido and Mardalbecco. The technical tools used in the research are based on the works of Capoferri, and the book by F. Della Sala, M. Molle, and M. Zanetti. This research focuses on utilizing handwritten text recognizers in a more efficient manner. Typically, these recognizers are initially used to transcribe the text from an image directly. However, we have developed an innovative approach where the handwritten text recognizer and a Generative Adversarial Network work together in a feedback loop. The handwritten text recognizer provides the generated text from step n-1 to the GAN, which then produces an enhanced image based on this text. This collaborative approach continuously improves both the image and the text through iteration. The integration of the handwritten text recognizer adds critical knowledge about the text's structure, including the layout, which significantly contributes to the image enhancement process. Moreover, this integration can also improve the robustness of the GAN by training on accurate, rather than flawed, text data. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this integrated approach in improving both the layout and the text's overall readability within degraded document images. We have specifically tailored this layout recognition component to match the specific requirements of the layout pattern in question, rather than relying on pre-existing knowledge, which would be limited to that of standard handwritten text recognizers. This novel combination of handwritten text recognizers and GANs in a feedback loop marks a significant advancement in the development of more effective document image enhancement techniques. Moreover, this approach is versatile and can be applied to various document image enhancement challenges beyond just layout and text. We have specifically tested this combination on handwritten text and mathematical notations, demonstrating its broad applicability to multiple domains. Additionally, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of the influence of handwritten text recognizers on the overall performance of the GAN. This includes assessing the impact of utilising handwritten text recognizers versus relying on pre-existing knowledge, as well as examining the stability of the GAN when incorporating these recognizers. The integration of the handwritten text recognizer is seen to significantly outperform the baseline performance in the absence of the recognizer, despite the presence of significant image degradations. We have also investigated the effect of varying the layout pattern on the performance of the integrated approach, as well as assessed its applicability to multiple layout patterns in various document types. Furthermore, we have explored the potential of this integrated approach in improving both the layout and the text from actual, rather than artificially created, document images. We have specifically examined the performance of the GAN before and after integrating the handwritten text recognizer for both line drawing and handwritten text, as well as comparing its output to that of a GAN that was not supplemented with a handwritten text recognizer. This research focuses on utilizing Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to extract personal data from ID cards with varying formats. Our goal is to apply deep learning models to optimize extraction accuracy and minimize the impact of structural discrepancies. Although most NLP applications rely on fixed input and output formats, ID card extraction presents a unique challenge due to the diverse layouts of identification information. To address this issue, we develop a new attention technique that adapts to non-fixed structural patterns. Additionally, ID card extraction poses another difficulty in normalizing the data format for comparison. To overcome this hurdle, we combine extracted data with an MD5 hashing method to validate our approach's effectiveness across different ID card layouts. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate high extraction accuracy rates of 97.5% for name extraction, 98.5% for ID number extraction, and 97.1% for birthdate extraction, with an overall average precision of 97.7%. Furthermore, our proposed method outperforms the control group's accuracy by 7.8%, showcasing its validity and effectiveness. We employ a deep learning strategy known as super resolution to enhance low-resolution astronomical images, specifically those taken by the ZTF camera at 105 per second. This fast frame rate enables the capture of rapid astronomical events such as novae, but the images are severely blurred, affecting the schedule and the success rate of the ZTF survey. We develop a convolutional neural network algorithm to enhance these fast frame rates into sharper images, utilizing a dataset of 144,000 low-resolution images collected over two years by the ZTF. The model is optimized to improve the extraction of celestial objects from blurred images, and we observe a significant improvement in the sharpness of the images through the comparison of the peak signal-to-noise ratios before and after the application of the algorithm. This enhancement enables the accurate identification of objects in the fast frame rates of the ZTF, and we anticipate the application of this algorithm to various rapid real-time astronomical surveys in the future. Additionally, we successfully tested our model on actual ZTF data by processing fast frame rates around the discovery of a nova, and the enhanced images revealed significant improvements in the signal-to-noise ratios by a factor of two, allowing us to identify a stellar counterpart at a later epoch that was previously undetected. Based on this success, we anticipate the application of the algorithm to significantly enhance the detection power of various rapid real-time astronomical surveys in the future. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) possess exceptional capacity for learning tasks, but they are susceptible to overfitting, which can be mitigated through regularization techniques, particularly effective ones that harness nearby data points to constrain the model's behavior.  Within the machine learning community, various graph-based regularization methods have been developed; nonetheless, these methods are limited to specific layers within the network and often disregard the dependencies between data points.  This paper proposes an innovative algorithm that incorporates regularization at the graph level for the entire ResNet, effectively constraining the model's behavior through a regularization signal derived from the nearby data points.  The algorithm creates an adjacency matrix that captures the dependencies between the data points, where the model's parameters are then updated using a novel optimizer that incorporates the graph-based regularization, thereby preventing overfitting and enabling the detection of latent data clusters.  Experimental findings on multiple datasets indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through an empirical analysis of the model's regularization effects, the detection of data clusters, and the prevention of overfitting using comprehensive metrics.  This research is an extension of our previous conference paper, providing additional experiments and a revised algorithm that incorporates the insights gathered from the conference presentations.  In particular, the presented results include the effects of graph-based regularization on the model's behavior, an in-depth analysis of the data clusters, and an investigation of the impact of data dependencies on the model's generalization capacity, all conducted on the CIFAR-10 dataset using the BNN.  Furthermore, the algorithm has been implemented in a public repository, located at https://github.com/Gurkit/RBN/treefeature/Reg_NAS. We introduce a new estimator that significantly reduces bias while maintaining the current accuracy levels in a wide range of econometric estimators, such as those used to measure the effect of treatments, connections, and other contextual factors. Notably, our proposal tackles a major limitation of existing bias-reduced estimators, which often assume a high level of smoothness. We overcome this limitation by leveraging a powerful mathematical technique, simulating unbiasedness, to derive an initial estimator with no smoothness assumptions. This estimator can then be improved using various techniques, resulting in several more efficient options. The new estimators surpass their counterparts in terms of accuracy, all while maintaining the same level of reliability. By means of simulated data, we demonstrate the superior performance of our proposal in a range of practical scenarios. Furthermore, we apply the new estimators to real-world problems, such as analyzing the effect of a medical treatment on patients with distinct symptoms and assessing how a large technology firm's connections influence its market dominance. The results reveal substantial correlations between these contextual factors and the estimated effects, which highlight the importance of considering these factors in such analyses. By making these estimators available on our website, we aim to facilitate their use in future research. Ultimately, the new estimators seek to enhance the efficiency of econometric research, particularly in scenarios involving multiple treatments, networks, and non-smooth data patterns. Given its generality, this method may also have applications in other fields beyond econometrics. By extending the traditional scope of econometric research, we seek to expand the potential applications of our approach. Additionally, we provide detailed information on how the proposed estimators compare to their counterparts in terms of various statistical criteria, such as mean squared error, variance, and bias. This comparison serves as a foundation for our recommendations on when to use the more efficient estimators. By making these estimators accessible through an available R package, we seek to simplify the process of implementing these new techniques in practical contexts. Moreover, we outline potential avenues for further research in this area, such as developing new estimators for this purpose and applying these techniques to real-world data sets. By seeking to enhance the efficiency of econometric research, we aim to contribute meaningfully to the field of econometrics. Furthermore, we describe in detail the theoretical underpinnings of our approach, including how we combine existing methods to develop these new estimators and why these specific techniques are necessary to achieve this goal. By expounding on these theoretical aspects, we seek to facilitate the extension of our method to other estimation problems.

Additionally, our model can be adapted to address entity ranking, the task of ranking entities based on their likelihood of being linked to another entity. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experimental evaluation on multiple benchmark datasets, showcasing its capacity to successfully predict missing links and entity rankings. Furthermore, we highlight the challenges associated with entity ranking and provide potential avenues for further research. This paper explores the mass spectrum of heavy quark-antiquark pairs in a hot and dense medium with negative baryonic chemical potential and zero electric chemical potential. The study is based on a gauge-invariant quark-meson model that incorporates instanton-induced interactions. When baryonic chemical potential is introduced, the study indicates a shift from Debye mass types I and II to Type III. The paper examines how heavy quark-antiquark pairs are bound in a hot and dense medium with negative baryonic chemical potential and zero electric chemical potential, revealing a previously uninvestigated region of the mass spectrum. The study discovers that heavy quark-antiquark pairs are bound in a certain mass range for a specific range of Debye mass parameters. The findings of this study may provide insights into quark-gluon plasma properties and potentially shed light on the mechanism of charmonium suppression in heavy-ion collisions. The paper discusses these implications. Furthermore, the study discovers that heavy quark-antiquark bound states are stable within a certain mass range for a specific range of Debye mass parameters and baryonic chemical potential values. Notably, the magnetic arrangement in Nd3RuO7 features in-phase spins, whereas Tb3RuO7 displays out-of-phase spins. Effective representation of low-dimensional signals is crucial for achieving good generalization results. Current methods utilizing the global functional representation, despite being efficient, have a limitation - they do not adequately account for local data distributions within input samples. Contrary to conventional wisdom, our research reveals that focusing on these local arrangements, as expressed through the lens of diffusion maps, leads to improved generalization results. Building upon this insight, we introduce the concept "learned diffusions" which utilize a learned, data-dependent Riemannian metric to enhance the diffusion maps' sensitivity to local data patterns. By incorporating this metric into the standard negative manifold minimization objective, our method achieves significant improvements in the consistency of manifold coefficients across sample permutations. As a result, our approach exhibits superior performance in the analysis of multi-manifolds and signal denoising applications, as evidenced by extensive experimental evaluations. We introduce a new class of probabilistic models called semi-generated models that analyze multi-dimensional sequential data with mixed structures of causes and effects. These models combine a hierarchical probabilistic model of intermediate variables with a set of deterministic functions that simulate the dynamics of the target variables. The models are trained using an innovative approach that incorporates both generative and regression techniques in an unified framework. This new method builds on the strengths of previous approaches and offers improved efficiency and flexibility. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach using both artificial datasets and real-world data from the study of cell signaling networks and stock market analysis, and our results demonstrate its ability to make accurate predictions and identify key variables that influence the behavior of complex systems. The proposed methodology and associated tools are freely available on our project website.

Deep learning's rapid growth has been bolstered by conventional approach methods, but these rely on long-standing mathematical assumptions from classical computing. It's time to reassess these premises using deep learning data. Our investigation explores the geometric underpinnings of a standard deep learning framework, uncovering novel insights that could lead to improved architectures, unparalleled performance, or even new computing paradigms. By reimagining the deep learning landscape, we might discover groundbreaking algorithmic innovations. This study marks the initial phase of this endeavor, setting the stage for a broader examination of the deep learning ecosystem. Our analysis has already inspired the development of novel neural networks, such as doubly-convolutional networks, which exhibit exceptional robustness against adversarial attacks. Additionally, it allows us to quantify the approximate data storage complexity of neural networks over diverse data distributions. This research opens up numerous research avenues, such as reshaping network geometry to boost inference speed, or creating learning methods that reconstruct neural structures by imposing data-driven geometric constraints. The problem addresses finding minimal elements in cubic fields of the form $x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 2$. When $x$, $y$, and $z$ are integers, the field's discriminant is a multiple of 3, which leads to two possible values for the discriminant, denoted $D_0$ and $D_1$. For each discriminant, a specific infinite family of cubic fields has radicands as the sum of three cubes, with all three cubes being integers. The identity of the minimal elements in these cubic fields has been completely identified. In particular, it has been found that one of the minimal elements is an infinitely large family that can be expressed as $(\pm 1, \pm 1, \pm 1)$. Additionally, it has been found that another minimal element is more difficult to identify and cannot be expressed in the form $(x, y, z)$ where $x$, $y$, and $z$ are integers, but rather has a more complex relationship and may have a non-integral $z$-coordinate. Notably, it has been found that one of the minimal elements is an infinitely large family that can be expressed as $(8, -z^2 - z^3, z^5 + z^6)$. This behavior is particularly notable in that the $z$-coordinate appears to vary freely. The identified minimal elements account for approximately $20.8\%$ of all lattice minima in cubic fields with a discriminant of $D_0$ and $7.4\%$ of all lattice minima in cubic fields with a discriminant of $D_1$. This model exhibits three right-handed and three left-handed quark generations with precise U(1)_F flavor symmetry breaking, save for the top and bottom quarks. Their distinct masses are a result of the E6 unification group's subtle influence on the minimal model, which can be attributed to an anomalous U(1)_F symmetry breaking effect or a non-minimal arrangement of the flavor symmetry. Notably, this model precludes flavor-changing neutral currents. It is based on a previously developed symmetry, known as A4, which can be mapped to E6, offering a natural explanation for the top quark's relatively small red decoupling and the enhancement of the hbb coupling. This model's minimal field content makes it an ideal candidate for further study using future precision top quark measurements at enhanced luminosity levels at the LHC and other forthcoming experiments. Recent advancements in container technologies, such as Virtual Private Networks and Cloud-Services, have increased the need for secure methods to determine the source of network attacks. Traditional methods, employing API calls to identify sources, are easily manipulable and deceptive in virtual environments, leading to false identities. To overcome these limitations, API-free methods utilizing system calls have been developed for determining IP addresses in Linux containers. Notably, our research introduces a new deep learning approach, Deep Private IP Mapping (DPIP), which employs system calls to precisely identify IP addresses in Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL2). Though challenged by the complexity and variability of system calls, our paper demonstrates the effectiveness of DPIP through experimental validation using real-world WSL2 configurations. Furthermore, we reveal the vulnerabilities of Malicious Private IP Maps (MPIPs) in virtual environments, which can be exploited for malicious activities such as attack fake identifications and malicious system call injection. Consequently, the malicious utilization of MPIPs could compromise the security of virtual environments. To mitigate this risk, our research proposes a new MPIP model based on the natural flow of system calls. Notably, our model can determine IP addresses with high accuracy across various Malicious Private IP Map configurations. Importantly, our method is the first of its kind to utilize system calls for precise IP identification in Windows Subsystem for Linux, showcasing its robustness and generalizability through extensive experimental validation. Furthermore, our model outperforms existing approaches by achieving up to a 15.23% improvement in accuracy on the MPIP dataset. Language models are now widely utilized across numerous languages, yet their suitability for handling unfamiliar languages is largely unexplored. This adaptability is crucial for open-world tasks where language data is constantly being discovered. We investigate how language models prepare for unfamiliar languages during inference and find that they fail to effectively adapt to new languages with similar scripts, often relying on familiar language data instead. To enhance language adaptability, we introduce a novel inference method called PromptPretrain, which fine-tunes prompts using pretrain loss before inference. This method significantly improves adaptability and is particularly effective for non-English languages. Moreover, we introduce zero-shot data augmentation using named entity replacement, enabling further enhancements to language adaptability. Our work is implemented in a publicly accessible repository. Reproductions can be found at https://github.com/yangyangyang-labs/LAMB. We evaluate our method using 20 languages from various language families, which can be accessed at https://github.com/yangyangyang-labs/LAMB/tree/master/language_list. Our results indicate that PromptPretrain yields superior results, with an average 10.3% improvement in median accuracy among languages with similar scripts, and an overall 6.1% improvement across all languages. Furthermore, it offers robust protection against zero-shot data augmentation, preventing performance degradation when language data increases up to 10 times. With an inference time acceleration of 57%, PromptPretrain demonstrates exceptional efficiency. Empirical analysis suggests that PromptPretrain enhances adaptability by minimizing temperature fluctuations and zero-shot prediction bias. As a result, it provides a pioneering solution for open-world language tasks and serves as a foundation for exploring various adaptability techniques. With n-gram error rates decreased by 2.3 and test set data augmentation coverage increased to 70.3%, it also demonstrates promising applications in natural language inference and zero-shot data augmentation. With applications in multiple open-world tasks and a 35% reduction in temperature fluctuations, it displays remarkable stability and is thus named LAMB. We extensively evaluate LAMB across diverse benchmarks, which can be found at https://github.com/yangyangyang-labs/LAMB/tree/master/results. Notably, it exhibits robust performance on languages with similar scripts, outperforming ZeroShot by 10.3%. This research introduces a novel multivariate aggregation function, m-ar-K function, to address issues related to data complexity and dimensionality. It serves as a parameterized, comprehensive tool for handling diverse problems, ultimately contributing to dimensionality reduction. Utilizing the m-ar-K function, we develop a new technique for generating minimal discrete ordinarily differential equations models on a finite grid, which can be applied to dimensionality reduction. Additionally, this method can be employed for tracking the dynamics of sparse differential equations models. Our study compares the efficiency of this new approach with existing dimensionality reduction techniques, specifically PCA, K-Means, LLAPC, LLMDS, LLMAPC, and LLDIM, using synthetic and real-world data sets. The results demonstrate that the m-ar-K function-based method outperforms these established methods in clustering accuracy and dimensionality reduction effectiveness. The associated algorithm, along with simulation codes, is made available open-source. Furthermore, our study highlights the potential of the m-ar-K function for use as a regulator in nonlinear control systems. This innovative application expands the scope of potential control strategies, paving the way for its further exploration in this domain. Moreover, our work formally establishes the m-ar-K function as a multivariate aggregation function, thereby contributing to existing literature on this topic. The proof presented can be adapted to other multivariate aggregation functions in the future. Lastly, our research extends the concept of multivariate aggregation functions to include parameterized forms, thereby providing a framework for studying parameterized multivariate aggregation functions. The study demonstrates its efficacy through practical applications, and this concept is also applicable to other real-world problems. The technique employed for generating discrete ordinarily differential equations models relies on a multivariate aggregation function, specifically the m-ar-K function, utilizing a multivariate optimization approach. This method, as well as the formulation of the underlying optimization problem, are discussed thoroughly. The Levenberg Marquardt Nonlinear Optimization algorithm is employed to solve the resulting problem, and the study verifies the correctness of the generated models through comparison with actual differential equations, as well as by examining their stability properties, specifically the condition of hyperbolicity. This would be the first known separation between PTIME and CPT. Additionally, we demonstrate that a super-polynomial EPC lower bound for PTIME would yield significant implications, such as establishing the optimal gap-hierarchy for EPC and proving that multiple natural decision problems are resistant against EPC-computable zero-knowledge proofs. Furthermore, assuming the hypothesis that efficient zero-knowledge proofs can be constructed for all verifiable predicates, we prove that a super-polynomial EPC lower bound for PTIME would allow us to construct a super-polynomial EPC lower bound for any fixed predicate in the class of VP0 (a subset of verifiable predicates with specific properties). Our analysis also reveals a surprising discrepancy between the computational power of PTIME and its ability to efficiently construct zero-knowledge proofs, as well as efficient proofs of correctness for arbitrary probabilistic computations, which could have far-reaching implications in the realm of theoretical computer science.
