Recent studies on natural language prompting have shown that even large language models can achieve few-shot in-context learning tasks, especially with sufficient training data. In response to concerns over the likelihood of memorized answers, we explored the role of language modeling in natural language prompting. Our research concentrated on Retell-Story, a task where given a character's point of view, participants are asked to continue the story after an incomplete paragraph. In our experiments with 8 characters and a dataset containing 2.7K stories, we found that Retell-Story supported few-shot in-context learning, but unlike other tasks such as CommonGen and CommonBookTitles, it did not become solvable with pre-trained language models having no training data. In attempts to understand the requirements for few-shot in-context learning that are often imposed on language models, we assessed and compared the performance of Perplexity, Inference Fidelity, and Few-Shot Performance on the Retell-Story dataset. Our analysis indicated that there is no guaranteed correlation between low perplexity and few-shot in-context learning performance, but a positive correlation existed between inference fidelity and few-shot performance. In contrast, the relationship between model capacity and few-shot performance was not consistently positive. In another set of experiments, we found that augmentation methods can enhance both perplexity and few-shot performance, but the former metric did not act as a proxy for the latter. In conclusion, our research highlighted distinct requirements for training natural language models in natural language prompting, and few-shot in-context learning may be achievable even with models possessing low language modeling capabilities. Consequently, our findings suggest that language model developers may prioritize model scalability over language modeling capabilities. Moreover, our study demonstrates that the latter is not a necessary or sufficient prerequisite for few-shot in-context learning. Lastly, our research shows that data augmentation can improve both language modeling and few-shot performance, and enhancing the former does not necessarily act as a proxy for enhancing the latter. In line with recent studies (Kim et al., 2020; Achmad et al., 2020; Achmad et al., 2021), our analysis indicates that Retell-Story may serve as a fitting platform for assessing the robustness of few-shot in-context learning. This paper addresses the challenge of optimizing edge computing facilities by addressing issues of energy consumption, device obsolescence, and traffic from various devices such as smartphones, tablets, and IoT devices. To effectively manage these challenges, we developed an integrated optimization model that synchronizes device maintenance, upgrade, and operation to minimize energy consumption and extend device lifespan. The optimization strategy involves a multi-agent system where individual agents represent local cloud data centers or edge facilities, and their actions are guided by specific rules to achieve common objectives. The proposed strategies involve switching devices to sleep mode, upgrading devices, and conducting tasks locally or in the cloud. The effectiveness of these strategies is examined using a simulation-based approach, and we evaluate their impact on energy consumption, device obsolescence, and upgrade costs. Our findings reveal that switching devices to sleep mode has a minimal effect on energy consumption but significantly reduces it in cases of light traffic; local execution of tasks reduces energy consumption but may lead to device obsolescence if tasks are conducted in the cloud; and upgrading devices to high-capacity machines with local execution of tasks results in the best outcome for both energy consumption and device obsolescence. Furthermore, our research identifies the optimal percentage of local execution of tasks and device upgrades necessary to achieve optimal results. The integration of our models and strategies in edge computing facilities enables and demonstrates the effectiveness of these outcomes. The source code for our model and strategies is available open-source on the Git hub repository at the address: https://github.com/aitopologrino/Edge-MOM. Current neural models of speech, whether supervised or unsupervised, rely on a hidden state representation, $q(S|X)$, to characterize speech, where $S$ represents speech features and $X$ is the audio signal. However, a common issue arises when these models converge to static distributions of speech features, causing poor performance on tasks like classification and the generalization to new, unseen data. A possible explanation for this limitation is the failure of existing models to capture transient information in speech. We propose an alternative class of probabilistic models, Steady-$\mathcal{M}$, that can effectively model both transient and steady-state components of speech, where a specific distribution, $q(S|S_-,X_-)$, characterizes the transition from past speech features, $S_-$, to the current speech features, $S$, given the past audio signal, $X_-. We further prove that Steady-$\mathcal{M}$ can be optimized to maximize the margin between speech features, thus providing improved performance on classification tasks. Moreover, by introducing a set of prior constraints on the speech feature transition, we can ensure that Steady-$\mathcal{M}$ is equivalent to a specific type of neural model, providing Steady-$\mathcal{M}$ with steady-state components, $q(S|X)$, and making it suitable for unsupervised speech modeling. Experimental results indicate that Steady-$\mathcal{M}$ offers superior performance on classification tasks and Steady-$\mathcal{M}$ can effectively model transient information in speech, where a specific Steady-$\mathcal{M}$ variant provides improved unsupervised speech modeling results compared to the current state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we demonstrate that Steady-$\mathcal{M}$ can effectively characterize the clustering of speech segments, where a specific cluster assignment matrix, $m$, is estimated by maximizing the margin between speech features, thus providing improved unsupervised clustering results. We further provide a novel unsupervised speech synthesis approach, Steady-Syn, built on the Steady-$\mathcal{M}$ model, where the posterior distribution, $q(S|X)$, is characterized by the transition to the current speech features, $S$, from the past speech features, $S_-, $given the past audio signal, $X_-. We show that Steady-Syn provides more natural sounding speech with fewer artificial breaks than the current state-of-the-art unsupervised speech synthesis approach

This paper introduces an optimized motion planning system for multi-limbed robots, enabling the calculation of precise trajectories in an under-ackermann model mobile platform environment. It leverages a multi-stage optimization framework, dividing the motion planning process into two distinct stages to analyze under-actuation and limb constraints separately. This stage-by-stage approach enables fast and efficient solving, by converting the original problem into a quadratic programming representation, which is then tackled through a novel multi-stage framework, resulting in a more robust and limb-optimal motion plan. We complement this framework with a filter strategy to eliminate suboptimal trajectory segments and propose a sampling method for optimal starting positions to enhance performance. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of this filter and the efficiency of our multi-stage optimization framework, yielding up to 4.5 times faster solution times compared to standard methods. Our approach utilizes a recently proposed more straightforward protocol for achieving maximally resourceful states, which involves overlapping the state with maximally resourceful pure quantum states. We analyze the trade-offs between the success probability and error thresholds in this process, and distill these findings into compact error probability expressions. By investigating these expressions, we identify key parameters that influence the trade-offs and characterize their relationship in various resource theories. This research investigates the convergence properties of Decentralized Regularized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DR-DSGD), a learning method used to solve convex and nonconvex optimization problems in a fully decentralized setting. By extending existing work, our findings establish the convergence rate of DR-DSGD to achieve $\epsilon$-accuracy, with a convergence rate of $O\left(\log(T)/\sqrt{K} + \Gamma/\sqrt{N} \right)$, where $T$ denotes the iteration number, $K$ represents the knowledge bound, $N$ signifies the number of devices, and $\Gamma$ is a regularization parameter. Furthermore, the obtained result exhibits stronger dependence on $N$ and $\log(T)/\sqrt{K}$ compared to some previously known results. To illustrate the efficacy of our findings, the regularized Allucas-Bach model, a nonconvex optimization problem, is examined as an example. The analysis shows that DR-DSGD achieves $\epsilon$-accuracy with an iteration complexity of $O(\epsilon^{-2}\log(T)/\sqrt{N})$ for nonconvex scenarios. The analysis also reveals that for nonregularized scenarios, DR-DSGD converges to a $(1-\rho)$-neighborhood of the true minimum, with $\rho$ denoting the level of decentralization, and attains an iteration complexity of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{K/\rho} + \sqrt{N}/\log(T))$. Notably, in the nonregularized case, increasing the number of devices $N$ leads to improved convergence, whereas in the regularized case, increasing $N$ has no impact on achieving $\epsilon$-accuracy. However, $N$ must be sufficiently large such that $\Gamma N > 1$. The analysis also illustrates that for the Allucas-Bach model, increasing the regularization parameter $\Gamma$ leads to improved convergence and may even guarantee the existence of stationary points. The analysis further establishes that for the Allucas-Bach model under the condition that its Jacobian matrix is positive definite, regularized decentralized learning achieves the same level of performance as centralized regularized stochastic gradient descent. Moreover, the analysis shows that for non-convex regularized decentralized learning, increasing the number of devices $N$ has no impact on achieving $\epsilon$-accuracy, whereas in the non-regularized case, increasing $N$ has a positive effect. Our current knowledge of the production of charged particles in nucleus-nucleus collisions is primarily based on the assumption that the pre-equilibrium phase maintains quark-gluon plasma (QGP) characteristics. We examine this assumption's validity by calculating the entropy production rate during the pre-equilibrium phase from initial gluon configurations created by high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions. Our pre-equilibrium calculations utilize the gluon saturation model, specifically the GLASQ model, to determine the amplitude of the initial gluon configuration. We find that the pre-equilibrium entropy production significantly depends on the nuclear logarithm and the Weiser-Nauenberg exponent. Our findings in this study may provide fresh insights into the equilibrium state and its precursor, thereby shedding light on the rapid evolution of the QGP from the pre-equilibrium phase. In the process of protostar formation, core mass accretion plays a vital role, which is characterized by two distinct phases: an early phase with rapid growth and a late phase with steady advancement. Our research focuses on modeling the early mass accretion phase, aimed at determining how mass is distributed and released during this process. Using numerical simulations, we examined how mass is transferred and ejected from the core, dependent on the initial mass of the core and surrounding disk structure. Our results indicate that massive disk fragmentation or magnetic field-induced mass ejection occur when the core mass exceeds a specific threshold, typically around one to a few tens of solar masses. In cases where the core mass is below this threshold, our models show that mass is predominantly fed to the protostar through magnetic flux, with little to no mass being ejected. In contrast, massive disk formation around low-mass stars is observed when the core mass is below a specific threshold, typically a few solar masses. Our research indicates that protostars with masses less than a few solar masses are surrounded by magnetic field-dominated disks, with little to no mass being ejected. This implies that early mass accretion is primarily focused on feeding the protostar, rather than being released or utilized in planetary formation. The study demonstrates that a specific algorithm can calculate the necessary rate adjustments in advance, allowing for timely DEV management and prevention of system failures. The study demonstrates that a well-designed base-case model can serve as a valuable safety management tool for complex systems. The research reveals the critical role of DEVs in limiting system performance and causing failures, underscoring the need for their active management. The proposed mechanism is essential for maintaining system safety in the face of DEST dynamics and DEVs. The research shows that safety management for a system comprising multiple DESTs requires careful analysis of DEVs to ensure reliable safe system exit strategies. The study confirms that corrective actions can be taken proactively to prevent system failures brought on by DEVs. The research has significant practical implications, extending to areas such as the development of safety critical software with a focus on reliability and the identification of quality indicators for safe system operation.

This study examines the magnetic and optical properties of twisted bilayer graphene within the tight-binding framework, focusing on achieving converged results among different approaches. We convert the orbital basis to the Wannier basis to ensure accurate description of the magnetic properties. Then, to rectify the shortcomings of the velocity gauge in capturing optical transitions, we apply a unitary transformation to the Hopfield model. We find that using the Maxwell equation average instead of the diamagnetic current is highly effective in describing the optical spectrum. Furthermore, by selecting key bands in the tight-binding scheme, we are able to obtain the optical spectrum with an accuracy comparable to that from the Dirac equation. We demonstrate that the optical transitions in TLG are characterized by both $\pm\omega$ transitions, resulting in two sets of inter-/intralayer transition energies. Notably, the optical conductivity shows both local and non-local responses, with the latter dominating and exhibiting a shift of charge density with a $\pi$ phase difference between the layers at low energies. Furthermore, the material exhibits both electron and hole carriers, with their ratios influenced by both the twist angle and the non-locality in the charge distribution. We analyze the effects of the non-locality on the carriers by treating the non-local potential as a perturbation, with the result showing that it adds a correction to the energy of the carriers that is a function of the non-locality parameter. We find that the non-local parameter in the charge distribution has a cut-off at a value of approximately 10% of the energy gap, with the non-locality in the charge distribution potentially impacting the transport in TLG and affecting the operation of electronic devices utilising photon-electron interactions. Additionally, the material exhibits both positive and negative circular dichroism in the absorption cross-section, with the magnitude of the effect increasing as the twist angle decreases and reaching a maximum at angles where the energy gap varies linearly with the angle. Our approach provides a versatile tool to design and study photonic devices and applications utilizing TLG, with the option to switch between velocity and length gauges through unitary transformations. This paper presents a robust framework for predicting the shape and appearance of an object from a single image. We approach this problem by formulating it as an energy-minimization problem within a graph-theoretic framework, allowing for the simultaneous calculation of the object's 2D/3D position, shape, and appearance features. To counter the influence of misleading data, our framework incorporates constraints on the changes to these features, weakening the impact of outliers through gradual adjustment. Upon initializing the object's features, we simulate possible changes, assess the impact of each modification, and adjust the energy function accordingly. We develop multiple message-passing algorithms for solving the problem, and evaluate the approach using real-world data from both synthetic and real experiments. The energy function is minimized using Belief Propagation, and we introduce a novel and efficient algorithm for estimating the object's 3D position. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches using robust optimization, with considerable improvements in both shape and appearance feature accuracy. The research benefits from recent advancements in graph optimization and feature estimation within computer vision. A comprehensive analysis of our method's efficiency shows promising prospects for real-time implementation on modern computers. This work establishes formulas for the maximum likelihood estimators of the parameters of a Cauchy distribution, given paired data observations. The distributions of these estimators are determined, leading to the derivation of a confidence region for the parameters. This confidence region is geometrically represented as a closed curve in the complex plane and is expressed in terms of an elliptical curve equation, using the estimators' variables. The confidence region's shape depends on the estimators' distributions being a 50/30 probability mix between a Cauchy and a 2D non-normal distribution, which can be approximated as a mixture of a normal and a Laplace distribution, both centered at the estimators' mean. Consequently, a confidence interval for a Cauchy distribution's parameters can be obtained by applying a transformation to the elliptical confidence region. The proposed methods are validated through numerical simulations, which include a study of the asymptotic behavior as the sample size converges to 100. Finally, the methods are applied to analyze paired data sets, resulting in the determination of a Cauchy distribution's parameters' confidence intervals. The entire analysis is supported with relevant code, provided in an online repository. We examine the essence of the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of a group and its interconnections with other group properties. Specifically, we explore how it relates to $R_\infty$-nilpotent groups, abelian groups, and their subgroups, as well as examine its connection to the length of group presentations. Furthermore, we consider the upper limits on this degree for particular groups of interest. Additionally, we introduce a new concept, $\mathscr{R}_\infty$-nilpotent groups, and establish the correspondence between $R_\infty$-nilpotent groups and those with this new property. Finally, we discuss the advantages and limitations of our nilpotency degree approach compared to others in the literature. This work partially stems from an undergraduate thesis. Our computations are largely accessible to and understandable by second-year mathematics students. This study aims to contribute to the existing literature on group properties and nilpotency, as well as the broader extremist functors in homological algebra, which we do not directly address in this work. \\

A significant portion of our study focuses on defining the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of a group and its two natural relaxations, as well as establishing its relationship with equivalent nilpotent degrees introduced by F. Benardete. We prove that for any group, the upper bound of this degree does not exceed its corresponding nilpotent degree by F. Benardete. We demonstrate that $R_\infty$-nilpotent groups are equivalent to those with the new property $\mathscr{R}_\infty$-nilpotent groups and that the former includes abelian groups, whereas the latter exclusively consists of abelian groups with commutative commutators. We find upper and lower limits on the $R_\ininfty$-nilpotency degree of particular groups like finite groups, symmetric groups, and non-nilpotent metacyclic groups. Moreover, we establish connections between this degree and the length of group presentations, examine the properties of the functors $R^nG$ for groups $G$, and explore upper bounds on the nilpotency degree of subgroups. Furthermore, we introduce an invariant notion to measure the nilpotency degree of groups with divided powers and demonstrate its correlation with nilpotent degrees introduced by F. Benardete. \\

A small prototype e+e- collider or a muon collider can play a crucial role in fine-tuning the top quark mass measurement through precise experimental analysis of top quark production at a near-threshold, low-energy state. This can be achieved by utilizing advanced theoretical models that account for the presence of a large spin-orbit coupling term, amounting to about 100 MeV. According to simulations, a few inverse femtobarns of integrated luminosity at a 1.85 GeV center-of-mass energy can provide a mass measurement with an uncertainty of approximately 20 MeV, complementing existing measurements from the LHC with an additional precision of 15 MeV. This ambitious project may face financial challenges but its scientific return would be substantial, making it a viable option to consider. Additionally, this research may also profit from advancements in theoretical calculations for exclusive double muon production in muon colliders, leading to an even more precise top quark mass measurement of 10 MeV. This study's findings on the role of the spin-orbit coupling term in top quark production could also profit from future experiments at J/ψ and ψ(2S) energy levels. This paper introduces CySGAN, a pioneering Segmentation GAN model that surpasses the performance of cutting-edge instance segmentation methods. CySGAN operates by converting the segmentation task into a nonlinear mapping between image features and semantic labels, leveraging two separate networks to achieve this mapping accurately. In contrast to conventional segmentation approaches that rely on category-specific masks, CySGAN utilizes a unified framework to tackle multiple categories simultaneously. Furthermore, CySGAN optimizes object detection accuracy by incorporating spatial alignment and weak supervision, effectively addressing the challenge of segmenting intricate objects within images. In our experiments, CySGAN demonstrated superior performance on the COCO benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art models by a significant margin. Specifically, CySGAN achieved impressive mAP scores of 45.47% and 43.85% for bounding box and mask AP, respectively, highlighting its remarkable efficacy. Our code has been publicly released on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ChenMiszyo/CySGAN. In addition, the project has been documented in a Jupyter Notebook, accessible at https://huggingface.space/CySGAN. If you experience any issues during replication, please refer to the repository README file for guidance. Ultimately, CySGAN embodies a novel and effective approach to instance segmentation, broadening the scope of GAN-based solutions and paving the way for further exploration of nonlinear segmentation transformations. Nonetheless, its application remains restricted to a single image at a time, necessitating the integration of a segmentation detector to function effectively in real-world applications. As a result, CySGAN's performance is contingent upon the quality of the input image features, which significantly undermines its overall performance. In an effort to mitigate this limitation, we investigated an alternative strategy involving coarse-to-fine segmentation using a mixed pixel map, a technique renowned for its robustness to various image conditions. In this variant, the CySGAN model is modified to operate on a pixel-wise basis, producing a segmentation GAN for multiple categories on a pixel-wise basis. In our experiments, this approach yielded compelling results, with a substantial +4.2% mAP improvement on the COCO benchmark. Notably, this technique is versatile and effective across various image conditions, underscoring its significance as a benchmark reference for semantic segmentation tasks. Our findings suggest that non-linear segmentation transformations using coarse image features can serve as a strong baseline for semantic segmentation tasks. Our analysis focuses on the far-ultraviolet and optical characteristics of the young star, PPI, which is known for generating extremely powerful solar flares in the H$\alpha$ and FUV regions. By utilizing fast spectroscopic observations obtained with the TESS satellite, we gathered spectra during three periods including one normal state and two intense flaring states. For the first time, we've discovered significant broadening of major hydrogen lines (like H$\alpha$, H$\beta$, and Lyman-$\alpha$) in relation to the star's increasing FUV emission. Notably, the observed line broadening in PPI is more pronounced than in the example solar flares provided by NY Dra, with a correlation observed between line broadening and energy output in both objects. Moreover, our study has revealed the presence of magnetohydrodynamic waves in the post-flare phase of PPI's spectra, with an observation of Balmer line asymmetry for the first time in stellar flares, replicating the findings from the solar flares of e.g. GJ 667.CC and RE J0555.89, with a distinction being noted in the line broadening and asymmetry features of PPI's H$\alpha$ and FUV Lyman-$\alpha$ emission lines, indicating distinct physical causes. The combination of these magnetohydrodynamic wave emissions and increased turbulence is considered to contribute to the broad hydrogen line emission, particularly in the case of the Lyman-$\alpha$ line. Building upon previous studies of (e.g. WW Vul, EI Eri, and RE J0444.85), our research has shown that hydrogen line broadening and asymmetry can serve as valuable indicators for assessing the magnetohydrodynamic wave activity during stellar flares. PPI's far-ultraviolet and optical spectral features offer examples of novel aspects to explore in the field of stellar flares, with implications for further research in this area, as well as the need for fast spectroscopic observations of future space missions like PLATO and SKYMAPPER to investigate the physical processes behind massive stellar flares. Based on their luminosity and proximity, it's anticipated that PPI and its counterparts could be among the targets for these missions to study stellar flares at an unprecedented level of detail. For example, detecting the magnetohydrodynamic wave activity during massive stellar flares could significantly improve our comprehension of these events through future fast spectroscopic observations of medium and bright stars exhibiting large H$\alpha$ and FUV emission fluctuations. We develop a concept for metric positivity on the parabolic invariant locus of $G_2$-instantons, and show that abelian $G_2$-instantons are rigid by proving this space is a point. Building on Chern-Simons theory, our approach relies on the unique properties of the gauge orbit within the invariant locus. The method also allows for a direct calculation of the index of the linearized operator of the $G_2$-instanton equation, which confirms an existing conjecture by Lovric and Müller. Additionally, our findings contribute to understanding the rigidity of abelian solutions in superpotentials of M-theory on $G_2$-manifolds. Lastly, mathematical generalizations relevant to monopoles and $M$-theoretic techniques are explored.

This difference is found to be a positive, $F_{p'p}$-core function, which can be expressed in terms of Eulerian numbers by investigating the inverse $\hat{F}_{p'p}(n)$, which equals the count of $U_{p'p}$-unpartitions of $n$. By examining both the ordinary and weight versions of this discrepancy, we establish various core partition formulas, some of which were previously conjectured. Additionally, this discrepancy reveals a surprising connection to modular arithmetic, leading us to define and study a related function, especially in the case of $p=2$. This generalized discrepancy may be expressed as a modular flow, which can be interpreted as the count of $(M_{p'p}(n))^{-1}$-partitions of $n$. This discovery leads to further analysis, including identification of the inverse of $M_{11}(n)$ and $M_{13}(n)$. Finally, this paper explores analogues of the Hilbert-Polya conjecture in relation to $F_{p'p}$, $\hat{F}_{p'p}$, $U_{p'p}$, and $M_{p'p}$. These analogues can be proven for $p=2$, but remain open for other prime $p$. If the Hilbert-Polya conjecture holds, it would imply that the generalized discrepancy is consistently $0$; this, however, is demonstrated to be impossible. Consequently, the discrepancy gives rise to an infinite family of counterexamples to the Hilbert-Polya conjecture. Additionally, this paper identifies further families of counterexamples, one comprising triangular numbers and another consisting of $F_{p'p}$-core partitions with largest $p$-core that have a specific shape and are counted by a $q$-analog of the formula for the number of partitions of $n$ into $p$ parts, each of which is either equal to $1$ or $p$. Recent advancements in geometric deep learning have led to the creation of point cloud models, but they lack stability against common real-world conditions like rotation and translation. Our proposed TPC framework provides precise guarantees for point cloud transformations, enhancing model stability and adaptability. In contrast to existing approaches, TPC incorporates a Siamese network to certify point cloud similarities, using a nested polytope enclosure method to increase efficiency. Our framework also provides a query complexity of $O(\kappa^{-2}\log^2M)$, where $\kappa$ is the confidence parameter and $M$ is the number of point clouds. By substituting the polytope enclosure with a convex hull of spheres, we achieved a significant reduction in query complexity to $O(\kappa^{-2}M^{2/3}\log^{2/3}M)$. In experiments with CPNet, our framework increased certified accuracy by 5.3% compared to existing polytope enclosure methods and allowed for a 2x increase in training data points. Furthermore, our framework enhanced the verified accuracy of PCD-Net by 10.6% and decreased the verification time by 30.8%. Like existing polytope enclosure techniques, our framework can be applied to other deep geometric models for enhanced robustness and generalizability. Our TPC framework's sources and accompanying polytope enclosure library are available on GitHub at https://github.com/floretmap/TPC. Our certified model can be accessed via an online verification interface at https://floretmap.github.io/TPC-Visualizer. Our results indicate that precise and efficient polytope enclosure techniques can significantly enhance the robustness and adaptability of point cloud models. At the same time, we observed that the currently available deep geometric models are limited by their inability to handle continuous and seamless transformations. Therefore, we propose the development of a new class of point cloud models, referred to as $PC^2$ models, that can smoothly transform under twisting transformations and maintain consistent output across these transformations. Our study on these $PC^2$ models demonstrates a significant increase in certified accuracy of 11.4% and verified accuracy of 14.2% compared to CPNet, with potential applications in various domains, such as robotics and computer vision, where smooth and continuous transformations are inherent in the underlying geometry. Our analysis also reveals that the known deep geometric models fail to achieve this level of smooth transformability and suggests the need for a new research direction in the development of these models

This paper explores the design of Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks, addressing the challenges associated with medium access through analysis of a single FMCW radar access channel. By developing an analytical framework for a random access FMCW radar network, we examine how packet formats, system parameters, and channel conditions affect the medium, with specific focus on the impact of chirps per packet, data rate, and signal-to-noise ratio on packet interference, system utilization, and network throughput. This paper ultimately provides guidelines for optimizing FMCW radar parameters to balance high throughput with low interference probabilities. Our findings are further validated through Simulations, with results demonstrating the effectiveness of this analytical approach in guiding FMCW radar design. This research identifies key design trade-offs for FMCW radar systems, including the relationship between system utilization and packet length, as well as the influence of data rate and SNR on interference probabilities, with simultaneous optimization yielding significant throughput enhancements while maintaining acceptable levels of packet interference. With increasing chirps per packet, both high throughput and low interference probabilities are achieved but come at the cost of prolonged system duration. Conversely, lowering the number of chirps per packet reduces system duration, with lower throughput and increased interference probabilities, although simultaneous optimization reveals that a low chirps per packet value can yield acceptable throughput and near-zero interference probabilities. Furthermore, increasing the FMCW data rate reduces both system utilization and interference probabilities, with nearly-linear relationships observed in high SNR conditions. Conversely, rising SNR conditions lead to decreased system utilization and interference probabilities, with nearly-linear composites observed. On the other hand, increasing radar pulse bandwidth decreases system utilization and interference probabilities, with nearly-linear composites observed in high SNR conditions. Additionally, rising SNR conditions lead to decreased system utilization and interference probabilities, with nearly-linear relationships observed. Notably, optimizing FMCW parameters in conjunction with data rate and SNR results in substantial throughput enhancements and near-zero interference probabilities. Overall, this research indicates that a limited FMCW parameter range yields optimal performance, with potential applications extending to other radar systems. This study further suggests that a random access FMCW radar network with multiple radar nodes, incorporating principles of node density, system duration, and interference, requires a more intricate analytical framework than a single FMCW radar access channel, posing additional challenges to medium access design. As such, this research is confined to a single FMCW radar access channel, with future work envisioned for multi-node random access FMCW radar networks.

By using a quantum scattering approach, we've calculated the probability of detecting paired photons after interacting with the material, and also determined the probability of detecting single photons. This allowed us to derive a formula for visibility that is linked to the quantum characteristic of double-slit interference. Notably, our findings align with an experiment's results, and offer insights into how to enhance visibility through adjustments to beam splitters' transmission probabilities. Additionally, we've developed a method to differentiate entangled two-photon absorption from regular two-photon absorption, and tested this approach using our visibility formula. Since our model starts from a fundamental principle and doesn't have any unknown parameters, it provides a useful tool for understanding the phenomenon and guiding future experiments. Ultimately, as visibility approaches 100%, our model indicates that the primary obstacle to detecting entangled two-photon absorption is likely the broad energy spectra of single photons. Therefore, by improving the selectivity of detectors to photon energies, it may be possible to surpass the current visibility record of 90% and firmly establish the phenomenon as a genuine manifestation of entangled two-photon absorption. Furthermore, our model highlights that selectivity could be enhanced by using lasers with even narrower spectral widths, and suggests that detection techniques involving grating structures could be particularly effective. Additionally, we've found that the phenomenon of entangled two-photon absorption is linked to the phenomenon of quantum engagement in nonlinear materials, and has the potential to be harnessed in order to reduce energy losses during absorption through alignment with the material's dispersive structure. This paper addresses the issue of temporal knowledge graph completion using a novel approach called cycle-aware time-encoding, which takes into account the cyclical nature of time. The method encompasses two key components: initially, a cycle discovery method identifies cycles within the knowledge graph and assigns appropriate time encodings; secondly, a time-encoding aggregation operation determines the most suitable time representation for each statement in the graph. Notably, our approach focuses exclusively on cycles containing a single time-sensitive statement - the one that needs to be predicted. The proposed method strives to enhance the quality of time-related knowledge by leveraging cycle structures found in the graph. Experimental evaluations using four diverse datasets demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art techniques, yielding up to a 7.5% improvement in ranking-based metrics. Further analysis reveals that our method successfully "learns from cycles" by identifying the most informative time encodings for each statement, thus enhancing the quality of time-related knowledge in the graph. The associated code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/jayjayng/CycleAware-Time-Encoding. Knowledge graph completion methodologies have seen significant advancement over time and their applications extend to areas such as natural language processing, semantic search, and data augmentation for deep learning models. The area of temporal knowledge graph completion (tKGC) is a notable sub-category that focuses on determining missing time-related attributes in knowledge graphs. Existing tKGC methodologies have achieved notable success but their efficiency is often hindered by the lack of adequate time-related structures in the graph - specifically, cycles containing time-sensitive statements that need to be predicted. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a novel approach called cycle-aware time-encoding to enhance the quality of time-related knowledge in the graph. Our research focuses on the effects of randomness in systems with non-Abelian symmetry, specifically in the Majorana chain, by examining how it alters the degeneracy of the flat bands and their critical points. Our findings demonstrate that the degeneracy of the flat bands in the Majorana circuit model is determined by the number of critical points and that randomized systems exhibit multiple critical points. Our theoretical model, the randomized Majorana circuit model, is distinct from the existing random bond Majorana circuit model and shares similarities with the random orbitals model. Our research shows that the degeneracy of the flat bands in the random orbitals model is reduced by the number of disorder configurations and that the randomized Majorana circuit model exhibits band splitting at the critical points. Our methods for determining the critical points involve analyzing the nearest neighbor correlation functions and the second central moments of the Wigner distribution. In the development of automotive driving systems, crucial safety assessments are carried out using formal verification techniques like model checking to evaluate whether system failures can be avoided. However, driving systems involving human input cannot be thoroughly analyzed through formal means due to the inherent unpredictability of human behavior. Therefore, safety assessments relying on formal verification methods in such systems are limited to certain parts, like basic control systems, whereas the remaining portions, like active safety features, are evaluated using simulation-based approaches that lack formal assurance. This paper introduces an innovative method to combine formal verification and simulation-based testing, yielding stronger validation of safety assessments for the entire system. The proposed method leverages learning algorithms from machine learning to create transitional models for system components, which are then checked against specified safety constraints using formal verification techniques. This allows for the coverage of complex system components, like active safety features, and provides enhanced formal assurance. The proposed approach was evaluated on a realistic case study involving a vehicle adaptive cruise control system, and the results indicate that it surpasses conventional simulation-based testing with formal verification. The integration of this method with existing formal verification tools for model checking produces an efficient and scalable solution. The proposed strategy is versatile and can be applied to various systems, as demonstrated by an evaluation of its applicability to two distinct automotive systems. Finally, the method was successfully implemented and confirmed to work on real-world systems through practical experiments involving an open-source formal verification tool for model checking. Although Leibniz's work on infinity is widely recognized, its actual meaning and impact are debated. Two possible interpretations - one that sees infinity as a conceptually bounded idea and another that views it as inherently unbounded - have been proposed. However, earlier scholars who shared Leibniz's views often misunderstood the nature of infinity. This study examines two specific scholars, Bernoulli and Clarke, to illustrate the varying ways infinity was conceptualized. Clarke saw infinity as a logically bounded notion, whereas Bernoulli used it as a metaphor for unbounded sequences and phenomena. Clarke's perspective aligns more closely with Leibniz's original intent, but Bernoulli's became influential in the development of the concept of mathematical infinity. This study reveals that the complex nature of infinity was not yet fully grasped even by those closest to Leibniz's ideas. Conversely, Clarke's work represents a more accurate reflection of Leibniz's innovation in treating infinity as a fundamental philosophical concept. This discovery highlights the challenges and nuances of transmitting innovative ideas through time. Furthermore, this study examines the varying uses of infinity among the scholars in question and explores their respective arguments to determine whether they successfully addressed the issues at hand. Lastly, this study points to the crucial role Clarke's Correspondence played in consolidating Leibniz's original contributions. In contrast, Bernoulli's correspondence, although extensive, failed to achieve this effect, instead focusing on presenting his own viewpoints. This study shows how Clarke's Response Correspondence served as a turning point, as it led to the solidification of Leibniz's legacy and marked a key point in the development of the Correspondence genre. In contrast, Bernoulli's correspondence, although considerable, did not have this effect, instead highlighting his correspondence as a rare example of a double-response correspondence where the participant, Clarke, chooses to respond not to a single counterpart but to two correspondents, each representing different perspectives. In order to optimize the GRAVITY detector's operational efficiency, it is essential to rapidly obtain these stabilization parameters in a limited number of measurements. In this research paper, we examine the statistical behavior of the stabilization parameters as well as the success rate of the GRAVITY detector and its detection time, utilizing a statistical approach to analyze and improve filter pattern settings. By applying an optimized filtering strategy, we were able to reduce the GRAVITY detector's operational time from 13 milliseconds to 5.4 milliseconds on a single science detector frame. This improvement is particularly significant, given that the GRAVITY instrument is now ready to observe at a much faster rate of 5.4 milliseconds. This advancement has the potential to significantly extend the lifetime of the GRAVITY instrument on the VLTI, which was previously limited to 6 months but can now operate for at least 2 years. In this paper, we outline the detailed statistical analysis of the GRAVITY detector and provide a publicly accessible Python code to facilitate future data analysis and parameter optimization. Furthermore, we propose two potential and efficient algorithms to rapidly determine the stabilization parameters, which can significantly reduce the GRAVITY detector's operational time to 2.4 milliseconds. This efficient timing will enable the GRAVITY instrument to accurately monitor the gravity field of gravitational sources at a much faster rate in the next observation run at Paranal. Additionally, we explore the possibility of further reducing the GRAVITY detector operational time to 1.3 milliseconds by utilizing all four filter patterns captured by the acquisition camera to determine the stabilization parameters at a much faster rate in future data analysis. This efficient timing will enable the GRAVITY instrument to accurately monitor the gravity field of gravitational sources across the entire VLTI field of view at a much faster rate in the next observation run at Paranal. We explore the approximate solvability of hard combinatorial optimization issues by examining a group of supplier location problems that involve selecting a subset of suppliers to minimize total service costs and meet demand requirements. The Capacitated k-Center problem, which seeks the smallest set of suppliers to serve the top k% of demanding customers, is particularly challenging and has proven to be computationally intractable when considering multiple suppliers per customer. In contrast, the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem, which allows a limited number of suppliers with some customers going without service, offers more flexibility and is thus relatively easier to approximate. The key difference lies in the issues' "highway dimension," which measures the cost of deviations from optimal solutions; according to our findings, this metric restricts the applicability of simple approximation algorithms for the Capacitated k-Center problem, whereas we can design more complex algorithms with stricter limitations on suboptimality. Furthermore, we have discovered an interesting linear programming relaxation feature: all feasible solutions to the relaxed problem have a minimal number of active supplier-customer pairs. These findings provide valuable insights into the nature of hard optimization problems and the complex relationships between similar problems. Additionally, we have proposed and tested approximation algorithms for the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers and the k-Medians problem with outliers, achieving ratios of 40 and 20, respectively, to the optimal costs involving no outliers; in comparison, we have established lower bounds of 20 and 14 for these problems, respectively. Furthermore, we have proved that no algorithm can solve the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers with a ratio smaller than 28, and the k-Medians problem with outliers ratio smaller than 17, under certain conditions. We have also analyzed variant problems allowing multiple suppliers per customer and established approximate algorithms and lower bounds for these issues. Lastly, we have examined an application involving the representative location problem in a scenario involving single-demand customers and demonstrated the difficulty of solving this problem approximatively under certain restrictions. In contrast, we have designed an efficient approximation algorithm with a ratio of 20 to the optimal costs involving no restrictions. Additionally, we have established a lower bound of 15 for this problem, assuming additional constraints. In the absence of these constraints, we have proved that no algorithm can solve the representative location problem with an approximation ratio smaller than 13, and 11, under two different sets of relaxable constraints. You can find the complete details in our research paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.

When a suitable coherent light source is present, it generates a highly intense binding force between the photon emitted by the first atom and the one emitted by the second, resulting in the creation of correlated parity states of the emitted photons. A novel equation of state (EOS) is developed specifically for alkali metals, utilizing a simplified Mayer-Sauerborn model, which incorporates a unified treatment of vibrational and entropy contributions suitable for the entire range of temperatures and densities found in natural settings. This EOS is utilized to analyze eosinomal temperatures and phase transition pressures for the elements lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, and caesium across various densities. Furthermore, the researched EOS is validated against experimental data from density measurements on rubidium and potassium via comparison with results obtained using the PRISMS software. This comparison reveals satisfactory agreement between theoretical and experimental data for rubidium, extending up to a density of approximately 3.8 g/cm³. However, the PRISMS results yield higher phase transition pressures and eosinomal temperatures for potassium than the experimental measurements. Additionally, the researched EOS is used to investigate how the elements' properties behave under the principle of corresponding states. Based on the eosinomal temperatures and critical constants calculated using the Meyer-Peter-Franck criterion, this principle is found to be satisfied for sodium, potassium, rubidium, and caesium up to a density of approximately 4.5 g/cm³, providing the basis for a universally applicable equation of state for these elements below this limit. The characteristics of vector mesons in a local parity violation environment, described by an inverse curvature gauge theory with Chern-Simons term, are investigated using a quasi-classical approximation with modified Boltzmann equations. By leveraging a specific U(1) Nambu-Goto type action for the vector potential, the integral over the collective coordinate can be resolved explicitly. Consequently, the quasi-classical equations of motion with source terms are derived, yielding source-dependent equations of motion for the complex-valued scalar associated with the vector meson. A specific caustic integration technique is employed to analyze the scalar distribution in the longitudinal space, resulting in two distinct distribution patterns obtained for right- and left-handed vector mesons. Our findings demonstrate that the latter exhibits two localized peaks, whereas the former displays a single peak. Furthermore, our theoretical framework allows us to examine the ratio of two vector mesons in a parity broken plasma and, potentially, detect signs of local parity breaking via future collider experiments. Moreover, our research can also be extended to include finite temperature and chemical potential conditions. Lastly, our formalism can be applied to vector-like particles, such as D-mesons and lepton leptons. A notable extension of our research is the incorporation of local parity breaking into the framework of conformal field theories. Conversely, our theoretical framework can be used to explore caustic integration within the context of Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity through a variational action of a string worldsheet. Additionally, our research has been further generalized to gravity's quasiclassical regime and even cosmological quasiclassical scenarios. Furthermore, our results have been found to be consistent with existing literature in various physical contexts. Lastly, our research has been found to have relevant applications in the following fields: condensed matter physics, atomic physics, string theory, Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity and cosmology. Some of these applications are still in the process of being explored. For example, we have not yet determined whether our formulation of the Cauchy stress tensor can be used to describe experimental observations in condensed matter and atomic physics. In this paper, we introduce a randomized distributed algorithm that enables accurate measurement of network node counts, including switches and routers, within a distributed system. By utilizing individual nodes' measurement capabilities, we develop an efficient method to estimate the network topology, focusing on irregular topologies with no assumed structure or regularity. We test the proposed algorithm on various irregular networks and evaluate its performance under different distribution types of network nodes. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of measurement errors on the accuracy of our estimate. We demonstrate that a limited number of measurements from each node suffices to achieve precise count estimates with high confidence, even in the presence of substantial measurement errors. We explore ways to enhance the proposed algorithm's robustness and study its application in symmetric topologies. Additionally, we consider extensions to address potential challenges and limitations of the algorithm. We complement our analytical findings with numerical simulations to illustrate the performance of the algorithm across diverse network configurations. Our work presents an alternative approach for network size estimation compared to established methods that rely on centralized collection and efficient sparse graphs. We discuss this new approach and potential improvements for future work. We also consider an extension to estimate the network diameter by building on the network topology obtained through our proposed algorithm. By combining our results, we present a streamlined process for network management and maintenance. We further investigate the replication factors, active nodes, and resource allocation in the network to deepen our understanding of distributed system architecture. By analyzing the network topology, we identify potential performance enhancements and illustrate poor system design examples. We discuss the feasibility of manually determining an efficient network structure and present an alternative, efficient algorithmic approach to optimize the system configuration. We conclude our paper by highlighting key research areas and challenges in the field of distributed system management. These areas not only require resolution of existing problems but also offer numerous opportunities for further research and development. To facilitate future work, we provide an overview of the existing literature in the field, emphasizing the distinct contributions of our proposed algorithm. This method differs from conventional strategies that utilize the minimum action principle to determine the conformal factor. Instead, our scheme utilizes the predictive power of the theory to establish the conformal factor as a function of the initial data. This new idea emerges from a broader framework of modified Einstein gravity with a potential gauge invariance. We demonstrate that, despite variations in the original theory, the conformal factor remains a function of the initial data rather than an arbitrary function. Furthermore, our approach builds upon this broader theory to reveal that the conformal factor is necessarily tied to the mean curvature of the 3D spatial section. This relationship gives rise to a nonlinear system of equations that mimics the constraints of modified Einstein gravity, allowing for the solution of the Hamiltonian constraint. This method may serve as an efficient alternative to outgoing wave conditions or other strategies that directly impose resonant conditions on the spatial section. Additionally, our approach opens up the possibility that the desired physical solution may resonate at specific frequencies, a notion that could be applicable to broad classes of gravitational systems. The Informer model has recently demonstrated exceptional performance in large-scale time series forecasting, but it is primarily designed to handle sequential data and may struggle with multidimensional time series. In this research, we introduce an enhanced Informer framework that can effectively handle complex time series data with multiple dimensions. Our model incorporates a novel informer encoder that leverages attention mechanisms to capture inter-dimensional relationships and incorporates positional encoding to effectively handle multi-dimensional sequential data. Our experimental evaluations reveal that the proposed framework not only surpasses the basic Informer model but also outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in multidimensional time series forecasting. Furthermore, our results show that the model is highly efficient, with a low computational cost of $O(KN_\text{head})$, making it suitable for large-scale time series forecasting even with a large number of heads. Our source code can be accessed at https://github.com/jay-jin/Informer-EA. JellyFish is used to create the plot in this paper, which can be found at https://jellyfishlib.github.io/.

This research presents a novel atmospheric dispersion correction system's prototype, which incorporates a four-lens design configured in a Stonehenge pattern, responding to multiple wavelengths. We evaluate its performance using the atmospheric dispersion models of Swindell and Reddish, which demonstrate that the proposed system effectively corrects dispersion across various spectral ranges. Nevertheless, the atmospheric dispersion model proposed by Swindell appears more suitable, particularly in the blue portion of the spectrum. Furthermore, the work outlines a feasible approach to implementing an adaptive optics system, which would enhance the performance of ADC systems by collecting near-field images of a star and utilizing these images to identify and compensate for atmospheric distortions through a deformable mirror. We explore the effectiveness of a fully adaptive system, as well as a system where only one of the lenses is adapted, which is found to still operate within acceptable limits. A comparison of the various models is presented in terms of their Strehl ratio, pointing towards an enhancement of the ADC system's performance by at least 1.5 times through the adoption of an adaptive optics system. We also examine methods for integrating an ADC system with an adaptive optics system, which involves adjusting the wavefront propagation equation and utilizing the point spread function (PSF) of the system to identify the optimal ADC lens positions and their corresponding distances. Notably, it is observed that the adoption of an adaptive optics system allows for the use of a wider range of Lancaster parameters. We investigate the feasibility of integrating an ADC system with a ground-based fast phasor vertex telescope (FPV), which is found to be challenging due to FPV's fast sampling rate and its inability to accommodate a larger Schlemm radius. As a result, it is concluded that a fast phasor vertex telescope cannot effectively utilize atmospheric dispersion correction. Finally, we investigate the potential of incorporating an ADC system into a liquid mirror telescope, utilizing a Schlemm radius that varies based on the wavelength, and by optimizing the lens positions, we are able to achieve a Strehl ratio of approximately 0.80 across the 350-450 nm spectral range. We verify through simulations that an ADC system can be effectively utilized with a liquid mirror telescope by sampling 5-7 points across the focal plane, which is found to be a more efficient approach compared to sampling the entire focal plane. We introduce Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), an innovative semi-supervised learning technique that iteratively expands label usage to maximize entropy in the prediction space, even with just two labeled samples, by performing pairwise label comparisons. PILE is a versatile method that can be applied to various models, including deep neural networks, and handles multiple label types efficiently. By iteratively maximizing the distance between predicted logits for positive and negative label comparisons, PILE is a robust solver for the semi-supervised learning problem. PILE outperforms state-of-the-art methods on popular benchmarks, such as CIFAR10-SL and real-world data, and its source code is available on GitHub at the URL https://github.com/argentus/LILE._journal_version.html. PILE can also be used as a robust test set validation method by applying it to existing datasets and observing its performance on that dataset's hold-out test data. This is demonstrated on CIFAR10 and can be seen in the results section of this report. PILE can be viewed as an alternative to Label Distribution Learning (LDL) when working with single-label datasets; thus, we present a modified version of PILE that handles single-label datasets, dubbed PILE-SL. Moreover, we propose an unsupervised version of PILE, called dPILE, that removes the need for label information by comparing predicted probabilities from multiple models. The performance of both PILE and its unsupervised variant dPILE surpasses that of state-of-the-art methods on benchmark datasets in terms of accuracy, and can be found in the results section of this report. The theoretical basis for this method, along with additional details including hyperparameter choices, can also be found within that section. Furthermore, the repository includes experimental results for our paper on semi-supervised learning with a reduced labeled sample size, available at https://github.com/argentus/LILE_journal_version.html. We investigated the behavior of the basis pursuit algorithm when the matrix entries follow a normal distribution with varying levels of correlation and non-diagonal covariance structures. Focusing on the basis pursuit problem with sparse solutions, we considered representative examples that demonstrate the impact of distinct spectral distributions on solution sparse representations. Notably, our findings reveal that the properties of the matrix spectrum significantly influence the accuracy and characteristics of the sparse solutions obtained through basis pursuit. In particular, we found that certain spectral patterns can induce a phase transition in basis pursuit solutions, where changes in the matrix spectrum lead to shifts from dense to sparse solutions, or from accurate to inaccurate representations. In addition to theoretical analysis, our research highlights the potential applications of basis pursuit in spectrally structured correlation datasets, using the example of genomic regulation analysis. By applying basis pursuit to correlated transcription factor activity data, we were able to uncover novel patterns in gene expression and identify key regulatory factors. Our results include a list of significant pathways associated with 124 distinct genes, including key drivers such as TRIM9, GFI1, and lncRNA profiles, which together highlight the critical role of 15 transcription factors in regulating these genes. These findings have important implications in understanding the functional mechanisms of genes. Our research on basis pursuit for correlated data sets could be extended to other areas such as imaging, financial analysis, and molecular chemistry by analyzing various examples provided in a companion technical report. Moreover, to validate our theoretical predictions, we developed a rigorous statistical testing approach to evaluate and reproduce the results presented in this research. Our code and associated data are publicly accessible for verification and reproduction purposes. In particular, our research has important extensions in the molecular chemistry domain, where we analyzed the performance of basis pursuit in recovering sparse coefficients from the low-frequency components of a random Pauli correlation matrix, by exploring the distribution of eigenvalues and corresponding geometric decay rates. Our findings indicate the presence of a phase transition at a critical threshold for the condition number of the matrix, where basis pursuit solutions become accurate at or below this threshold, by analyzing the resulting critical phenomena and scaling behaviors. It draws comparisons with existing methods, which often involve calculating gradient-type problem mini-max optimization problems with non-differentiable objectives in the context of adjoint-based gradient calculation. In contrast, our formulation yields a problem with differentiable objectives in a lower-dimensional space, facilitating more efficient computational adjoint gradient-based optimization. A comprehensive set of numerical experiments further demonstrates the robustness and performance of our proposed method. Specifically, it outmatches a commonly used standard approach in the transport literature by achieving more accurate results, particularly for larger error thresholds. A detailed analysis of the observed discrepancies is provided. All the source code and data utilized in this study are available at the specified repository. Furthermore, our method offers a flexible framework that enables the incorporation of various discontinuous Galerkin mesh decomposition methods. It is worthy of note that our formulation is capable of handling vector fields with diverse magnitudes and directions within each element. Lastly, our approach is adaptable to a range of transport scenarios involving diverse source functions and velocities. It possesses robust stability, making it suitable for use in conjunction with the discontinuous Galerkin method. As machine learning models increasingly influence high-stakes decisions, it's essential to address their lack of fairness. This deficiency can originate from various factors, such as biased data and model design. To tackle this challenge, researchers have been introducing new concepts of fairness. This study introduces a unified framework that evaluates the metric's statistical requirements and computational complexity as function of the data partitioning method within federated learning. Findings from this examination can inform the selection of fair learning techniques. Furthermore, this study explores the ethical implications of leveraging differential privacy to ensure fairness. Results indicate that a combination of differential privacy and minimax fairness provides a robust framework, but comes with a trade-off due to an increase in communication complexity. This study also implements the new framework using Nearest Neighbor Search, revealing constraints that impact its performance when data is partitioned horizontally. When data partitioning is complex, simpler metrics like Equality of Odds demonstrate better computational efficiency. This study demonstrates the efficacy of its concepts through extensive experimentation with popular fairness metrics on various datasets. Findings from this study can be applied to actual use cases, as seen in its accompanying case study on face recognition systems. This research introduces a novel class of continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods that expand upon existing discrete-stage versions, enabling accurate solutions for Hamiltonian problems and certain types of stiff problems. By constructing these methods with inherent Hamiltonian structures, they maintain a consistent level of efficiency, regardless of the problem's stiffness, making them versatile for use in various problem settings. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that traditional discrete-stage methods can be reimagined as special cases of the continuous-stage framework, utilizing constant coefficients, and that many well-established methods, such as CKF, DPS, and WKS methods, naturally fit within this continuous-stage paradigm. By exploring this continuous-stage interpretation, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms of traditional methods. Additionally, this study provides a theoretical foundation for developing continuous-stage methods by proposing and analyzing explicit Hamiltonian Fehlberg methods, along with continuous-stage counterparts, providing a significant advancement in the field. Importantly, this research offers a significant innovation in the design of continuous-stage methods by introducing a free variable condition to optimize method performance, allowing for the first time a wide range of efficient, explicit, and stable continuous-stage methods to be developed with three stages, two evaluations, and two free variables per stage. This approach facilitates an extensive exploration within a given problem domain of many suitable methods, often surpassing traditional methods in accuracy and robustness, as exemplified in various numerical examples. Furthermore, this research confirms the superiority of these novel continuous-stage methods over traditional methods in various problem settings, such as Hamiltonian problems, stiff ODEs, and differential algebraic systems. This research introduces an innovative method to accelerate the training of Convolutional and Recurrent Neural Networks by dividing the network into independent modules. Each module is then trained separately using multiple critic modules, which provide gradient estimates based on its own input alone. This local critic training approach enhances training efficiency by minimizing communication overhead between modules. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques in running time and accuracy. Furthermore, we examine the effect of module splitting on the performance of Neural Networks and discover that our method remains efficient even after splitting is implemented at the module level. Additionally, we propose a simplified version of our method that is computationally lighter but still achieves notable speed improvements. This work is inspired by the Distributed Gradient Evaluation network (DGE), a distributed training framework that uses local critics to evaluate gradients in parallel. By integrating our method with DGE, we achieve significant improvements in training time and efficiency. Our research also identifies potential pitfalls in splitting training of Neural Networks and contributes to an understanding of the effectiveness of local critic training. Moreover, we investigate the trade-offs between model efficiency, communication overhead, and accuracy. This study is unique in combining the efficiency of model splitting with local critic training, thereby offering alternative solutions when model splitting is impractical. We conduct extensive experiments on popular image classification benchmarks, as well as benchmark benchmarks for Recurrent Neural Networks, and our method emerges as a speed-up comparator, outperforming existing methods as well as its own variants. Our research is unique in exploring the effectiveness of model splitting for Neural Networks, as well as their potential use in distributed training. To facilitate replication, we provide the code used in this study at: https://github.com/alexrame/Local-Critic-Training. Specifically, the relevant experiments can be accessed via https://github.com/alexrame/Local-Critic-Training/tree/master/local_critic_training. This code is designed to work with the DeepSpeed framework, which can also be accessed at https://deepspeed.ai/. Additionally, the experiment configurations used in this study can be found at https://github.com/alexrame/Local-Critic-Training/tree/master/local_critic_training/experiments. The muon's magnetic anomaly, denoted as $a_\mu$, is investigated in this study with a new generation precision ring magnet system at the CLIC site, utility tunnel 2 at CERN. A muon beam is introduced at the entrance of the precision ring and analyzed using beam monitoring methods. Given the significance of $a_\mu$ in particle physics, this research aims to determine the feasibility of utilising the precision ring at CLIC as a future experiment, referred to as R&A Ring, to examine the associated parameter space linked to the observed $a_\mu$ anomaly. Primary considerations for this experiment involve optimising the muon beam's characteristics, tracking accuracy, and implementation costs. Alternative designs for the precision ring are evaluated to minimize costs without compromising performance. Furthermore, this study explores the potential for utilising existing CLIC facilities and discusses necessary upgrades for the implementation of R&A Ring. Finally, this study discusses potential challenges and future development pathways for pursuing this groundbreaking experiment. Based on the investigation results, this study recommends conducting a more in-depth study to further establish the case for R&A Ring as a future experiment. This will involve reviewing the muon beam generation method's impact on background radiation and investigating Muon Collider's compatibility with the CLIC site's utility tunnels. Ultimately, this study aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion on the future of precision physics at the CLIC site by introducing a new case to evaluate. Hmmm-Captioning, a challenging task in computer vision, entails generating a video caption by precisely pinpointing key objects and their interactive relationships. Prior methods often utilize recurrent neural networks, attention mechanisms, and visual cognition models to analyze video content, however their effectiveness is limited due to over-reliance on general representations, overlooking crucial details in the process. Our proposed solution, HAN, leverages a hierarchical attention network that deciphers the temporal structure within video data by focusing on distinct spatial areas across multiple frames, thus tracing the movement of objects through the composition of multiple steps of temporal attention. To further enhance accuracy, we introduced Multi-FGME, a novel evaluation metric that assigns higher weights to smaller objects based on area proportion, ultimately leading to a substantial 15.1% and 13.6% improvements in our experiments using METEOR and BLEU-4 metrics, respectively. Our results demonstrate that HAN with MFGE outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, specifically on VidCap, with a substantial 41.2% and 35.2% improvements under METEOR and BLEU-4 metrics, solidifying its position as a top performer. A thorough qualitative analysis reveals that our model's unique spatial-temporal attention mechanism, combined with MFGE, allows for more accurate detection and tracking of objects at diverse scales, resulting in more comprehensive and precise video captions. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Qianhewang/HAN. HAN with MFGE can be directly applied to other video datasets, such as VideoParse@TRECVID, by substituting the corresponding annotation structure. With continued advancements in video data collection and processing, we anticipate HAN with MFGE to remain compatible with future large-scale datasets, potentially unlocking new possibilities for advanced video analysis. Ultimately, our model's hierarchical attention mechanism presents a promising approach for tackling detection and tracking challenges in video content representation. This methodology can be adapted and refined to process other type of temporal data, such as audio, by modifying the network structure accordingly. Furthermore, our multi-objective optimization technique can be integrated into various video processing methods to improve accuracy in specific applications. For instance, integrating our method with video parse on TRECVID would likely yield better results, exceeding the current state-of-the-art performance. In conclusion, our research highlights the significance of accurately capturing object movements across video content through hierarchical attention mechanisms, accompanied by suitable evaluation metrics, to achieve top-notch performance in captioning tasks. In cases where the underlying probability distribution is not directly known, 
its entropy cannot be calculated in a straightforward manner. Even if the distribution
is known but has an infinitely large support, standard entropy computation methods can
overestimate the result or fail to converge. This paper introduces a new framework combining
Markov chains and piecewise arithmetic functions to accurately estimate entropies in such scenarios. 
The proposed arithmetic Markov chain method determines the distribution's dominant features 
or "faces" and utilizes them to minimize estimation error. The study includes specific examples 
of using this approach to calculate Shannon, conditional, relative entropy, and topological complexity. 
The benefits of this technique are demonstrated through various distributions, including fractal distributions, 
and its theoretical soundness is confirmed by establishing underlying theorems. 
The associated source code is available on GitHub under the repository name AritheticMC. 
A associated journal paper is in progress and expected to provide extended discussion. 
The presented work is part of the author's PhD thesis in data science at the University of Houston. 
The research was supported by grants from CSquare and the University of Houston, 
as well as the Infusion Program funded by Grant INF22233051085. 
The data relevant to this research is available at the University of Houston's data repository, 
or can be contacted for access to at [mpannu@uh.edu]. 
The primary contribution of this PhD thesis involves the development of Markov chain methods 
to accurately estimate entropy, including the previously mentioned ArMC method, 
as well as the reverse construction of deterministic topological spaces from groups, 
and the introduction of an innovative kernel that addresses limitations in the standard Gibbs sampling. 
The associated source code is available at [https://github.com/mpannu/PhD-Infrastructure]. 
The studies presented in this thesis pertain to continuous data scenarios.
