We analyze systems that process products at a rate governed by a stochastic process with independent increments, blurring the lines between queueing theory and topology. Measures of system performance are evaluated using Borel measures, enabling us to compare weights on sets of flow diagrams and efficiently calculate costs. A crucial application involves evaluating ages on orbits of dynamical systems, allowing us to analyze ages in semiconductor production lines. These results lead to insightful correlations between system performance and topological properties of the system's phase transition diagram. The measures of system performance are expressed as integrals or sums of weights on sets of flow diagrams, and efficient sampling schemes are developed to estimate these integrals with low variance, such as stratified sampling or importance sampling targeted at high-performance regions. The approach is adaptable to various weight functions and can be applied to multiple manufacturing systems, including those with multiple product types and complex dynamics. A case study on ages in semiconductor production lines showcases the practical value of our methodology, and extensive mathematical proofs and supporting simulations are included. The companion software allows users to replicate our findings and make adjustments to match their own system's specifications. A tutorial outlines the necessary steps to use our approach in a real-world setting, and numerous open challenges are identified within queueing theory and dynamical systems. To exploit vulnerabilities in IoT devices, it is necessary to classify attacks quickly, but this requires a precise prediction to be effective. Unfortunately, deep learning technology, which has high accuracy, consumes too much memory and computation power, making it unsuitable for immediate deployment on devices such as routers and sensors. We have developed a tool called NBcoded, which converts neural networks into efficient decision-making systems for classifying attacks by compressing the complex model into a series of simple rules. This  tool utilizes an automatic method to choose the factors that accurately predict attacks, thereby reducing the size of the model and saving resources. We tested NBcoded on 19 datasets and found that it successfully reduces the memory requirements of neural networks by 20-40% and computation power by 25-40%, while maintaining high accuracy of classification. The detailed information about NBcoded's performance can be found at: https://github.com/akmese/NBcoded. We have also implemented this tool as an open-source service, which quickly identifies attack classifiers using the most efficient neural network for the specific device's resources. This service can be accessed at: https://iim.nstu.ru/nbcoded. The growth gap issue for metabelian groups has been explored, leading to distinct outcomes depending on whether these groups are finitely presented or torsion-free. This research introduces the concept of growth gaps, specifically the growth gap ratio, and demonstrates that finitely presented metabelian groups have a limited growth gap, whereas non-torsion metabelian groups with infinite subgroups have an unbounded growth gap. Furthermore, it has been discovered that torsion-free metabelian groups with infinite subgroups and finite rank have an unbounded growth gap, but this constraint on the rank can be relaxed to require only finite primitivity for the same property to hold. Additionally, this study examines the growth gap in solvable groups of finite rank and non-primitivity, finding it to be finite. Interestingly, it was found that solvable groups of finite rank and non-primitivity can be constructed as subgroups of finite rank solvable groups, explaining why their growth gap ratios converge to 1. Conversely, it was discovered that finitely presented solvable groups of finite rank and non-primitivity can be constructed as subgroups of metabelian groups of finite rank and non-primitivity, but with a distinct property where the latter group's commutator quotient is isomorphic to the cyclic group Z/2Z, resulting in a fundamentally different behavior. This research also discusses open questions regarding the growth gap in specific classes of groups, specifically finite groups and lattices within adjoinable groups. To conclude, the study highlights that the growth gap ratio can serve as an invaluable tool for distinguishing between different classes of groups. Lastly, extensive mathematical notation has been utilized to formulate the various open questions of an algebraic-nature that appear in this paper. The list of these questions is presented in the provided appendix.

The advancement of biotechnology has made it possible to create living entities that can be distinguished from non-living objects based on their movement. This paper explores ways to identify biological entities through their locomotion patterns, which are often intricate and less common than non-biological movements. To tackle this challenge, we employ a cutting-edge artificial intelligence technique known as Generative Adversarial Networks. By utilizing GANs, we can learn the underlying structure of biological movement data and generate novel, biological-like movements, thereby establishing a baseline for distinguishing biological movements from non-biological ones through data-driven approaches. To this end, we have developed a new benchmark dataset featuring various biological movements performed by living creatures, which, along with our method, can be utilized to test traditional machine learning algorithms for object classification. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, revealing significant improvements in classification accuracy for the proposed benchmark dataset. This research has far-reaching implications for addressing unsupervised problems in biology, medicine, and electronics, where distinguishing living movements from non-living movements is crucial. Moreover, this research can potentially transfer to areas such as distinguishing plants from non-living objects, which holds significant practical value. This study investigates the effectiveness of hybrid quantum approaches in solving complex partitioning problems within power network distribution. By utilizing superconducting hybrid qubits, we evaluated the performance of two such approaches, compared them to classical methods, and explored their scalability. Our results reveal that a hybrid quantum approach outperforms a classical alternative in solving smaller-scale partitioning problems, although its efficiency declines for larger problem sizes. Moreover, a another hybrid quantum approach was found to be less proficient in solving partitioning problems, yet demonstrated better performance in solving a related optimization problem, and could be adapted for various other applications in future studies. Such research has significant potential to advance the performance of energy systems by leveraging quantum computing technology. This research demonstrates a novel Bayesian method to estimate an object's initial conditions based on its observed behavior, specifically its falling motion through a fluid medium, where measurement noise and unpredictable drag forces are factored in. By developing a straightforward statistical model, we can accurately reconstruct the object's trajectory, identify uncertainty associated with its path, and make reliable predictions about its future location. Notably, our approach effectively manages noise from multiple sources, including measurement error, unpredictable fluid dynamics, and statistical fluctuations, to provide a reliable model of the objects falling process. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method using both real-world data and simulated scenarios, which include varying levels of measurement accuracy, drag force magnitude, and acceleration variability. The results indicate that our model is capable of providing a detailed and accurate description of the objects falling motion under diverse conditions, thus serving as a useful tool for physical ininvestigations in this domain. Furthermore, this study illustrates the applications of two uncertainty quantification techniques to analyze the effects of variable parameters on the falling motion dynamics. We also provide a publicly available Python code for the entire process to facilitate future studies and adaptations of our model. \\

Keywords: Bayesian inference, Object identification, Falling motion, Noise analysis, Uncertainty quantification, Physics, Predictive models. \\

By applying this model to silicon, we investigated the damping of longitudinal sound waves within the framework of the linearized Boltzmann equation. Our results show that this damping follows the same universal law across all materials, including silicon, but its calculation depends on knowing the detailed structure of the lattice, particularly how it interacts with itself at a quantum level. In multimodal optimization, multiple optimal solutions are sought, whereas in multi-objective optimization, a comprehensive set of optimal solutions is sought. Our proposed BIC (Boundary Interval Calculation) method leverages the efficient global solution finding capability of NSGA-II to identify high-quality solutions, which are then analyzed using the Delaunay triangulation to estimate the boundaries of the efficient frontier in a two-objective domain. Subsequently, an intermediate set of points is generated within these boundaries through smooth surface interpolation and an inverse distance method, following which an inverse logistic transformation is applied to adjust the fitness function values of the individuals. The main contribution of this study is the integration of a new inverse logistic transformation technique, in conjunction with BIC, to balance fitness adjustment and preserve genetic diversity, effectively enhancing the performance of multi-objective optimization algorithms and facilitating the discovery of optimal solutions in complex domains. Our experimental findings, based on the hypTSP problem, reveal a notable increase in the diversity of high-quality solutions, when compared to a leading state-of-the-art algorithm, while SGA-BIC successfully identifies all 260 hypTSP optima. Additionally, an empirical analysis of the hypTSP solutions suggests that SGA-BIC's increased diversity yields a significantly higher probability of obtaining the optimal hypTSP solution. Our study also examines the utilization of BIC for facilitating a seamless transition from multimodal optimization to multi-objective optimization, illustrating the versatility of this method in optimizing both types of problems effectively. To promote reproducibility, the proposed algorithm has been implemented in a public repository, along with the experimental data used to guide researchers in applying BIC in their own optimization tasks. Furthermore, a theoretical study on the boundary estimation in Delaunay triangulation is conducted to provide foundational knowledge that can guide experts in optimizing their own specific domains using this method. Our investigation into the theoretical properties of Delaunay triangulation also reveals its inherent shortcomings, such as an uneven distribution of nodes, that may compromise its efficiency as a general-purpose optimal solution finder. Ultimately, an analysis of the computational complexity of BIC provides insights into its practical applications and potential limitations in real-world optimization tasks. This leads to a novel characterization of clouds with non-trivial stabilizers in their stabilizer group and the existence of a center. This characterization is significant as it holds for all clouds, whether they are locally compact or compact. Building on this finding, we've demonstrated that there is a common metric that makes the stabilizer group path-connected and has a center in any universal cover of a graph whose links correspond to non-trivial stabilizers. This result has practical implications; for example, it allows us to define a metric that turns the universal cover of a simply connected graph into a contractible space. A low-cost, compact Antenna, approximately half-wavelength in diameter, was designed to operate within a 5 GHz bandwidth. The result of these findings is an economical antenna solution suitable for 5G applications requiring wide coverage areas. To tackle the challenge of decoding noisy quantum circuits, researchers utilize a variety of methods such as probabilistic analysis or exhaustive search. However, these approaches are limited due to increasing input lengths. This paper presents a novel approach using reinforcement learning to develop a correct decoding strategy for quantum error correction. By creating a suitable state space representation, researchers developed a compatible agent to verify the effectiveness of this method. Specifically, they applied it to correcting steerable qubits suffering from random errors and compared the efficiency to other existing methods. The results show that reinforcement learning can efficiently decode quantum errors, surpassing standard probabilistic methods. Moreover, the encoded agent successfully corrects steerable qubits with up to 20 qubits, outperforming a known efficient algorithm in this domain. Additionally, the research involves a detailed analysis of the policy learned by the agent to understand its workings and provide additional support. The developed code is accessible on GitHub at the URL https://github.com/kuusst/reinforcement_learning_decoding. As future work, the researchers intend to apply a similar approach to tackle other quantum circuit problems. Furthermore, they plan to investigate whether reinforcement learning can be used to develop quantum circuits that are more efficient. Currently, the researchers are working on developing a correct synthesis algorithm for noisy intermediate-scale circuits, a crucial goal in contemporary quantum computing development. We introduce a novel measurement technique based on quantum jumps that enables precise angle estimation in optical interferometry. This method surpasses the standard quantum limit, achieving faster convergence without the need for numerous probes. Building on this idea, a simple and efficient quantum network can be implemented to facilitate the measurement of remotely connected optical interferometers. This quantum approach offers a desirable trade-off between accuracy and the number of measurements required. Additionally, we examine the limitations of this quantum jump measurement technique when data analysis is constrained by a limited number of data points. This research lays the groundwork for integrating quantum resources into optical metrology experiments. \\

This research examines the interplay between parton fragmentation and parton-hadron fragmentation in relativistic heavy ion collisions. A parallel is drawn between the yields of various hadrons in proton-proton collisions and non-identified hadrons in Au-Au collisions, based on their momentum fraction, z. While there is a significant decrease in yields of hadrons with increasing p_T in Au-Au collisions for quarks representing the majority of the parton population (z > 0.5), a minor decrease is observed for those representing a lesser part of the population (z ≤ 0.5). This investigation suggests that hadron yields, affected by parton fragmentation, also exhibit a parton-hadron fragmentation component, more prevalent for lower-momentum quarks. Estimates of the parton-hadron fragmentation yield in Au-Au collisions increase with the parton's lower momentum, indicating that lower-momentum quarks produce a greater number of final-state hadrons. An numerical assessment of the system's energy loss by the parton, ΔE, in Au-Au collisions shows that lower-momentum quarks experience a greater energy loss, consistent with the findings of as-yet-unconducted hydrodynamic studies. Furthermore, this study calculates nuclear modification ratios, R AA, for hadron production in Au-Au collisions across the measured p_T ranges. A substantial suppression, up to 20%, is observed for low-momentum hadrons. Nuclear modification ratios increase as the parton's momentum is decreased, indicating a greater effect of nuclear effects on the momentum transfer from the nucleus to partons. An empirical power-law function, used to describe the p_T dependence of nuclear modification ratios for high-p_T hadrons in proton-led collisions, fails to adequately represent the data for Au-Au collisions below a certain p_T threshold. Instead, this study develops a double-power-law formula to fit the R AA data across the measured p_T ranges in Au-Au collisions. The parameters of this function, which quantify the nuclear modification factors for hadron production in heavy ion collisions, are reported. Additionally, this study computes the centrality dependence of nuclear modification factors for hadrons in Au-Au collisions at 200 GeV, using the parameterized formula double-power-law for z-dependent yields. The findings of this research demonstrate that nuclear modification factors for hadron production in heavy ion collisions exhibit a distinctive behavior, influenced by the parton's momentum. In digital-analog quantum computing, a mix of digital and analog techniques efficiently simulates complex physical models, notably the Fermi-Hubbard model, on a small-scale grid. This paper explores the possibilities of analog quantum error correction in DADC systems by adapting the horizontal shift correction method. By incorporating this method into the interaction circuit, the error correction of superconducting nanowire quantum-potential tunnels has been successfully demonstrated using two stations separated by a lossy channel. This breakthrough brings us closer to a fully functional DADC system that can accurately model the Fermi-Hubbard model on an large-scale grid, paving the way for quantum simulation of complex physical phenomena. Furthermore, this error correction technique has potential applications in future quantum devices, such as quantum switches and simulators. Currently, research is being conducted to expand the technique and use it for correcting errors in DADC systems with multiple units and varied potential barriers. Additionally, efforts are being devoted to develop and implement an efficient decoding algorithm for the error correction technique. Upon completion, this development is expected to significantly reduce the threshold displacement required for correcting errors in the quantum-potential tunnel experiment. In the long term, our goal is to integrate this error correction technique into the digital-analog quantum computing chain to create a highly robust and versatile quantum simulation platform that can be utilized for studying various physical models at different temperature and density levels, including realistic models of materials that can be measured with current technology. This development has the potential to accelerate research in this field and, ultimately, contribute to a new generation of quantum technologies. Furthermore, this error correction technique could be applied to future quantum devices by adapting it to various contexts, such as matrix multiplication, parameter estimation, and random number generation, which are critical functions in phase measurements, quantum chemistry calculations, and cryptographic applications, respectively. In particular, if incorporated into the measurement process of the quantum double slit experiment, this technique could potentially reveal random interference patterns that can be utilized to improve current models of reality, such as the de Broglie-Bohm theory, by comparing them to data measured with high precision. In the event that this experiment is successful in revealing such patterns, this development has the potential to significantly alter our understanding of nature, leading to new philosophical perspectives and a deeper appreciation of quantum mechanics, even if the inherent uncertainties associated with its principles cannot be completely eliminated. In conclusion, the application of analog quantum error correction in digital-analog quantum computing offers promising prospects for enhancing the performance of this promising quantum technology. This paper introduces Bonsai, a novel algorithm that develops minimal, interpretable feature representations for machine learning models by compressing dated, sequential multimodal time series data. Bonsai discovers a compact, structured representation by utilizing two innovative techniques: sequential exploration of the data and incorporation of a hierarchical, mixed-type graph neural network. Its unique combination of rapid data exploration and efficient feature encoding enables Bonsai to outperform current approaches in both efficiency and performance, as evidenced by our empirical evaluation across diverse datasets and scenarios. Additionally, the paper highlights the cognitive benefits of Bonsai's features over other state-of-the-art methods. You can access the code and model information at the repository https://github.com/ChunYuan-Research/Bonsai.

This study presents a weighted-mutation variant of a genetic algorithm, known for its potential applications in oceanography, medical imaging, and computer vision. By incorporating adaptive mutations, the algorithm enhances its ability to accurately reproduce complex images with high level details. In our research, we examine the effectiveness of this approach in improving light transmission and detail restoration in three-dimensional scattering media. Our findings indicate that the weighted-mutation genetic algorithm successfully restores both the shape and spectrum of a laser pointer's image, achieving better results compared to a standard genetic algorithm. Furthermore, we evaluate the algorithm's sensitivity to noise levels and find that it remains effective across various noise intensities. Our work includes a comprehensive analysis of parameter settings, extensive numerical experiments, and a detailed comparison with existing methods for image reconstruction and transmission. This research sheds new light on the potential of evolutionary algorithms for optical thinned-planar waveguides, offering a viable alternative to established techniques. Our findings could influence the development of novel optical devices and systems, including integrable optical transformers, and contribute to ongoing research in oceanography, medical imaging, and computer vision. Our main contribution is a modified genetic algorithm, known as WMGA, capable of accurately reconstructing complex images in three-dimensional scattering media. Our code is versatile and can be applied to various image reconstruction problems in optical thinned-planar waveguides. In policy learning, using multiple task-oriented paths in sampling can significantly boost the efficiency of value function estimates. This "back-and-forth" approach in off-policy sampling is particularly beneficial as it allows each testing sample to contribute to multiple training iterations. However, our research reveals that the maximal benefits come with a corresponding increase in the testing sample size, ultimately leading to diminished returns. This paper presents an alternative method to reach optimal results with a reduced number of testing samples, involving leveraging multiple training datasets to maximize the value of each testing sample. The proposed technique is a self-verifying method that does not necessitate any additional parameters, making it suitable for a wide range of existing value function estimation techniques. Through experimental analysis using a variety of representative tasks, we demonstrate that our method yields superior results when compared to a baseline back-and-forth approach, achieving better sample efficiency and overall performance, especially on demanding tasks. The code underlying this research is publicly accessible on the Gym-CarLA platform at: https://github.com/gym-carla/Gym-CarLA. A corresponding implementation on OpenAI's Benchmark suite can be found at: https://github.com/alevans/BackAndForth-OA-Benchmark. A video illustrating our research can be viewed at: https://youtu.be/7pMQtRwXgGw. In terms of future work, we envision a near-future reinforcement learning environment where back-and-forth sampling is an essential tool for efficient value function estimates, spanning a broad spectrum of applications and settings. In order to realize this vision, there needs to be standardization around this technique, as well as a corresponding need to investigate its broader theoretical and practical implications. Given its potential for improving current reinforcement learning methods and achieving optimal results with a reduced number of testing samples, we urge the community to take active interest in this area. In order to accelerate progress, we provide our code and research data to the public, with the hope of spurring innovation in both near-term and long-term projects. Furthermore, we propose the establishment of a benchmark suite for back-and-forth sampling methods, where researchers can evaluate and compare their approaches in an objective and transparent manner. By means of open discussion and collaboration, we believe that collective efforts can be focused on developing efficient value function estimates through the advancement of a unified, consistent, and efficient reinforcement learning ecosystem. In order to facilitate collaboration, our research data and code can be accessed at: https://github.com/alevans/BackAndForth-OA-Benchmark.

This study investigates the characteristics of monolithic small collection-electrode CMOS sensors with a single photodiode, which includes a thin sensitive layer and a p-type substrate through which charges can be transferred. To model these sensors, we utilize the numerical simulation tool SYNOPSI, which enables the calculation of signal loss due to impact of fairchild noise through which parameters such as sensitive layer thickness can be determined. Furthermore, we develop an analytical model to predict signal loss under various conditions. Experimental validation of our findings is achieved via measurement of charge collection in 16-nm FFinFET CMOS technology using a laser microbeam, under conditions simulating flux rates equivalent to 10 and 100 minimum ionizing particles per millimeter. Our simulations demonstrate that in small collection-electrode sensors, the thin sensitive layer enhances charge collection, while an overly thick p-type substrate can impede signal transfer. For fairchild noise with a maximum distance of 10 micrometers, our analytical model shows that the threshold energy levels for signals and signals from two separate particles coincide, occurring at a flux rate of approximately 10 particles per millimeter. In our experiments, the threshold energy levels for signals and signals from two separate particles appear at flux rates of around 70 and 120 eV, respectively, when the sensitive layer thickness is set at 0.7 micrometers. Our results establish a threshold energy limit of 70 eV for signals, which is in line with data on nuclear transition responses as well as data from other sensors such as PICO, FAIRCAST, and WEKA. Our findings on small collection-electrode CMOS sensors provide valuable insights into sensor design that can minimize signal loss due to fairchild noise, thereby enhancing nuclear transition response. In particular, we establish that a 0.7 micrometer sensitive layer thickness offers the optimal charge collection properties. Furthermore, this thickness can be adjusted in accordance with process parameters such as type substrate thickness and resistivity. Lastly, our study demonstrates that small collection-electrode CMOS sensors with monolithic single photodiodes can be highly effective in recording nuclear transitions beyond 70 eV. Such sensors have promising applications in various fields including particle physics research and space exploration for detecting intense gamma-ray emissions. Advanced data processing methods are significantly enhancing the exoplanet detection capability of ground-based telescopes by improving signal extraction algorithms. These algorithms analyze data from multiple frames to identify exoplanet images, but they have a slow processing rate due to their complex nature, making them unsuitable for rapid analysis. The application of machine learning techniques, specifically deep learning methods, has successfully detected exoplanets in crowded fields and demonstrated faster processing speeds. However, these models require large datasets of labeled data, which is scarce in this field due to the scarcity of exoplanet images. We introduce a new approach where we represent each image of a night as a point in a multidimensional space, aiming to improve the detection of exoplanets in large datasets. This method analyzes the temporal variations of a dataset and its statistical characteristics to identify exoplanets, and it does so by using two dimensionless maps that pinpoint the locations of exoplanets and distinguish real signals from noise. This method is versatile and can be applied to different types of datasets; our results show that it effectively detects exoplanets in large datasets, and it outperforms other algorithms in terms of performance metrics. The method is fast and efficient, allowing it to process large datasets quickly. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness by applying it to a simulated dataset of 200,000 frames that contains real data from the TYSKY telescope's observation of the HIP114470 star, and our analysis reveals two distinct planet candidates at 3 and 6 AU, respectively. This new method is an innovative detection algorithm for exoplanets in large datasets and may be used in future surveys such as EChO and PFS. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/Li-ZhenCheng/Li_ZhenCheng.github.io. Any questions regarding the code can be directed to lizc@ustc.edu.cn. Additionally, the project's website, which includes videos and images, can be accessed at https://li-zhencheng.github.io/deml/.

Investment strategies can be effectively guided by stochastic models tailored for negative interest rates. We introduce a novel model that incorporates the log-normally distributed short rate process, enabling seamless alignment with existing Swaption pricing methodologies. Moreover, this model makes it possible to calculate Annuity prices in the presence of negative interest rates. Our model's parameters can be estimated using Real World Measure data, and we demonstrate that it aligns with market expectations, thereby facilitating the transition to the Risk-Neutral Measure. This model offers a valuable tool for managing investments under negative interest rates and also serves as a starting point for developing future models. Several numerical examples are included to showcase its applications. Furthermore, the model has been implemented in an open-source library, AnnuiLib, for use in production environments. This library is comprised of Python functions that allow users to simulate short rate processes, calculate Annuity prices, evaluate sensitivities, and simulate trading scenarios, all while taking into account negative interest rates. We provide thorough documentation for the library to ensure maximum usability. We contend that the proposed model represents an advanced solution for addressing negative interest rate phenomena and also observe that it exhibits desirable statistical properties, thereby making it an attractive choice for practical applications. We acknowledge the significant challenges involved in forecasting future interest rate directions and welcome any potential improvements that may arise from future developments in the field. We intend for the model to serve as a valuable resource to both practitioners and academics, offering a valuable point of departure for further study. We intend to maintain and updating the model, the accompanying open-source library AnnuiLib, and the associated documentation to ensure they remain compatible with current market conditions. We intend to keep the model and the library AnnuiLib open to users, and to continuously update them to ensure they remain accurate and usable for applications involving negative interest rates. This research introduces enhanced cluster-robust estimators that tackle existing drawbacks, such as massive variance in the estimators and significant weight of observable error in the predictions. The newly proposed estimators are tested and compared with existing alternatives in a simulated environment, specifically with our proposed method where the cluster-robust estimator is integrated with the Demlzer-Willmot model. The results demonstrate improved performance of our proposed method over the existing estimators, particularly in small sample scenarios. Additionally, the mathematical properties of our proposed method are validated through theoretical proof. The methodology is then applied to analyze the effect of observable error on the predictions of terrorist organization membership. The findings reveal significant impact of the observable error and provide guidance on choosing suitable cluster-robust estimators based on the relative sizes of the observed clusters. The research is built upon previous findings that individuals with certain characteristics are more likely to join certain terrorist organizations, and the analysis is conducted using the SocioEcon data from the University of Maryland's Terrorism Research Program Center. The results provide insights into how various socioeconomic factors influence the likelihood of an individual joining a particular terrorist organization, and the findings are shared for further replication. The companion software, available through the Replication Data tab, facilitates the replication of the research by allowing users to download the necessary packages and data files. This study enhances the computational efficiency of direct numerical simulations of turbulent channel flows with multiple solid particles within them by utilizing an optimized integration algorithm. The multiple-time-step integration algorithm (MTSA) accelerates simulations by merging distinct physical processes onto a single time scale. We expand upon this approach, combining it with the steady-state characteristics of particle-laden flow simulations. By grouping simulations into steady-state and transient phases, and applying the MTSA on the latter, the algorithm significantly reduces the total computational time required for convergence. Compared to conventional methods, this strategy leads to a substantial decline of up to 80% in the number of time steps needed to achieve steady-state conditions, without any additional memory demands. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the optimized algorithm maintains the same level of numerical stability as the standard method. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in simulations of multiple particle-laden turbulent channel flows, showcasing its potential to greatly decrease the computational time and expense of such simulations, which are commonly used to study particle suspensions in engineering applications. The improved algorithm is expected to greatly benefit simulations of even more complex configurations, such as particle assemblies and flows within 3D turbulent channels. The analysis provided in this work is now utilized to guide simulations of flows with dilute particle suspensions, and is made accessible through an open-source code for the benefit of the community. Lastly, possible avenues for further optimization of the algorithm through the regularization of the particle Reynolds number are explored, offering potential for continued reductions in computational time in the future.

This breakthrough has enabled researchers to gain insights into the thermodynamic properties of extensive systems, such as the critical points of fluids and magnetic phase transitions, by applying holographic theory. Building on this success, researchers extended the framework to define particle number definition in extended systems containing multiple particles. This led to a new understanding of particle number definition and its potential to illuminate complex systems, such as the behavior of quark gluon plasma at large collision energies. The extended framework has also enabled researchers to derive thermodynamic state equations for dense fermion systems, allowing for precise predictions of how certain physical properties change with density and effective mass. Furthermore, researchers used the framework to investigate how the properties of dense fermion systems change in response to changes in their chemical potential and degeneracy pressure, discovering intriguing similarities with the theories of neutron stars and quark stars. Finally, researchers have also explored the potential of the framework to understand the properties of non-relativistic black holes and how they relate to the theories of dark matter and compact stars. The new theoretical framework has the potential to revolutionize our understanding of particle number definition in the context of black holes and dense systems, offering a novel approach that can be applied to study various physical phenomena across multiple dimensions. The approach can be further generalized to study systems containing multiple types of particles and may hold potential for understanding the properties of intricate systems such as neutron stars, quark stars, and other condensed matter systems. The impact of the dipole model on the nuclear broadening of high-energy particle collisions has varying interpretations depending on the model used for the dipole-nucleus interaction. This study investigates how different models affect the nuclear broadening by comparing predictions for the transverse momentum shift and scaling factors in proton-proton collisions, utilizing reconstructions of proton-lead collisions from the LHC. For a given dipole model, changing the treatment of the impact parameter leads to significant variations in the predictions for the transverse momentum shift. Specifically, the saturation model yields a larger shift at a given impact parameter than the color glass condensate model. Additionally, models that incorporate the nuclear geometry in the dipole model enhance the shift relative to a geometrically universal model. However, these differences are diminished in the rapidity-yield ratio, highlighting the necessity of considering multiple channels and system-scale effects in high-energy proton-lead collisions. This study's findings and methods will guide the analysis of nuclear broadening in the context of exotic states decaying into photons and nuclei. Furthermore, the techniques developed can be applied to the study of quarkonium nuclear broadening and the exploration of new phenomena at the LHC via photon-nucleus collisions. This research was carried out as part of the PHENIX collaboration. The research presented utilizes data from the PHENIX detector at the LHC, consisting of 14 Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV and 14 p-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV, involving the reconstruction of exclusive photon-nucleus collisions based on event centrality up to 60%. The analysis focuses on transverse momentum shifts in photon-nucleus collisions and the associated scaling factors. The reconstruction of the photon four-vector events is utilized to calculate the transverse momentum shift and the scaling factors. The results for the transverse momentum shift are compared to quark-saturation and color glass condensate models. The analysis reveals significant variations in the transverse momentum shift when considering saturation and color glass condensate models at a given impact parameter. However, these differences are diminished in the rapidity-yield ratio, emphasizing the necessity of considering multiple channels and system-scale effects in high-energy photon-nucleus collisions. The Diophantine equation $7^m - 7^n = x^2$ has been studied since the 20th century. A particular case, not solvable with rational numbers, was initially considered. A middle term $7^{n-m}$ was linked to the value of $m-n$. However, it is suspected that this equation has no solution as integers shift towards each other. Nonetheless, the opposite case, with the difference being a fraction, reveals that for any irrational number $r$, the equation $7^{m-n} = r^2$ has an infinite number of solutions. A fundamental question remains whether the equation $7^m - 7^n = x^2$ has an infinite number of solutions when $m-n = k$, a positive integer. A partial answer was given by Vincenzo Re and his colleagues, providing infinite cases with specific conditions applied to $m-n$. Furthermore, the study explores similar problems with equations of higher powers, such as $15^{m} - 15^{n} = x^2$ or $15^{m} + 15^{n} = x^2$. Interestingly, the first of these equations has an infinite number of solutions when the difference between its terms is 1, while the second has an infinite number of solutions when the difference is a multiple of 2. A key observation in this study revolves around the number of solutions to the equation $15^{m} - 15^{n} = x^2$ when the difference between its terms is $r$. If this equation has a solution, then the equation $(15^n - 15^m)^2 = 15^{m+n} \cdot 15^{m-n} \cdot 15^{m-n}$ has a solution as well. Consequently, the study discovers an infinite number of quadratic polynomials that have no solutions with rational parameters. A notable example is the polynomial $x^2 - (15m^2 - 15n^2 - x^2) = 0$, which has an infinite number of solutions if $m-n$ remains a non-zero constant. A corresponding relationship also exists for equations of higher powers, such as a polynomial of the form $x^2 - (31m^2 - 31n^2 - x^2) = 0$, which has an infinite number of solutions when the difference between its terms is a fixed integer. This work examines the dynamics of a liquid jet that flows through a narrow passageway filled with air. As the jet moves through the channel, it encounters resistance that causes it to deviate from its original path and develop unstable fluctuations. To study this behavior, we use an experimental setup consisting of a vertical tube filled with air, connected to a reservoir of moving liquid. A high-speed camera captures the dynamics of the jet, which are then analyzed in three-dimensional reconstructions. Notably, the method employs advanced image processing techniques to remove oscillations resulting from the free surface of the liquid. We investigate how the ratio of liquid to air densities and the rate at which the liquid moves through the channel influence its behavior. Importantly, our findings highlight the significance of considering the movement of air in dynamical systems. This is accomplished by tracking the flow of air around obstructions and measuring the velocities of fluid elements within both phases. Our results show that when the rate at which the air moves is similar to the rate at which the liquid moves, the two phases become closely linked and the behavior of the system appears to be uniform. However, when the rate at which the air moves slows down or speeds up compared to the rate at which the liquid moves, the two phases develop distinct patterns and the behavior of the system appears non-uniform. We observed that when the ratio of liquid to air densities is low but the rate at which the air moves is high, the behavior of the system appears to be uniform and the flow of air assumes a leading role. Conversely, when the ratio of liquid to air densities is high, the behavior of the system appears to be non-uniform and the flow of air assumes a supporting role. To summarize, the system's behavior appears uniform when the flow of air is the primary factor and non-uniform when the flow of air is secondary. Furthermore, we developed a simplified model to study the system's behavior, which consists of two phases and is governed by the Reynolds number. Our results show a close match between the model's predictions and the observed patterns. Notably, the model holds significance as it identifies key parameters that dictate the system's behavior and demonstrates how the movement of air and the system's density ratios impact the system's dynamics. This research has far-reaching implications and can be applied to study a wide range of natural phenomena and engineering systems. Moreover, our study provides a foundation for exploring the system's stability through linear stability analysis and identifying the governing parameters that dictate the system's behavior. Non-volatile memory, such as NVRAM, is an innovative technology that enables fast persistence without the need to frequently flush cached data to storage. Unlike traditional volatile memory, NVRAM allows for single system call operations, including read and write accesses, resulting in faster performance. This attribute makes NVRAM useful for building fast data management systems with consistent data persistence. However, ensuring complete data consistency across all systems in a distributed setting remains an open challenge. This paper introduces Fferri, a NVRAM-based key-value store that employs algorithm-driven approaches to maintain total consistency and thus preserve data consistency across all systems. In particular, Fferri relies on the Redelivered Vector Protocol (RVP) and the Fowler Ralph Token Pass Protocol (FRTPP) to ensure strong consistency and linearizable consistency, respectively, while maintaining high performance and low overheads. Through comprehensive testing, we demonstrate that Fferri meets its consistency requirements and outperforms existing NVRAM-based key-value stores by factors of 1.35 and 1.42 for protocols RVP and FRTPP, respectively, while only introducing a minimal performance delay of 6.45 microseconds. Furthermore, we examine the practical implications of employing Fferri in distributed systems by considering various system sizes and performance metrics. This study provides new insights into ensuring data consistency in distributed NVRAM-based key-value stores. Details of this work are available online at https://ferri.github.io/. In the context of Inference-based Information Network Analysis, we have developed a new method, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), which utilizes a stacked Dirichlet Process Mixture Model (DPM) to identify overlapping clusters of information entities. By employing the slide-and-project technique, we have developed a practical and efficient algorithm for learning the upper and lower layers of HDTM. Our experiments with real-world data have shown that HDTM can effectively detect latent hierarchical structures in information networks, outperforming existing statistical techniques, such as Hierarchical Clustering and Nonnegative Matrix Factorization, due to its ability to capture complex and nested patterns. Furthermore, the robust topic modeling capabilities of HDTM enable it to handle large datasets, even in cases where the data distribution does not meet the requirements for maximum likelihood estimation, such as data sparsity. We have validated the robustness of HDTM through comprehensive testing and verified its applicability to practical information network analysis by evaluating the quality of the learned topics and the accuracy of the proposed Information Network Parser (INP), which enables the extraction of relevant information from an information network. Our experiments have shown that HDTM can accurately detect latent topics in an information network with an average precision of 0.79 and an average recall of 0.73, and the proposed INP can accurately extract relevant information from the network with an average F-measure of 0.76. Our work on HDTM marks the first application of stacked DPMs in information topic modeling and the first use of DPMs to analyze hierarchical networks, making HDTM a pioneering method in Information Network Analysis. Our algorithm is also unique in its ability to handle large datasets and learn robust topics from incomplete data, outperforming existing methods in this regard. In terms of scalability, HDTM can handle datasets more than 30 times larger than Hierarchical Clustering and more than 10 times larger than Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. While the time complexity of HDTM is higher than NMFP, its robust topic modeling capabilities make it suitable for large datasets even when the data distribution does not meet the requirements for maximum likelihood estimation, such as data sparsity. In terms of applicability, HDTM can be applied to any information network, whether it is a network of documents or a network of entities, and is more versatile than NMFP in this regard, as it can learn latent hierarchical structures in both types of networks. Our work on HDTM marks the first application of DPM

The LHCb collaboration has presented the initial investigation of prompt $\psi(2S)$ and prompt $J/\psi$ meson suppression in PbPb collisions at 5 GeV/c. This analysis utilized data containing around 220 million events, equivalent to 1 nb$^{-1}$ integrated luminosity, and revealed a 15% $\psi(2S)$ suppression relative to $J/\psi$, with both mesons exhibiting a dependence on transverse momentum that becomes more pronounced with increasing momentum. Notably, the observed $\psi(2S)$ suppression surpasses that of $J/\psi$ in the 2-4 GeV/c transverse momentum range. This study serves as a foundation for evaluating medium effects on the $\psi(2S)$ and $J/\psi$ mesons and their respective fragmentation processes. Furthermore, the data suggest that prompt $\psi(2S)$ and $J/\psi$ mesons are affected differently by the quark-anti-quark pair velocity in the nuclear medium. Based on these findings, the study estimates a upper limit for the elusive $\psi(2S)$ fraction at around 7.6%, aligning with current theoretical predictions. This analysis also verifies that prompt $\psi(2S)$ and $J/\psi$ mesons are produced via the same fragmentation processes and suffer from similar factors in the $J/\psi$ suppression observed in the LHCb experiment. Next, the study considers that the observed prompt $\psi(2S)$ and $J/\psi$ meson suppressions, in the transverse momentum ranges examined, are caused by the effects of the nuclear medium. By using data from the ALICE collaboration for comparison, the results from the LHCb experiment reveal a notable discrepancy in the nuclear factor between $\psi(2S)$ and $J/\psi$, with around 2 times more suppression for the former in the 2-4 GeV/c transverse momentum range. Finally, the study rules out a purely conservative explanation for the observed prompt $\psi(2S)$ and $J/\psi$ meson suppressions by indicating, with around 5 standard deviations, that the suppression factors in PbPb collisions are significantly higher than those encountered in proton-proton collisions at the same energies. As a result, the study asserts the need for new theories involving charm quark interactions with nucleons and nuclei to explain the prompt $\psi(2S)$ and $J/\psi$ meson suppressions observed in the LHC

This research develops an analytical framework leveraging the capabilities of approximate singular value decomposition. The objective is two-fold: initially, it aims to identify the underlying structure within a software project's evolution over time by applying the learned models directly to new, unseen commits; secondly, it intends to improve the maintainers' ability to detect and manage evolving changes within software systems by employing the derived component models. By managing complex variations, this framework aims to support software evolution analysis, particularly in detecting and measuring changes. The effectiveness of this approach was evaluated using eight popular open-source projects from various domains, involving the manual examination of 1,940 commit patches and the application of 779 component models. The analysis indicates high accuracies in identifying application components from commit patches, both across different projects and individually, with an overall accuracy of 85.94%. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that variants of SVD can effectively support software evolution analysis, including the detection of changes and measurements. The integration of this framework with existing tools enables software maintainers to utilize the derived component models to detect and manage changing changes at scale, thus supporting practical software evolution analysis. Theoretical predictions for the compass state variance, characterized by both classical and quantum uncertainties, are derived. This analysis focuses on a linearized version of the system in question, with its restoring force modeled as a single planar force. The variance calculations yield expressions in terms of two key parameters: the Anandan-Virbhadri angular displacement and the parameter $\gamma$, which is proportional to the ratio of the planar to the perpendicular restoring forces. The behavior of the variance as a function of $\gamma$ exhibits distinct non-analytical points at $\gamma = \pm 1/3$. Notably, our results show that the variance is dominated by quantum uncertainty for small $\gamma$ and a combination of classical and quantum uncertainties for larger $\gamma$. The consequences of this research are particularly relevant to the study of the ring laser experiment, where the dominant variance term is found to be insensitive to damping parameters. However, the second-harmonic coefficient offers insight into and could potentially quantify damping parameters, with its contribution varying greatly with $ \gamma$. The structure of this coefficient suggests that its measurement could be optimized by adjusting $ \gamma$ to align with the non-analytical points at $ \gamma = \pm 1/3$. Furthermore, varying $ \gamma$ could enhance the precision of the variance measurement, making it a valuable asset in metrological applications. The potential for this parameter to be adjusted through modifications to the resting conditions is also explored in depth. The study concludes by estimating the required variance precision to measure $ \gamma$ to the level of $10^{-3}$. Finally, the relationship between the compass state variance and this parameter is found to be most sensitive at $ \gamma = -1/3$, requiring a precision of $10^{-5}$; at $ \gamma = 1/3$, a precision of $10^{-4}$ is needed; and for $ \gamma$ values between these points, a precision of $10^{-5}$ is required. The study concludes by estimating the potential for the variance measurement of the compass state to be used as a precision meter for $ \gamma$. The study's findings can be extended to investigate the behavior of the ring laser experiment when subjected to various forms of noise and damping. The study is particularly relevant to the field of ring laser gravity spectroscopy and may be used to investigate multiple forms of gravitational damping. The study is self-contained and can be used as a pedagogical tool to educate students about the theoretical and practical aspects of the ring laser experiment,

The molecular machinery driving the rolling of viruses along host cell surfaces has yet to be clearly defined. A notable exception is the case of influenza virus, where the presence of specific host cell proteins is essential for recognizing and binding to target cells, which initiates a metabolic process on the viral surface that ultimately leads to successful infection. This process involves the activation of dormant genetic material and the subsequent expression of viral genes within the host cell. Our study aims to examine whether a similar metabolic process is involved in the rolling of HIV on immune cells, which could provide additional insights into viral dynamics and infection mechanisms. By analyzing time-resolved images of HIV interacting with target cells, we observed changes in viral movement patterns, which suggested the presence of a metabolic process governing viral behavior. Notably, the presence of certain proteins in the viral Rous Sarcoma virus-based expression system revealed a self-organizing mechanism regulating viral movement, which could provide valuable insights into viral behavior, host interactions, and the therapeutic targeting of HIV. This novel metabolic process is deemed "ViroMovement Metabolism" (VMR) – the first description of a metabolic process governing the behavior of a virus, which could open up new avenues for investigating viral dynamics and the development of infection. Moreover, the application of VMR could extend to understanding the behavior of other microorganisms, such as bacteria and viruses, as well as engineered viral systems, which could facilitate therapeutic targeting and the design of more effective antivirus therapies. Ultimately, the study of VMR holds promise for making significant contributions to viral research and biomedicine. We introduce a novel numerical approach to simulate galactic warps by utilizing precise orbit polynomials up to a high degree (four). This method leverages the galactic potential's gradient and curvature to model warps as unpredictable, low-frequency phenomena. We apply our technique to a diverse range of 178 galactic disks, incorporating realistic spiral and stellar mass distributions. The results show that warp patterns, influenced by environmental factors, significantly vary in shape and orientation. The classification of warped galaxies into "S-type" and "U-type" based on warp geometry is examined. The analysis reveals distinct environmental effects for each type, with S-type warps predominantly influenced by the nearby galaxy Coma Leo and U-type warps largely affected by the galaxy NGC 3097. Additionally, we find substantial warp lengths in both S and U types, exceeding previously estimated maximum limits. The calculated warp lengths demonstrate a positive correlation with galactocentric distance and an inverse correlation with the central surface brightness of the galaxies. The application of our approach to simulated galaxy catalogs could serve as a reliable tool for understanding galaxy evolution and disk instability through comparisons with observed galaxy populations. The approach has been successfully applied to a variety of materials, including insulators, conductors, and semiconductors, and shows favorable comparisons with experimental and ab initio values for some materials. Furthermore, we've observed that non-adiabatic Born effective charges for clean conductors exhibit significant discrepancies due to the issue of overbound charges at the boundary with vacuum, in addition to varying in response based on polarization drive. On the other hand, non-adiabatic Born effective charges for insulators are relatively less sensitive to boundary conditions. The study demonstrates that non-adiabatic Born effective charges can be accurately calculated using first-principles methods, and lays the groundwork for improving density functional theory, particularly with respect to the approximation of exchange-correlation effects. The results of this calculation will contribute to a more refined understanding of how to model and describe lattice vibrations in ionic materials. Additionally, we've used these findings to explain the low-temperature emergence of a finite dielectric response in two-dimensional materials, and to account for the significant variances in the dielectric properties of two-dimensional materials made from transition metal dichalcogenides. The calculations demonstrate that these properties are primarily driven by the non-adiabatic response of the charge transfer between atoms within these materials. The findings of this study have potential applications and implications for the use of transition metal dichalcogenides in optical modulators, and could contribute to an improved understanding of how these materials respond to light at the atomic level. The fluctuating Navier-Stokes equation, an application of the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation with fluctuating viscosity, has been established as a reliable mathematical model for turbulent flow at intermediate scales in incompressible turbulent fluids. This model has been proven to statistically replicate the properties of the 3D turbulent flow observed in nature across a wide range of Reynolds numbers. Conversely, the deterministic Navier-Stokes equations, which form the basis for the fluctuating model, are known to break down in describing turbulent behavior on intermediate scales due to their inability to account for random fluctuations. By deriving the fluctuating Navier-Stokes equation as a mathematical model for turbulent flows, this study provides statistical evidence for the validity of the model across a wide range of Reynolds numbers. This proof of concept can be extended to other fluid dynamics equations to develop statistical models for various dynamical systems characterized by random fluctuations. This research has applications in modeling chaotic dynamic systems observed in natural phenomena. This statistical model can be utilized to analyze and understand turbulent behavior on small scales in incompressible fluids, guiding numerical simulations and experimental analyses. Furthermore, this study sets the groundwork for developing statistical models to monitor and detect early signs of developing turbulence from deterministic Navier-Stokes simulations or experimental data. This research can be extended to investigate the statistical significance of rare events in dynamical systems, evaluating whether their occurrence could be an indication that the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation is breaking down. Lastly, this study can be used to investigate the statistical errors of global models of turbulent flow that ignore random fluctuations and are instead based on the deterministic Navier-Stokes equations. Global models of turbulent flow that account for random fluctuations, on the other hand, are known to be accurate and effective. This research can provide a comparison between these two types of models, evaluating their differences and effectiveness across a wide range of Reynolds numbers. This knowledge can help inform whether attempting to correct the random fluctuations term in the fluctuating model for a particular Reynolds number is warranted, potentially guiding future developments in this area. This research can be extended to investigate the statistical behavior of global models of turbulent flow at extremely high Reynolds numbers, such as those observed in the turbulent flow of deep space gas. Under specific conditions, such as positive definiteness of $\mathcal{A}$ and a bounded delay, we establish the diffeomorphism between a neighborhood of the manifold defined by $x(t) = x_0 e^{\mathcal{A}t}$ and the system's non-delayed counterpart in the Banach space $\ell^1$. This paper presents a denotational and operational probabilistic semantics for higher-order programs that incorporate continuous probability distributions over domains, such as domains representing real numbers or unstructured state. Unlike existing probabilistic operational semantics, our denotational framework directly defines a probability measure on the program domain, while our operational framework introduces a probability space for each program configuration. We demonstrate that these semantics are equivalent, as proven through a bi-relation proof. Additionally, our work extends existing type-and-probability systems to include denominators, thereby allowing for the reliable analysis of probabilistic programs that incorporate unstructured state. Using our framework, we prove reliable versions of probabilistic soundness theorems for flapping equality and test q-may properties. Finally, we showcase the utility of our approach by applying it to the reliable analysis of programs constructed through probabilistic lifting and probabilistic guarded commands. A companion Isabelle/HOL formalization documents our development and serves as a reference for future research. It can be accessed through the following link: https://bitbucket.org/jdolphin/relprobsemantics/. A brief overview is also available in arXiv preprint 2202.11392. \cite{mypaper}.

Researchers in design mining study how to effectively utilize large-scale commercial product data to refine design generative models, aiming to produce more stable and cross-product relevant outcomes. In this paper, we develop an innovative method to enhance the stability and cross-product relevance of design mining conclusion results. Our approach leverages large-scale commercial product data to create class-specific similarity matrices, which are then used to refine the latent design codes of each product through matrix completion and diffusion. By testing our method on an industrial-scale dataset of 65,000 products, we demonstrate its effectiveness in producing more stable and cross-product relevant design mining conclusion results. In particular, our method achieves a 25.6% improvement in stability and a 21.3% improvement in cross-product relevance compared to state-of-the-art baseline approaches. Notably, our method also enables the retrieval of more accurate and diverse design samples for each product, which can inform and refine the design generative models in an iterative manner. Specifically, it has been found that if $I$ is weakly $1$-absorbing but not a $1$-absorbing prime ideal, then $I^3$ is a $1$-absorbing prime ideal. Additionally, in a Dom-S with a non-nilpotent maximal ideal $M$, if $I$ is a prime ideal that is weakly $1$-absorbing but not a $1$-absorbing ideal and $M^2 \subseteq I$, then $M \subseteq I$; in this scenario, $I$ is also a weakly $1$-absorbing valuated ideal. Although the arrival of these rays is random in time, their correlation with large-scale structures in space can be measured using techniques sensitive to tiny orientation changes. This research investigates the use of massive datasets containing simulated cosmic rays to quantify their correlation with large-scale structures, focusing on their arrival directions and energy levels. By employing machine learning tools, we found that cosmic rays form distinct groups based on their arrival directions and energy levels, and these findings match well with simulations. In pharmacological research, relational machine learning models are employed to derive correlations between molecular structures and their effects. Typically, these models rely on graph data, such as protein structures or small molecule interactions, represented in standardized formats. However, different datasets characterized by diverse graph schemas, relations, and attributes complicate the comparison of their performance. Furthermore, evaluating models depends on specific characteristics of the data context. Therefore, we suggest utilizing contextual evaluation metrics that take into account dataset features, such as graph connectivity, size, and degree distribution. We developed four novel evaluation metrics to gauge the predictive capability of a model relative to a specific data context. These metrics include assessment of its ability to learn relations, prediction accuracy, capacity to generalize, and preference for training data characteristics. We applied these metrics to evaluate six relational models applied to two small molecule translation datasets and one protein structure validation dataset, analyzing their ability to derive meaningful relationships between molecular components. We observed that a simple supervised model outperformed more advanced, inclusive models in our evaluation context, highlighting the importance of dataset influence on model performance. We provide an implementation of our evaluation metrics in the RGF dataset evaluation tool (https://github.com/rdkit/r-distr), accessible through R packages rGF and GFR. A Python equivalent is in progress as part of the PyRF project on GitHub (https://github.com/rdkit/pyrf). Our evaluation context, along with the novel evaluation metrics, encourages further research on contextual model evaluation, fostering informed discussion on relational model assessment, and motivates the development of more advanced models that can effectively leverage diverse data characteristics. Ultimately, this could lead to development of more effective pharmacological models. Imitation learning is commonly used to transfer knowledge from experts to agents but relies heavily on environments that accurately reflect the expert's behavior. Any differences between the two environments can hinder learning or cause the agent to fall back on suboptimal behaviors. Our research explores how discrepancies between expert and agent tasks affect the learning process in scenarios where tasks aren't explicitly defined. We utilize a system that generates tasks on the fly based on the two trajectories' similarities. When the environments match, the effective transfer of knowledge enables the agent to easily learn the tasks. However, introducing discrepancies between the two environments leads to partial or incomplete learning, and in some cases, causes the agent to perform significantly worse. We analyzed these results to provide a framework for predicting learning outcomes based on the nature of discrepancies. This research provides unique insights into imitation learning, demonstrating its limitations in scenarios where task discrepancies arise. It also offers a potential solution by providing on-line support to help the learning agent navigate uncertain tasks. This support enables the agent to successfully learn the intended tasks in diverse environments. Our research further establishes the complexity of cross-domain imitation learning by presenting a practical solution to the problem and providing a benchmark for comparisons in the future. The research was conducted using the continuous control benchmarks, including HuTap Push and Parkour, and the results are available on our website at: https://ziggywiz.github.io/cross_domain_imitation_learning. All the necessary code can be found on https://github.com/ziggywiz/cross_domain_imitation_learning. Our research further explores the development of efficient reinforcement learning algorithms. We developed SimPIT, an efficient algorithm for simulating exploratory experiences that enhances the learning process. The algorithm identifies the most informative virtual exploratory experiences based on their impact on the learning agent. SimPIT leverages variational inference to determine these experiences and has shown superior performance in comparisons with current reinforcement learning algorithms. Our research further establishes the potential for efficient reinforcement learning algorithms to solve complex problems in the future. Our research delves into the connection between imitation learning and the ability to make counterfactual reasoning. We developed a system that generates counterfactual trajectories using the variations in expert behaviors. The generation of these trajectories is guided by the exploration agent's intentions, making it possible to identify the most informative variations. This research further establishes the potential for counterfactual reasoning to facilitate cross-domain imitation learning. This question explores whether protostars with such high masses can form both inside and outside of established disks, assuming these disks have not lost excess angular momentum. It is proposed that stars with high masses can form through the collapse of a gas cloud either by direct collapse or through the fragmentation of a disk, influenced by factors such as anisotropy and external pressures. The study considers which factors promote or hinder the process of disk fragmentation and evaluates the validity of this theory using existing observational data on protostars and their distributions. The conclusion drawn is that while non-uniform distributions of properties among protostars are observed, there is currently insufficient evidence to confirm or reject the theory of disk fragmentation due to observational ambiguities. Furthermore, potential detection methods and future lines of research are explored to clarify this issue. It is proposed that studying the distribution of a specific property in protostars, formed both inside and outside of established disks, could help confirm or reject the theory of disk fragmentation. The study suggests that a specific parameter, equivalent to the mass-to-angular-momentum ratio, could be used to distinguish between protostars formed through the collapse of a gas cloud or through disk fragmentation. Using available data on protostars with high masses, it is observed that those born inside established disks generally have lower mass-to-angular-momentum ratios compared to those formed outside of these disks. However, there is a need for more accurate measurements of both mass and angular momentum in protostars born outside of established disks to confirm or reject the theory of disk fragmentation. The study proposes that a future research focus should be placed on accurately determining the mass and angular momentum of protostars, particularly those with lower masses, to test the idea that disk fragmentation contributes to the formation of high-mass protostars. The discovery of protostars with mass ratios close to the critical value, as calculated in the study, could provide robust evidence for or against the theory of disk fragmentation. Association rules have far-reaching applications in databases and data mining. The concept has been expanded to cover partial orders and patterns in data, among other areas. The current study tackles the issue of characterizing coverage among these rules, using a logical framework. By representing entailment between sets using a monotone modal logic, we show that it's possible to determine the consistency of assertions involving coverage relationships. The approach also enables us to identify unique properties of coverage and establish an order among association rules. The model generalizes to partial orders; however, it's inconsistent for distributive lattices. The approach offers a theoretical generalization of existing results in databases and opens up new avenues for research in data mining. The model is applicable in various domains, such as text mining, where a text's meaning can be partially unknown. The approach has practical implications, as it allows us to identify essential rules using query reduction and essentiality of minimality principles. The model also enables us to compute minimal-covariance and minimal-consistency association rules. The computations were successful for small datasets; however, they became infeasibly slow for larger datasets, such as those found in the UCI repository. The approach has practical limitations, as it enables us to characterize redundancy, coverage, and consistency using a first-order logic with 2 variables, but fails to generalize to n variables. The approach has practical implications, as it enables us to identify redundant rules and reduce computation time by eliminating them. The model also enables us to identify essential rules and compute minimal-covariance and minimal-consistency association rules, which can aid data miners in drawing meaningful inferences from large datasets. Anomalous process states can be effectively detected without relying on labeled data using unsupervised learning methods. This is particularly advantageous in cases where anomaly labels are scarce or obtaining them would be impractical. One such unsupervised learning technique employs a neural network model that identifies anomalies by recognizing patterns of normal operation and detecting deviations from these norms. By utilizing this method, the detection of anomalous conditions in a gas detector has been achieved. The model was trained on noise data mimicking normal operation and accurately identifies anomalies with high sensitivity and robustness. The model's performance was evaluated in terms of its ability to select relevant features from the data and distinguish between normal and anomalous operation with high accuracy. The model's efficacy was further confirmed by testing it on a dataset collected during an actual experiment and verifying that it can run independently without requiring human expertise. The model's advantages include its ability to adapt to variations in detector settings and its capacity to provide probabilistic outputs representing the likelihood of normal or anomalous operation. As a result, this model can effectively detect anomalies in this particular gas detector and likely other similar systems as well. In contrast, C$_3$H$_2$ column densities prove less sensitive to both factors. We examine a branching population model subject to random movements and a cost function that is not constant over time, within the context of mean field games. The objective is to achieve an equilibrium that minimizes the average cost over time, under the constraint of having a completely regular population flow. It is demonstrated that satisfying regularity conditions significantly increases the complexity of finding an equilibrium compared to the constant cost scenario, as seen in reference [2]. Specifically, there may not be an equilibrium that is continuous in the initial condition, even when a constant cost function is used. Furthermore, when the cost function is not constant, the existence of an equilibrium that is continuous in the initial condition is possible only if a particular transversality condition known as the 'transversality condition of Lagrange' is satisfied. If an equilibrium is present, it may not be unique when subject to minor alterations in the model parameters. Gallium nitride's holes have a significantly lower mobility compared to its key component, gallium, making it a major constraint for developing high-power electronic devices. Research has shown that pairing GaN with a compatible nitride semiconductor, such as ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$, at the lattice level can greatly improve the room-temperature hole mobility. Our study focuses on thoroughly examining the structural, electronic, and transport properties of two scenarios: fully incorporating GaN with ZnGeN$_2$ (GZN) and MgSiN$_2$ (MSiN), and near-lattice-matched combinations involving a thin GaN buffer. We utilize a unique theoretical framework that integrates first-principles calculations with a device simulation. Our results indicate that the average room-temperature hole mobility in GZN and MSiN is approximately 4800 cm$^2$V/s and 2200 cm$^2$V/s, respectively. In contrast, mobility levels in two near-lattice-matched configurations are significantly lower, at about 10 cm$^2$V/s and 70 cm$^2$V/s for GZN and MSiN, respectively. Our investigation also reveals that the optimal mobility in GZN and MSiN is largely attributed to distinct sp and p-distribution of the valence charge of the holes, favoring a more balanced distribution for better mobility. Furthermore, our study shows that the transport properties are largely controlled by the N-Zn and N-Mg bonding configurations in ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$, respectively, which have a significant influence on the hole mobility across these semiconductors.
