Natural language modeling has made significant advancements in generating coherent and contextually relevant content, but it still falls short when it comes to accurately answering specific questions. Unlike traditional static language models that rely on pre-trained weights and are applied universally, our proposed OREO-LM architecture incorporates a dynamic question-aware layer that fine-tunes for question-answering (QA). Building upon the success of prefix-tuning in efficiently improving model performance, OREO-LM prefix-tunes a layer dedicated to interacting with input questions. This layer, which we call the Knowledge Interaction Layer (KIL), is specifically designed to mesh well with pre-trained language models, is efficient in terms of requirements, and is adaptable to various QA datasets. Our experimental results demonstrate that OREO-LM surpasses state-of-the-art QA performance on multiple datasets, with an impressive 87.6% relative improvement in eval loss and 23.4% in eval FMiA F1 score. Notably, our method outperforms comparable QA baselines, achieving state-of-the-art results on datasets such as Quad (80.0) and TAT-B (71.1). Given its remarkable results and relatively low computational needs, our OREO-LM architecture is an ideal choice for enhancing natural language models' ability to answer questions accurately. Recent advances in NLG have been accelerated by pre-trained language models, which have significantly improved the quality of generated text. However, the effectiveness of these models can be limited when they're asked questions that were not part of their training data. To better understand this phenomenon, known as out-of-distribution (OOD) behavior, we conducted experiments using prompts that were either similar to those used to pre-train the models or significantly different. We assessed the performance of six leading language models in terms of their text generation capabilities when given OOD prompts, examining both their ability to follow instructions and produce high-quality text. Our research reveals that while strong pre-training helps language models adapt to OOD prompts to some extent, it often falls short, and these models are unable to effectively handle such scenarios. Interestingly, we discovered that the performance of models on OOD prompts is largely determined by their performance on in-distribution prompts, and there's a noticeable disparity in the quality of generated text. Furthermore, we found that the likelihood of a model displaying OOD behavior increases with the complexity of the prompt. To mitigate this issue, we explored ways to reduce the impact of OOD factors and developed methods for effectively handling unfamiliar prompts, including analogizing to similar scenarios in the training data, active learning to identify and prioritize such scenarios, and fine-tuning the model to produce more consistent text when given OOD prompts. Our research indicates that these approaches can significantly improve the quality of generated text when given OID prompts, and we've developed a tool to facilitate the discovery of effective OOD behaviors. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first research to systematically investigate the phenomenon of OOD behavior in NLG using prompts, and we've made our code and data available for other researchers to build upon. Moreover, we've developed a research direction that could lead to the development of more reliable language models that can adapt to a wide range of applications and domains. Our goal is to understand the extent to which these models can be improved, and we welcome collaborations from the community to achieve this goal. The results show that the integrated approach effectively counteracts environmental noise, enabling the model to achieve high fidelity measurements in challenging conditions. The model's versatility makes it suitable for applications beyond Rydberg atom-based systems, including multi-agent sensing systems. This breakthrough opens up new possibilities for precise measurements in such systems, paving the way for their practical implementation. The source code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/indigo-lab/RLRA. Experimental demonstrations using Rydberg atoms and artificial neural networks have validated the model's effectiveness, laying the groundwork for its application in quantum sensing. The theoretical precision limits of the model have also been explored to assess its performance under different scenarios. Furthermore, the study investigates the resilience of the model against deliberate distortions in its data, which could be useful in protecting it against cyberattacks in future quantum networks. The analysis shows that the model remains accurate within a certain range of distortions but eventually fails outside of this threshold, highlighting its vulnerability to data corruption. This discovery raises potential security risks, which need to be addressed to ensure the model's safety in such scenarios. The research has far-reaching implications, opening the door to utilizing deep learning in practical quantum applications, while also highlighting important challenges that need to be overcome. Ultimately, the success of quantum computing and networking depends on the solution to these issues. The study is part of a broader series on quantum computing and networking, exploring the integration of deep learning with Rydberg atom-based models. Upcoming papers in this series will present alternative approaches to the current research, presenting a unified perspective on the field. This unique arrangement allows us to study the distribution of HII regions in relation to a well-defined reference frame, rather than relying on ambiguous spiral arms. By analyzing HII regions within a radius of 4.5 kpc from the galaxy's center, our study reveals a clear imbalance in the population, with more abundant star-forming regions situated inside the bar's edge. Notably, nearly all identified HII regions are located within a 2 kpc radius of the galaxy's center, where a lack of HII regions at larger radii suggests may be due to dust-obscured star-forming activity. This paper introduces a novel approach to limited data audio synthesis, leveraging a spectrogram-based technique different from existing magnitude spectrograms. Our method utilizes a conditional Wasserstein GAN with a spectrogan-based perceptual loss and a generator optimized for spectrogram synthesis. This new framework yields high-quality audio output, exhibiting superior voice quality and accuracy in its spectrogram representation. Our tests utilizing the VCC2018 challenge dataset demonstrate that it surpasses the benchmark voice cloning system, boasting a significant improvement of 0.03 in MOS scores. Furthermore, the spectrogan approach outperforms magnitude-based techniques in voice synthesis tasks involving unseen frequency ranges, exhibiting increased robustness and the ability to produce more authentic spectrogram representations. The associated code and dataset used in this research are available on GitHub at https://github.com/uwjunqi/Spectrogan. Additionally, our audio generation model has been made available through the Vocoder Zoo at https://vzo.uwjunqi.com.

A new efficient training method has been developed that implements a threshold-based gradient masking approach when the gradient magnitude exceeds a set limit, preventing exploding gradients.  This technique combines seamlessly with gradient clipping and is compatible with various loss functions.  The research demonstrates the integration of this method with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for handling sequence-based time series forecasting tasks.  The new technique surpasses the performance of conventional RNNs and achieves comparable results to state-of-the-art models in multiple forecasting challenges. Similar to other global crises, the COVID-19 pandemic has led to a bitter debate between medical professionals, politicians, and the general public regarding the best approaches to combat the outbreak.  Two primary methods, strict lockdowns and voluntary public health measures such as self-isolation, have been implemented to balance the concurrent goals of minimizing deaths and economic losses.  Our research leverages a sophisticated epidemiological model that allows for the simultaneous evaluation of lockdowns and self-isolation measures.  Our results show that, at the national level in the United States, a timely middle-course approach that combines both types of measures can successfully achieve this balance.  Specifically, we found that a moderate course of action implemented in early February 2020 can concurrently reduce COVID-19-related deaths by nearly 60% and lower economic losses by nearly 50%.  Our analysis also highlights the significance of geographical differentiation in the model to accurately assess the effectiveness of both types of measures.  Finally, we found that a mixed strategy of voluntary self-isolation and social distancing can effectively mitigate the spread of the virus and reduce hospitalizations, even in the absence of a national lockdown.  Notably, we observed that this approach can reduce COVID-19-related hospitalizations by nearly 70% when implemented early in the pandemic.  Our research provides valuable insights for policymakers at the national and local levels, enabling them to make data-driven decisions that balance the concurrent goals of minimizing pandemic-related deaths and economic losses.  Our analysis confirms that a timely middle-course approach that combines lockdowns and self-isolation can successfully achieve this balance, not only in the United States but globally.  Our research is precluded from presenting specific recommendations for particular countries, given the unique challenges posed by different pandemic trajectories, varying population behaviors, and distinct governmental responses.  Nevertheless, our analysis offers a foundation for future research on pandemic control, focusing on the concurrent evaluation of lockdowns and self-isolation measures in the context of emerging vaccine policies. Debugging data processing pipelines, especially those utilizing large datasets in machine learning applications, can be an exceptionally time-consuming task. Current methods typically involve running configurations multiple times with varying parameters, yet provide limited insight into the actual data flow within the pipeline. Our research introduces DataScope, an innovative data debugging tool that enables efficient detection and resolution of data issues by capturing a partial, static image of the pipeline's state during execution. By combining this snapshot with a purpose-built debugger and analysis capabilities, DataScope enables the pinpointing of faults at scale, providing actionable insights to fix related problems in a timely manner. Experimental results demonstrate that DataScope significantly outperforms state-of-the-art data debugging tools, with an average improvement of 10x in diagnosis latency and 15x in total diagnosis effort compared to alternative approaches. Furthermore, DataScope's efficiency and effectiveness have potential applications in a broad range of data-intensive pipeline domains, including SQL queries, data analysis workflows, and NLP pipeline debugging. Our work is accompanied by an open-source implementation and supplementary materials available at https://github.com/uc-barcelonaml/data-scope. A corresponding video tutorial can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4e2TPxRwGqY. Our paper is presented under the CC-BY-NC-ND license. Our data, consisting of large-scale debugging jobs, is available at https://arxiv.org/docsExtent/2110.04612, with an accompanying technical report providing additional context to our research. Our project is co-hosted at https://data-scope.github.io/, serving as a central resource for further developments and related initiatives. Researchers investigating magnetic materials, particularly those based on transition metals, have identified unusual and stabilizable magnetic phases using advanced simulations and experimental analyses. For instance, recent studies of Mn$_3$Sn have revealed a surprising trimerization effect that contributes to its stable ground state. Although similar compounds with additional transition metals exhibit complex magnetic behaviors, precise predictions of their magnetic structures remain challenging due to increased computational complexity. To overcome this limitation, a new approach is introduced, using a specialized method to efficiently calculate magnetic structures, especially in compounds with multiple transition metals. By applying this method to a specific compound, LuFeCh$_2$(Ch = Ge, Si), the research demonstrates how this technique can provide accurate predictions of magnetic structures, especially when other computational tools fail. Furthermore, the predictions show that LuFeCh$_2$ exhibits a long-range magnetic order, with properties similar to Mn$_3$Sn. The analysis also demonstrates how adjusting crystal parameters can stabilize distinct magnetic phases, offering potential pathways for engineering magnetic properties in transition metal compounds. The techniques developed can be extended to study a wide range of magnetic systems. By combining these findings with ongoing experiments, the research opens up new avenues for controlling magnetic properties in transition metal compounds. The code used for the simulations is available at https://git.io/JlZKQ for public access. Additionally, the research provides refined estimates of magnetic energies for LuMn$_2$ with multiple magnetic structures, including a tetrameric arrangement, showing excellent agreement with experimental findings. By leveraging artificial intelligence, the research's findings can be used to inform future experimental investigations of magnetic transition metal compounds. The supporting data, such as magnetic phase diagrams, crystal structures, and other calculations, is available at https://git.io/0KMJQ. The research also presents an updated visual model of the crystal structure for LuMn$_2$, with P4/mmm space group at https://git.io/6MmTP. Recent advancements in Deep Neural Networks have significantly influenced improvements in Relation Extraction (RE) techniques. Despite the success, standard supervised approaches' performance drops significantly when tested on unrelated data. This study aims to bridge this gap by developing a novel approach, Relation Embedding, to leverage pre-trained models and unsupervised knowledge for more effective RE. The method involves two key components: generating relation representations that capture crucial features across multiple dimensions; and creating a neural model that integrates these elements with target sentences to predict relations. The proposed model leverages knowledge from General Conceptualized Zero-Shot Learning (GCZSL), a new framework that establishes a framework for generating relation representations and choosing relevant relations. Experiments on FBK-88 and CONDOR datasets demonstrate that our method achieves top results, surpassing state-of-the-art models under both zero-shot and non-zero-shot conditions. The study also includes an analysis of relation representations, demonstrating their effectiveness and variability. Supercapacitors hold great promise for storing energy, and their potential impact on reducing greenhouse gas emissions is significant. To maximize their efficacy, researchers seek to optimize their design through computational models. This study employs graph analysis techniques to represent and study the structure of supercapacitor electrodes, specifically those composed of porous materials. To expand their analysis, researchers proposed an abstract algebraic structure known as the hypergraph, but its practical application is limited when data is presented as a projected graph. This study examines the problems of reconstructing hypergraphs and understanding their properties in graph data analysis, specifically focusing on the analysis of supercapacitor electrodes. Our findings indicate that certain analytical approaches are feasible, but others are essentially impossible. To facilitate further research, we developed methods for creating and translating hypergraphs from and to supercapacitor edge degree distributions. This work is the first to utilize computational algebraic methods to analyze hypergraphs and their connections to graph data analysis, ultimately contributing to the optimization of supercapacitor design through a graph-theoretic framework. This study demonstrates that the ideas presented can be employed with existing datasets in the materials science domain to obtain meaningful insights about the size and composition of supercapacitor electrodes. This study contributes to the field of supercapacitor research by providing a methodology to examine the validity of the supercapacitor model assumption and to compare different supercapacitor designs using an algebraic structure. We investigate the broadside chirp pulse compression (BCPC) scheme, which uses a pair of chirped BCPC gratings to compress high-power laser pulses in the time domain. A detailed analysis of the phase and group delay effects, as well as the transverse spatial properties of the beam, is carried out. Notably, we identify that lasers with a higher divergence angle and those with elliptical beams are more susceptible to spatial distortions during the compression process. Interestingly, we find that the difference in phase delay across the beam's diameter can lead to irregular shapes and even spirals, which may cause beam breakup and instability during free space propagation. To evaluate the beam's temporal and spatial characteristics after compression, we consider key factors such as the initial pulse duration, divergence angle, and spatial beam profile. Our findings provide valuable insights and practical recommendations for employing BCPC in laser systems. A comparative study with the phase-coded chirp pulse compression (PCPC) scheme is also presented, along with suggestions on how to optimize this method to achieve better output stability and spatial smoothness. Moreover, we examine the feasibility of adapting BCPC for directionally emitting lasers, such as DFG (difference frequency generation) lasers and micro-lasers, which often require maintaining the original beam's spatial profile. A detailed analysis is performed on these specific cases to evaluate the effects of category of directional emission, such as single-mode, multi-mode, linearly polarized, circularly polarized, and elliptically polarized, on the compression process. By varying the parameters, we find that linearly polarized DFG lasers exhibit minimal spatial distortion during the compression process, making them suitable for BCPC. However, the resulting compressed pulses may still exhibit different phases across the beam's diameter, which could lead to temporal beam breakup during free space propagation. To mitigate this, we suggest combining BCPC with a spatial beam smoother, thereby reducing beam instability and providing a method to refine the temporal profile without affecting the original spatial pattern. A case study employing a spatial beam smoother to compress a 30 fs linearly polarized DFG laser is presented, demonstrating the removal of spatial irregularities, correction of phase delay across the beam's diameter, and the successful compression of this laser to 10 fs. Furthermore, our research maintains the original beam's spatial profile, thereby making it suitable for enhancing the efficiency of parametric amplifiers in chirped pulse laser systems. This study investigates volatility forecasting for cryptocurrency markets by examining volatility relationships among individual cryptocurrencies and their price indices. Notably, as cryptocurrencies have evolved over time, their characteristics have become more diverse, potentially influencing their own stability. To explore this trend, we compute Pearson correlations for a large selection of cryptocurrencies daily opening prices from 2020 to 2022. Our findings indicate a positive correlation shift in later years, signifying increasing interdependence among certain cryptocurrencies during this period. Employing the Dynamic Conditional Score-based Method from the Ugarte et al. (2022) study, we discover significant evidence of forecastable volatility in both individual cryptocurrency markets and their price indices. Moreover, our results reveal the Mean Absolute Percentage Error of the Predictive Regressions for the cryptocurrency market as a whole to be around 10% less than the Ugarte et al. (2022) study's findings, suggesting an improvement in volatility forecasting. This research also introduces a novel application of the Dynamic Score-based Method, utilizing realized quadratic variations from cryptocurrency daily opening prices to predict volatility. To validate the robustness of our study, we conduct threshold-dependent tests and explore the dynamic score models' responsiveness to cryptocurrency category labels, revealing distinct volatility patterns among different groups, such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, and other altcoins. Lastly, our study investigates the impact of cryptocurrency daily trading volume on volatility relationships, revealing a more complex relationship than initially thought, but finding that the Dynamic Score-based Method remains effective in modeling this relationship. To address potential criticisms of the 2022 Ugarte et al. study's findings and methodology, we undertake several robustness checks, such as using alternative specifications for the Ugarte et al. (2022) study's Equation (1), testing for asymmetries, and evaluating the performance of our predictive models through a Monte Carlo-like process. Furthermore, the study's findings on correlation shifts and volatility relationships are verified using alternative methods, such as the Joint Generalized Method of Moments and the Full Information Maximum Likelihood Estimator. Building on the non-linear noise framework established in recent research, we derive a robust formulation of the KPZ equation that incorporates noise-induced effects in dislocation-based models. This formulation is obtained by integrating noise into a dislocation-based model through a weak perturbation framework. The resulting noise is then analyzed and characterized using existing tools in the non-linear noise theory, thereby providing a novel and valuable method for quantifying noise-induced impacts in models of dislocation-based plasticity. Furthermore, our findings implicitly validate the conventional noise formulation of the KPZ equation, which underpins a broad range of numerical simulation strategies. The approach developed here provides a valuable alternative to conventional simulation techniques and may find applications in scenarios where high-precision simulations are required. On a broader scale, our work showcases the potential of the weak noise theory to underpin the conventional noise formulation of complex non-linear models. The approach is versatile and may be adapted to various physical models of importance. Lastly, our calculations yield noise-induced impacts on the scaling of typical impact distances in dislocation-based models that differ significantly from those obtained via the conventional noise formulation of the KPZ equation. The numerical implications of these differences are explored in detail. The mathematical framework developed here is likely to be useful in scenarios where dislocation-induced impacts are negligible due to small time or space scales, where a dimensionless scaling framework is adopted to analyze these effects. The approach developed here is versatile and may be adapted to various physical models of importance. The FPI instrument on MMS observes small-scale solar wind turbulence via its two components, which measure the electron and ion velocities, respectively. However, these components often provide different insights into turbulence. While the electron component reveals the rapid variations in spacecraft potential, the ion component measures the actual electron fluid velocity. Understanding these differences is crucial for analyzing the turbulent energy distribution and direction along the spacecraft's trajectory. In this study, we compared the data from the SWEIA instrument, which analyzed the potential measurements from FPI, with the actual data from other experiments on the same spacecraft. Our investigation demonstrates that there are distinct differences between the turbulent energy distribution measured by the electron component and that measured by other experiments. Additionally, we found a notable right-hand polarized wave mode in the frequency range of 0.1-0.4 Hz when examining the ion component, which did not appear in the electron component. Our findings indicate that the electron component is affected by the spacecraft potential, causing it to provide unique, yet flawed, insights into solar wind turbulence. Our research contradicts previous studies that suggested the electron component and the ion component provide equivalent information for analyzing the turbulent energy distribution. Based on our analysis, we recommend using the ion component, which measures the actual electron fluid velocity, as a more reliable method for understanding the turbulent energy spectrum. Our work also emphasizes the value of multiple measurements from the same instrument, particularly when contacting diverse spacecraft, for confirming or disagreeing with each other's findings. Our investigation further highlights the significance of in-flight instrument calibration, as the difference between the electron component and the ion component shows that the latter is generally more reliable. Lastly, our study suggests that the ion component, which measures the actual electron fluid velocity, is a more reliable method for understanding the turbulent energy spectrum, which can have a profound impact on understanding the physical processes of the solar wind at the scale of a few hundred kilometers. Our research, however, requires more extensive data sets from other similar experiments to confirm our results and ensure the sufficiency of our analysis. Our investigation, therefore, paves the way for the use of the ion component as a more reliable method for understanding the turbulent energy distribution, which can be utilized to study the solar wind on a scale of a few hundred kilometers via comparative observations with other similar spacecraft. A supplementary method to enhance ultrashort pulse generation in free-electron lasers operating in the XUV and soft X-ray range has been developed. It involves introducing a modulated infrared drive current into the electron beam, which can be realized using a chirp-taper technique. Computer simulations demonstrate that this supplementary method significantly improves the performance of existing facilities and potentially increases the peak electric field of future machines by an order of magnitude. It significantly mitigates coherent oscillations in the free-electron laser signal, enabling higher average powers and greater stability in the generated ultrashort pulses. This innovative technique is expected to play a crucial role in overcoming current limitations of FELs in this wavelength range and opening up new applications in fields such as ultrafast physics, chemistry, and biology. Furthermore, it has the potential to benefit other types of lasers and other areas of advanced photon source research. For example, it could improve the performance of SASE FELs, develop new types of free-electron laser undulators, and enhance the performance of self-modulation effects in plasma wakefield accelerators. It is also versatile and can be adapted to various free-electron laser architectures for generating infrared coherent radiation. This promising approach could lead to the creation of powerful new tools for fundamental research in the fields of physics, astrophysics, and engineering. Examples of its potential applications include the development of a powerful X-ray source for the exploration of fundamental physics in the study of dark matter and the investigation of the properties of superconductors at the interface with quantum mechanics. It is also suitable for research in the biological and chemical fields as well as in the fields of chemistry and physics associated with electron storage rings. This promising approach has numerous applications across multiple research areas and is expected to have a significant impact on the advancement of free-electron laser technology in the near future. It is specifically analyzed in the context of the HIBEF line at the CTA, a facility that is part of the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory's (FNAL) research efforts, but its findings and results are universally applicable to this type of facility as well as to other research initiatives. It is specifically evaluated at two energy levels - 20 MeV and 5 MeV - but its results can be assessed at any energy level. This presentation will provide an overview of the concept, assess its feasibility, discuss its potential, and explore its various applications across multiple research areas. Presently, this concept is at the evaluation stage, but it is expected to be a crucial part of the research efforts

This study explores perturbations against a stable stratified background in a channel using the modified Taylor-Goldstein equation, which was initially developed to account for vertical velocity fluctuations. By assuming the perturbations have exponential vertical decreases, the problem is reduced to a Sturm-Liouville eigenvalue system. However, since the eigenvalue problem does not satisfy certain boundary conditions in the literature, the solution space has two distinct sets of solutions. Furthermore, due to the non-diagonalizable Jacobian matrix of the equilibrium, the linearized problem exhibits significant regularization difficulties when applying certain non-physical boundary conditions to the modified Taylor-Goldstein equation. Conversely, imposing physical boundary conditions leads to incomplete eigenvalue problems that successfully capture the most influential solutions. Using a parameter variation method, the eigenvalue problems can be continuously connected and the missing zero frequency eigenfunctions can be captured, ultimately enabling the construction of optimal states and an effective diagnostic tool for measuring how far the equilibrium is stable. A companion paper will investigate the dynamics governed by the complete eigenfunction system. The findings of this study will be used to guide the modeling in that paper. Additionally, this study's method can be applied to other similar eigenvalue problems in geophysical dynamics and the investigation of the model's behavior will be explored in future research. A brief review of the Taylor-Goldstein theory is included in the appendix for reference. The District of Columbia's redistricting process is unique due to requirements for one-district representation and for ten council members elected by population.  We investigate how Simulated Annealing contributes to analyzing the fairness of districting plans by examining neighboring configurations, their quality, and transitions between them.  Focus is on evaluating plan symmetry, its connection to fairness, and generating highly qualitative plans.  Through experiments, it is revealed that Simulated Annealing produces notable improvements in the overall quality of districting plans.  We also discovered that Simulated Annealing favors asymmetric plans, and these plans outperform uniformly drawn plans in terms of fairness and overall quality.  However, Simulated Annealing may generate plans with unusual shapes when seeking to maximize fairness.  Notably, Simulated Annealing's ability to analyze the fairness of districting plans can be utilized even in the absence of its optimization capabilities.  This analysis enabled the creation of highly qualitative districting plans that surpass those of uniform drawings in terms of fairness and overall quality.  These plans serve as a foundation for future research and can be utilized as a reference for districting efforts in the District of Columbia.  A tool for exploring Simulated Annealing's contributions to analyzing and improving the quality of districting plans is available online at https://caesarmathis.github.io/Redistricting-Annealing/.  This project is part of a larger effort to improve the quality of districting plans through mathematical techniques, with more information available at https://redistricting-annealing.github.io/. However, an agent may fail to extract meaningful information from its observations if they are unconnected to the actions it takes. This research focuses on detecting incidents in distribution grids that feature energy storage systems (ESS). Current methods rely heavily on predictive models, which do not fully utilize the data collected from advanced sensors in the community microgrid tested at the Georgia Tech Smart Grid Community Knowledge Share site. We tackle this issue by developing a data-driven incident detection system (DIDS) for identification of power quality disturbances and anomalies within microgrids with ESS and phasor measurement units (PMUs). This DIDS employs machine learning algorithms to analyze the features extracted from the disturbance-free template of the grid's power system, which is created using fundamental frequency components of the voltage and current signals. We assess the performance of the DIDS under various incident scenarios, including active and reactive power imbalances, power factor disturbances, and false data injection attacks. The results show that the DIDS can effectively detect incidents in both in-service and off-grid configurations of the microgrid, with an overall detection accuracy rate of 95%. The DIDS presents a novel approach to incident detection that integrates data-driven and machine learning techniques, offering improved detection capabilities for incidents involving ESS and operating guidelines for the evaluation process. This research makes significant contributions to the development of incident detection systems, including the definition of proper evaluation metrics, the assessment of false data attack impacts, and the identification of areas for further improvement in optimizing detection performance. Ultimately, this effort aims to facilitate the utilization of data-driven techniques in detecting incidents associated with energy storage systems, a key technology in modernizing distribution grids. The associated software code is available at https://github.com/asharath/DIDS_for_SMGrid_SMGRIT. The analysis comprises two procedures: directly calculating the amplitude through Fadde'ev equations and subsequently convolving this with the photon flux from the Regge trajectory analysis. The latter method involves the regression of virtual photons from Regge trajectories, modeled after leading production amplitudes. Notably, our calculations indicate that omega and rho meson contributions are relatively close. The findings from this study show that spin-1 contributions significantly prevail over spin-0 ones, thereby providing meaningful insights into the X(3872)'s internal composition. The comparative decay widths to J/psi and pi pi gamma suggest a stronger coupling to the pi pi channel, supporting this interpretation. The computational approach allows for the extraction of structural parameters of the X(3872), such as the relative distance between the charmonium parton and the di-proton parton, as well as the momenta of the constituent hadrons, thereby enhancing our understanding of X(3872)'s composition. The advancement of machine learning techniques has led to significant growth in the availability of simulated training data for complex problem-solving. The Simulated Reality III agent, an advanced model pre-trained on text-based simulations, has exhibited exceptional performance across various tasks, however its large dataset-dependent throughput hindered its broader application. In response, we present TextWorldExpress, a substantial dataset of 25,000 training samples in an interactive format that can be utilized for on-the-fly sampling by Simulated Reality III. This innovative approach replaces the traditional batch training method with a online, non-batch training protocol. As a result, TextWorldExpress boosts the throughput of text game simulations by 3.5 times and showcases the potential for incremental learning from diverse datasets, a capability yet to be fully explored. When combined with prior knowledge, the Simulated Reality III agent trained on TextWorldExpress achieves a 12.1% increase in reward on the Classic Game Tracking benchmark, encompassing 17 diverse game scenarios. Additionally, we analyze various factors influencing the performance gains and offer code repositories for RepROBERT and TextWorldExpress at the provided links. \href{https://github.com/ai4rj/Propbert}{https://github.com/ai4rj/Propbert}, \href{https://github.com/ai4rj/TextWorldExpress}{https://github.com/ai4rj/TextWorldExpress}.

A deep learning approach to 3D object estimation in RGB images relies on accurate representation of object shapes. Current models, however, struggle to generalize when the input image lacks clear defining features, such as in the case of canonical poses. Our proposed solution involves early stage training with easily recognizable images, followed by a multi-stage training protocol that gradually shifts to canonical poses. This improved model achieves higher accuracy in discovering canonical poses and performs better on complex 3D object estimation tasks compared to standard approaches. The 'Early Shift' training method is available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/hirosearavine/EarlyShift. Evaluation was performed on the ModelNet dataset (Learnin et al., 2020) and the results can be found in the paper's supplementary materials. Specifically, our method reduced the Mean Absolute Diameter error from 0.042 to 0.036 when discovering canonical poses, and improved the accuracy of 3D object estimation from 40.3% to 44.6% with a 3D bounding box volume of 0.172, indicating a 26.2% decrease. These performance gains indicate that our method represents a more effective general-to-specific approach to learning canonical poses and can easily be integrated into existing deep learning architectures for 3D object estimation. Moreover, Early Shift's stage-wise training strategy can be applied to a broader range of computer vision problems where predefined conditions are involved. Its adaptable nature makes it suitable for various specific tasks without affecting its potential to improve general performance. Ultimately, our goal is to advance the state-of-the-art in learning canonical poses and discover new applications for stage-wise training methods. As such, we have made our code publicly accessible at the provided GitHub repository. Additionally, we provided early access to our paper for researchers at the DeepLearn2019 conference and incorporated feedback into the final revision. Throughout our research, we found that Early Shift's performance gains could also be achieved by increasing the training time for modelnet40, however this would come at the cost of significantly prolonged training duration from 3 days to 1.5 months. As such we determined that a more efficient approach was to apply our method. Furthermore, our approach is versatile and may be used in learning various predefined conditions in future applications. Last but not least our research indicates that learning general conditions first can greatly improve the discovery of corresponding canonical poses. By taking advantage of easily recognizable general conditions, we can greatly improve the accuracy of corresponding canonical poses. As such we have named our method early shift.

A range of computational approaches has been created to evaluate the effectiveness of vaccine misinformation, but they have yet to be consolidated into a unified framework that can consistently determine whether a given piece of public feedback supports or goes against such misinformation. Our new framework, designed for English language feedback, uses machine learning to analyze the context of each feedback and determine its alignment with proven scientific facts, specifically regarding COVID-19 vaccination. Each context is examined across a broad spectrum of linguistic and contextual factors. This framework is called ALCHEMI and is comprised of various components: a tokenizer, a BERT-based language model, a data encoding system, a machine learning algorithm, and a knowledge base that is regularly updated. ALCHEMI's reliability is guaranteed through two sets of tests. Firstly, it is tested against a range of benchmark datasets to confirm its accuracy and consistency in determining the truth behind vaccine-related misinformation. Secondly, an independent team of experts is employed to manually assess and verify the effectiveness of ALCHEMI in real-world scenarios. As a pioneering approach to understanding public attitudes towards vaccine-related misinformation, ALCHEMI successfully determines the truth behind a given piece of feedback with an accuracy rate of 88.5%, significantly surpassing existing baseline methods. Furthermore, it is shown that ALCHEMI's reliance on natural language processing is minimal, and its performance can be enhanced through data augmentation techniques such as changing font sizes, adding sarcasm, and implementing counterfactual reasoning. By leveraging this improved framework, known as ALCHEMI+, ALCHEMI's accuracy is elevated to 90.2%, establishing a new standard in evaluating vaccine misinformation-related public feedback. Our detailed study of the binary system Algol~C, carried out using 211 nights of data collected between 2007 and 2016 at the La Silla Observatory, reveals noteworthy findings. By analyzing the system's orbital motion, we determined that the orbital period remains stable and consistent with historical records, remaining constant at 2.876 days over the past 110 years. Additionally, our research focused on searching for any changes in the system's brightness, known as non-periodic variability, but did not uncover any significant patterns or variations that could be attributed to the system's gravitational interaction. Furthermore, we investigated the possibility of magnetic activity on the system's component stars, specifically Algol~C and Algol~D, by examining observations from conjugate pairs, but did not find any conclusive evidence of this activity despite having data sets that include individual and mutual minima. Our final conclusion is that the system's bright star Algol~A, which makes up a significant portion of the system's total brightness, likely dominates any expected signals of this activity, but that further in-depth research is required to accurately determine the magnetic activity on the system's component stars. Moreover, our study serves as a foundation for future investigations of this system, which we suggest should continue to be observed and studied utilizing diverse spectroscopic and photometric techniques to gain a more in-depth understanding of its intricate behavior and its potential implications for theoretical models of binary system interaction. Lastly, we would like to express our deep gratitude to the researchers who, over the years, have shared their data and findings with us. Our work would not have been possible without their contributions, which have enabled us to build upon their previous discoveries and follow in their footsteps as observers of the binary system Algol~A.

Recently, the effectiveness of Gabor filters (GFs) for robust image representation and matching within image retrieval systems has been established. However, these traditional GFs are limited in their ability to handle various image degradation. A proposed extension to GFs, called Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), incorporates central-symmetric rotation symmetry features, along with diverse Gabor filters, to enhance the robustness of image representation and thus improve the precision of image matching and retrieval. A method for generating LGFs is described, along with an efficient alignment technique for matching images represented by LGFs. Experimental results confirm the superior performance of the proposed LGF system compared to traditional GFs, particularly in terms of the number of false positives eliminated and the precision of image matching and retrieval increased. Additionally, the novel feature representation shows potential in reducing alignment errors and improving the precision of image matching and retrieval. It is worth noting that the LGF technique is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of image modalities and content-based image retrieval applications. As such, LGF-based image retrieval systems have the potential to greatly expand the range of target datasets and accurately match images within them. A collection of test images and related data is available for public download at: http://vassar.academic.edu/mediawiki/index.php/Main_Page. Additionally, a demonstration of the proposed LGF image retrieval method can be viewed at: http://vassar.academic.edu/mediawiki/index.php/Demonstration.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become popular for graph classification. A typical GCN gathers features from neighboring nodes within a specified radius, processes them through a convolution operation, and reduces dimensionality through a dropout operation and gateway combination. However, the sequential nature of this feature gathering can lead to biases in the learned features. We address this issue by introducing a novel method that involves shuffling the feature gathering order in each convolution layer. This order shuffling can be computed in advance and does not require any additional parameters, thus making the approach efficient. We further propose a strategy to determine the best feature gathering sequence automatically. Our experiments show that the implementation of this strategy outperforms existing methods, including Relational Graph Matching Network, indicating the benefit of unsupervised learning of graph parameters. Moreover, the approach achieves significant reductions in computational complexity compared to previous methods, specifically a substantial decrease in memory usage, from O(V^2) to O(V), making it suitable for large graphs. The code for our method can be found at https://github.com/jhrudt/dynamic-GCNE. Evaluations on well-known benchmark datasets reveal that the approach competes favorably with current best practices in graph classification, offering a simpler alternative. Furthermore, the method is generalizable and can be applied to various GCN variants, as demonstrated by our evaluation. The approach is also compatible with existing methods, such as DeepGCN and Layer-Wise Assessment of Graph classifiers. Researchers have developed various forms of Trojan attacks that enable them to exploit neural networks and extract sensitive data without explicit consent. While current Trojans are generally triggered by specific input patterns, they have limitations that affect their reliability in real-world applications. To overcome these drawbacks, we propose a unique type of Trojan attack that forces a trained network to make specific decisions on target classes without relying on specific triggering inputs. This innovative approach involves modifying the target classes' log likelihood ratios during backpropagation, enabling more precise control over the network's output. Moreover, we have created an advanced generative adversarial model that can effectively restore the original clean data from Trojaned networks' output, thereby enabling the extraction of sensitive information. Our proposed attack, dubbed LogSTO, has several key advantages, such as its ability to be effective in various scenarios, and its ability to be effective after the training data has been completed. Additionally, we have established several metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of our attack. Through extensive experiments on different datasets and defenses, we have demonstrated that LogSTO outperforms current state-of-the-art Trojan attacks, showcasing its remarkable utility in real-world applications. This research has significant implications and will contribute to the advancement of AI security. An implementation of our approach is available at https://github.com/ChunFENG-2021/logsto. In massive MIMO systems with complex signal constellations such as 64-QAM, channel state information may become inaccurate due to feedback noise. This inaccuracy violates the standard assumption that full channel knowledge is reliable. This paper addresses this issue by developing an attention-based deep learning approach that enhances system performance by utilizing imperfect CSI. A massive MIMO system with 64-QAM and noise-affected CSIs is used as the test bed for this research. Results show that the proposed method surpasses conventional benchmarks by 30% in terms of energy per bit per unit bandwidth, highlighting its efficacy in noisy CSI scenarios. To validate the findings, this research uses multiple simulated channels from different datasets, including one widely used reference standard. This innovative approach is shown to improve system performance in the presence of noisy CSIs, thereby expanding the applicability of deep MIMO systems to a broader range of scenarios. Additionally, it is observed that the model is capable of adapting to diverse channel conditions without requiring frequent data replenishment. This makes the approach highly efficient in terms of data requirements for training. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the model achieves superior performance using significantly fewer propagation data samples than existing deep MIMO methods. This research further examines the computational complexity of the proposed method and finds it to be predominantly determined by the number of trainable parameters, which is comparable to conventional deep MIMO systems. This provides further confirmation of the efficiency of the approach. Ultimately, this paper showcases a cutting-edge deep learning technique that is poised to enhance the performance of massive MIMO systems, paving the way for innovative applications in wireless communication systems. To facilitate reproducibility, the research provides a publicly accessible code repository that includes all necessary information. Specifically, it is stated that our research's findings are available at the following URL: https://github.com/t-qian/Attention-Based-MIMO/tree/master/README.md. In 1990, Vitzthum proposed a hypothesis suggesting a division of the integers greater than 5 into two categories, based on whether they could be used as the maximum degree in a bipartite graph that requires at least k colors for edge coloring. This idea was later known as the Vitzthum Conjecture. Researchers found evidence supporting the conjecture by establishing a threshold, beyond which the assumption holds true for all relevant numbers. This proof uses the approach proposed by Vitzthum but also introduces new insights and observations. Furthermore, our research builds on previous findings by Tregenz-Katz and Vitzthum (2002), who provided partial evidence by showing that, assuming an unrelated hypothesis called the Erdos Fool's Gold Conjecture, the Vitzthum Conjecture would hold true, and we take this further by establishing the Vitzthum Conjecture solely on this latter hypothesis. This means that, in taking the product of k and the maximum degree to be an odd prime, k can be seen as essentially prime, which is in line with commonly held views on this problem. By reexamining this problem with constraints relaxed in regards to bipartite structures, we discover a new hypothesis, the Generalized Vitzthum Conjecture, which pertains to maximum degree 4 graphs in general graphs and not just bipartite ones, and we provide evidence supporting this new hypothesis up to a certain degree of magnitude higher than previously existing proofs for the original Vitzthum Conjecture. This new hypothesis is further strengthened by proving that its failure in certain instances is actually impossible, which in turn provides further insight into an unrelated problem known as the Erdos Fool's Gold Conjecture and grants new progress on it. Lastly, in examining a still more relaxed constraint system, we discover yet another bipartite structure hypothesis, which we prove up to a certain degree of magnitude higher than previously existing proofs for a related but more restricted hypothesis, known as the 3-Edge Coloring Conjecture. This new hypothesis is further strengthened by proving that its failure in certain instances is actually impossible, which in turn grants new insight into an unrelated problem known as the Fool's Gold Conjecture. In our research process, we also fortuitously discovered and solved an entirely new problem, which we term the Hypergraph Coloring Problem, and this solution yields the most efficient known result thus far for a more specific problem within this larger hypergraph coloring family, which we term the Hypergraph Complete

COPASI is a highly versatile biochemical network analysis and simulation tool, offering a wide range of features such as model editing, advanced algebraic and stochastic simulation capabilities, and extensive statistical analysis tools. The original COPASI application, designed for desktop use, has now been replaced by a cutting-edge web-based version called ShinyCOPASI. Built with R Shiny, this innovative platform enables seamless interaction with COPASI models, along with regular updates through the bioinformatics tool library Bioconductor's versioning system. Users can access ShinyCOPASI directly in their web browser, eliminating the need for initial setup or downloads required by the original application. The web-based interface not only expands access to COPASI capabilities but also enhances user convenience, including the ability to share and collaborate on models more efficiently. The transition to ShinyCOPASI as a web application marks a significant step in advancing COPASI's development, allowing for greater scalability, flexibility, and responsiveness to user needs. The new platform is compatible with models featuring mass action kinetics, quantitative biochemical networks, and multi-scale stochastic modeling approaches. With its powerful simulation capabilities, users can perform a wide range of analyses such as optimizing model parameters using evolutionary algorithms or other methods, conducting sensitivity and parameter scans, and simulating random processes. Additionally, ShinyCOPASI includes a built-in server allowing users to run simulations, even on models requiring significant computational resources, by submitting jobs for processing. The implementation of task queues helps streamline simulation workflows and improve overall performance, as demonstrated through the implementation of a protein synthesis model. The integration of R provides users with access to an extensive library of statistical analysis tools, as demonstrated through the application to a protein network involved in cell signaling, where users can leverage available libraries such as RBase for more advanced bioinformatics tasks or connect to other R packages for specific tasks. The future development of ShinyCOPASI will focus on incorporating new features requested by the user community, while ensuring seamless interaction with emerging technologies in biochemical network analysis and simulation. The next steps will involve enhancing web-based collaboration tools to enable real-time, simultaneous model editing and sharing among multiple users. Furthermore, the integration of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and machine learning will be explored to expand COPASI's capabilities and maintain its position as a leading platform in biochemical network analysis and simulation. The new version of ShinyCOPASI is now available for public use through a combination of Bioconductor's versioning system and public GitHub repositories, allowing for community-driven contribution and collaboration. We introduce inexact policy iteration for large-scale multi-dimensional grid-world MDPs with nonlinear function approximations. By allowing approximate evaluations in each step, inexact policy iteration significantly outperforms traditional policy iteration, with remarkable speedup. In our tests on a 1000x1000 dimension grid-world MDP, inexact policy iteration is 5-10 times faster than direct policy iteration, and 20-50 times faster when using sample-based evaluation. We also develop an inexact version of GMRES policy iteration and find that it converges even more quickly, outperforming traditional GMRES by a factor of 10-20 on the same grid-world MDP. Seeding an initial coarse approximation to the optimal policy with either inexact GMRES or evolutionary policy search enables the generation of near-optimal policies in grid-world MDPs, a capability that direct policy iteration and sample-based policy iteration lack. Additionally, inexact GMRES policy iteration proves resilient to significant levels of evaluation inaccuracy in both multi-dimensional grid-world and continuous state MDP settings, maintaining its convergence at rates comparable to exact GMRES policy iteration. Given its high performance, inexact GMRES policy iteration presents a practical option for large-scale multi-dimensional grid-world MDP problems and is a valuable contribution to the field of reinforcement learning. A related implementation, called inexact GMRES policy iteration with sample-based evaluation, is available online at https://github.com/jxjmath/InexactGMRESPI.git. We examine weighted oriented graphs and their edge ideals, along with the symbolic powers, to investigate equality between ordinary and symbolic powers, which implies unweighted equivalence. We draw inspiration from Ringel's cycle space theory and utilize edge ring generators to analyze certain oriented graphs, specifically those with a single edge weight. Furthermore, we identify a specific class of weighted oriented graphs where ordinary and symbolic powers converge to a common ideal, and find that this class is composed of graphs where the symmetry axis turns into a mirror axis. Additionally, we study the degree of an ideal divisor and its relation to the parameters of a weighted oriented graph, as well as determine the number of minimal prime ideals in the edge ring, based on these parameters. Finally, we compute some specific examples of edge ideals from weighted oriented graphs. We introduce a concept of normality for weighted oriented graphs, and explore how this property translates to their unweighted counterparts, presenting several examples along the way. Moreover, we establish a connection between this normality property and the characteristics of the weighted orientation, specifically the degree of an ideal divisor, and relate it to the graph's parameters, as well as its embedding dimension and the number of minimal prime ideals in the edge ring, based on the degree of an ideal divisor. Hints are provided for further research in this area, including determining whether there are oriented graphs that satisfy the normality condition but are not necessarily equivalent to their unweighted counterparts. The simulator modeled and predicted rock properties based on various geological features and was treated as a black box. Our results indicate that C C M successfully detects critical input variables and their interactions, which corresponds to the theoretical expectations of experimenter expertise. Specifically, for concept classes with large diameters, sample complexities grow exponentially with the query radius, whereas those with smaller diameters exhibit more gentle growth. By leveraging prior distributions and observing numerous sources, the Prospector algorithm generates posterior distributions for these parameters by weighting these two factors. Pet populations can serve as valuable indicators in environmental studies, yet accurately estimating pet ownership demographics is difficult due to the expense and complexity of census data. This paper explores the development of Bayesian spatial models for estimating unobserved pet population characteristics, such as density and demographic trends, using data from pet encounters detected through camera traps. This approach is applied to data from the San Francisco Bay Area, where camera triggers are utilized to inform estimates of unobserved pet population characteristics, including density and demographic trends. Two model variations are examined, incorporating information about pet owner demographics to adjust estimates and account for biases in camera placement. This research evaluates the effectiveness of camera-trigger data in estimating pet population characteristics, including species count, age structures, and sex ratios, for both domestic dogs and cats. Our findings indicate that model precision improves when more camera units are utilized and when cameras are dispersed evenly across a study area. This study estimates that the human-owned pet population in the San Francisco Bay Area comprises approximately 46.9 million dogs and 27.6 million cats. Our results also indicate that pet population characteristics exhibit spatial variability, with higher densities observed in urban areas, particularly for dogs, and that species count ratios exhibit distinct spatial patterns, particularly in the Bay Area's central region (e.g., dogs to cats ratio ranges from 1.13 to 1.46). This research represents the first application of Bayesian spatial models to pet encounter data, offering opportunities for enhancements, such as the integration of multiple data sources, careful selection of relevant predictor variables, and the implementation of data augmentation techniques to address issues of over-dispersal and skewness in pet encounter data. Additionally, this research may be modified to estimate free-roaming pet populations by adjusting the density function to account for differences in species marking behaviors. Furthermore, this approach can be adapted to estimate the characteristics of other mobile species, such as humans, using data from activity records, sensor data, and self-reported information. This research has the potential to provide precision estimates of species count, demographic trends, and human activities, thereby supporting conservation, urban planning, and public health initiatives. To model the intrinsic variation in type Ia supernovae, we utilize a Bayesian approach with Gaussian process priors on the luminosity and time. By incorporating a correlation penalty term, the model's output improves significantly. The correlation penalty term effectively constrains the variability to be cohesive, achieving this constraint without artificially influencing the data fit. We apply this model to the SNLS dataset and observe reduced randomness in our inference results, with the correlation penalty term achieving a significant 45% reduction in posterior sample variability. Furthermore, the model reveals a more precise inference of the H0 parameter, with reduced variability by a factor of two in our inference results. The improved constraint on variability allows us to investigate the structure of type Ia supernovae variability with greater detail, with further development expected to lead to more precise cosmological applications. For example, we estimate that future improvements in cosmological parameter estimation could be limited by the current level of variability restriction, meaning that reducing variability by a factor of two could result in a corresponding factor of two improvement in parameter estimation. By taking into account the correlation structure of the variability, we can make this variation and its effect on the parameter estimation assessment more accurate in the future. Furthermore, the improved model allows us to analyze the distribution of the variability, determining that a beta distribution provides a more precise fit than earlier models. By incorporating this more accurate model of the variability, we can refine our inference results and make new predictions about the cosmological applications of type Ia supernovae, such as a more precise estimation of the H0 parameter that could potentially differ by up to 3.4 km/s/Mpc. With further development, we anticipate that this improved model will enable significant breakthroughs in the study of cosmology, enabling precise testing of universal expansion models and potentially yielding new insights into the fundamental physics of the universe. The refined model is expected to contribute significantly to future research in this field. When a jet of fluid with varying density flows through a layer of a different density, typically a fluid with lower density, it develops characteristics that are not dependent on its initial conditions due to the self-organizing nature of the flow. This study investigates the characteristics of an isolated jet with variable density in a thinner layer of a different density flowing into a larger layer of a different density. Observations of a jet with variable density entering a larger layer of a different density reveal that it undergoes rapid and intermittent changes in its shape as it moves laterally. This process is influenced by the contrast in densities between the jet and the surrounding layer, and well-studied phenomena such as blockage, penetration, and deflection can occur. However, the present study reveals a newly identified phenomenon, 'flicking,' which involves the lateral movement of a variable-density plume in a larger-body of fluid with a different density. This process can occur when the effective density of the plume is higher than the surrounding fluid or when the fluid density within the plume is lower. A theoretical model has been developed to describe the process of flicking and determine the critical parameters that influence it. These parameters include the ratio of densities between the fluid within the plume and the surrounding fluid, as well as the Reynolds number, which characterizes the fluid flow. This model indicates that the maximum rate of lateral movement increases in proportion to the square of the Reynolds number and is independent of the Reynolds number above a certain threshold. This is in accordance with observations of laterally moving jets with variable density. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that the rate of lateral movement increases either gradually or suddenly, depending on the relative densities of the fluid within the plume and the surrounding fluid. A theoretical analysis indicates that sudden changes in the rate of lateral movement are unexpected and are therefore likely to be uncommon. These findings enhance our understanding of laterally moving jets with variable density and the underlying physical processes involved. This knowledge can be applied in various fields, such as experimental studies and numerical modeling, to better understand and describe sudden changes in laterally moving jets with variable density. Additionally, the study finds applications in the field of environmental engineering, where it has the potential to describe sudden changes in laterally moving jets with variable density that occur in response to environmental stimuli. This knowledge can be utilized in various settings, such as the disposal of wastewater, to describe sudden changes in laterally moving jets with variable density that occur as a result of environmental factors. We examine a hypergraph contagion model, where each hyperedge represents simultaneous exposure to a group of nodes. The transmission risk is characterized by the probability that a node becomes infected given that all nodes in a hyperedge have the infection. This model is applicable to settings such as social networks, transportation systems, and media outlets, where transmission risk is associated with interconnected groups. Notably, our framework allows the transmission risk to be non-uniform, affecting individual nodes differently and dependent on the infection status of other nodes within a hyperedge. This leads to a complex contagion process represented by a polynomial-time solvable problem under specific conditions, but otherwise a challenging issue. The model's unit of analysis is a hyperedge containing a group of nodes, where our simulations demonstrate that infection spread can result in a large proportion of nodes in a hyperedge being infected. This phenomenon is particularly evident in scenarios with a low number of nodes per hyperedge and is observed less frequently with a larger number of nodes per hyperedge. The probability distribution of infected hyperedges can vary depending on the model parameters, leading to skewness in the distribution of infections within a hyperedge. This effect is most pronounced when the transmission risk is high and the number of nodes per hyperedge is small. As a consequence, approximate methods may be ineffective in simulating the contagion process, particularly when the transmission risk is high and the number of nodes per hyperedge is low. Our research explores the impact of lateral pressure on magnetic properties within ferromagnetic bilayers composed of ultrathin layers grown on compressively strained substrates. We've developed an efficient method to model strain effects at the atomic level and examine the spin alignment in a 3D ferromagnetic bilayer system. Our findings show that compressive strain causes key characteristics of the spin arrangement, such as magnetic anisotropy and the spin polarization pattern, to significantly change at the atomic level; interesting patterns emerge in the spin alignment within these bilayers when the strain is varied gradually. Our work lays the groundwork for a theoretical understanding of how strain affects magnetic properties at the atomic level in collinear ferromagnetic systems and has practical applications in the design of strain-engineered magnetic devices. The formation of planetary magnetic fields within their parent stars is closely tied to the presence of a star's magnetic field.  A significant factor influencing a star's magnetic field is the kinematic dynamo, specifically its expression as an alpha-effect that generates a star's magnetic field through fluid motion within the star.  Observations suggest that stars with slowly rotating speeds of less than five kilometers per second frequently exhibit magnetic cycles.  A numerical simulation model was utilized to investigate whether the application of an alpha-effect would result in long-term magnetic fields within slowly rotating stars.  The results indicate that, when an alpha-effect is applied, stars with very low rotation speeds may fail to develop a sustainable magnetic field.  However, stars with slightly faster rotation speeds are able to generate a long-term magnetic field due to geometrical considerations.  The findings suggest an essential role for the kinematic dynamo in the formation of a star's magnetic field, particularly relevant to the study of magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars.  The discovery could have implications for the study of magnetic activity in ancient stars and the generation of planetary magnetic fields.  A graph illustrating the relationship between rotation speed and magnetic cycle duration was developed based on the simulation results.  The findings can be incorporated into one-dimensional models for the study of magnetic activity in stellar clusters and the event evolution over cosmic time.  The research was funded by a DLR B research grant and an DFG PhD research grant.  A PhD thesis was associated with the research, entitled "Magnetic cycles in ancient stars" (2021). The development of models capable of efficiently processing multiple input signals and producing tailored outputs has been crucial for advancing applications in medical imaging and predictive chemistry, among others. Traditional models, however, have difficulty adapting to complex multi-input, multi-output tasks due to their inherent lack of structure. To address this challenge, we propose a novel attention mechanism that facilitates learning from multiple signals and produces a weighted output, effectively treating MIMO tasks as a composite of SIoT (Single Input-Output Task) processes. By incorporating this mechanism into a SiMViT (Shift-invariant Multi-Channel Vision Transformer) model, we demonstrate improved performance in a range of MIMO benchmarks, noting that the proposed model also yields superior results on traditional SIoT tasks. Additionally, we explore how the model's weighted output can be utilized to generate aggregate predictions for dynamic MIMO tasks. Multi-threaded programs are becoming increasingly prominent, with their complex interactions potentially leading to program crashes and data corruption.  Current checking methods based on finite state machines are restricted by their state spaces, making them impractical for complex programs and data-intensive paths.  In contrast, our McMini model checker leverages McSki, a framework for sketching finite state machines, to circumvent state space limitations, offering an order-of-magnitude speedup over traditional methods.  Specifically, McMini exhibits performance improvements of 10-100 times over existing model checkers when verifying basic multi-threaded operations and data structures, such as atomic variables, locks, and data structures in standard text books.  Additionally, McMini can check programs with arbitrary data sizes, including primitive data types, strings, and structs, which would be uncheckable for by other model checkers.  Furthermore, McMini's efficiency enables it to verify more advanced multi-threaded scenarios, such as client-server applications with data parsing, including those with large data sizes.  By checking these complex multi-threaded programs, McMini has been used to identify over a hundred previously reported bugs as well as over a hundred newly discovered ones in standard text books.  All McMini's model checking algorithms are fully formalized in Isabelle/HOL and can be found on the McSki repository at https://skwi.cs.umass.edu/mckwi-doc/index.html. All benchmark inputs used in this paper can be accessed at https://skwi.cs.umass.edu/mcmmini-doc/benchmark.html. Mobile messaging app WhatsApp has seen significant growth in usage, particularly in countries with limited internet access. While facilitating direct messaging, WhatsApp also enables the dissemination of information, including misinformation. To address this concern, WhatsApp has introduced a "Forwarded" label on sent messages to identify duplicated content and a "Simple Messages" option to limit shared media. Furthermore, WhatsApp has partnered with fact-checking organizations to flag suspicious messages. Additionally, WhatsApp has launched an education initiative comprising educational tools, such as infographics and a website, to raise user awareness of the potential dangers of spreading false information. As part of this effort, we created infographics in five languages representing significant languages in countries with limited internet access. This project aims to contribute to WhatsApp's efforts in combating the spread of misinformation. Our work is unique in that it directly affects users who may struggle to differentiate fact from fiction. By targeting low internet connectivity areas, our solution also considers technical and cultural constraints typical in these regions. We evaluated the effectiveness of our strategy through user testing with 40 participants across diverse languages. Our findings indicate that simplified infographics required significant time to process and understanding but still demonstrated a notable improvement in comprehension compared to standard infographics. By leveraging clear and concise visual elements, we created effective infographics that can be utilized to raise user awareness of the potential issues with duplicated and misleading content on WhatsApp. Our research has resulted in actionable suggestions for future improvements, such as incorporating more prominent visual elements and reducing text complexity. Furthermore, we have developed a set of infographics and source files that can be customized for various languages, cultures, and fact-checking initiatives. Lastly, our study highlights the importance of considering both technical and cultural factors when crafting clear visual messages to users. By combining these aspects, we can create an effective mix of educational visual content that is accessible, clear, and understandable for WhatsApp users. Our efforts in combating the spread of misinformation on WhatsApp are ongoing, and we intend to share future updates on this initiative to continue supporting this endeavor. Our primary goal is to utilize design as a catalyst for change, and we welcome collaborations from fact-checking organizations and visual communication specialists to aid us in this quest. Our vision is to utilize design as a social responsibility tool in combating the spread of false information, and we are committed to sharing our knowledge and expertise with others through our ongoing projects on WhatsApp Design for Good. In the long-term perspective, complex models of genetics involving multiple types of mutations and a large number of sites can be simplified to a single key factor influencing the shape of a population's genetic structure over time. This factor, which determines the similarity of a population's genetic makeup with their ancestral genome, is primarily influenced by the average rate of mutations per generation across all relevant genetic locations. When multiple types of mutations have different effects on the genetic structure, the ultimate outcome resembles that of an error-prone reproductive process where mutations of any kind lead to genetic divergence from ancestral genes. This factor, therefore, accurately predicts the degree of such genetic disruption. On the other hand, in scenarios involving non-fixing mutations that do not drastically alter the effect of any single mutation, the rate of mutations per generation still dictates the overall rate of genetic change within a population over time. This rate is calculated as the sum of the rates of mutations leading to permanent changes in the population's genetic makeup, an value previously studied, and the rates of mutations leading to temporary changes in the population's genetic structure. This temporary alteration rate is calculated to be equal to the population size times the probability of a mutation becoming fixed in the population, and is therefore highly sensitive to changes in the population's effective population size. This mathematical framework can be used to study the long-term effects of various genetic mechanisms on a population's genetic structure.
